title: Lesson 1
text: Lesson 1 Lesson 1 Conversation: At the Bus Depot John Wood, an American, goes to the bus depot to get a bus for Colombo. He approaches the conductor of a waiting bus for help. JOHN mehee මෙහේ here in̆dəla ඉඳල from koləm̆bəTə කොලඹට to Colombo bas-ekak බස් - එකක් a bus tiyenəwaa තියෙනවා there is də ද question marker mehee in̆dələ koləm̆bəTə bas-ekak tiyenəwaa də? මෙහේ ඉන්දෙල කොලඹට බස්-එකක් තියෙනවා ද? Is there a bus from here to Colombo? CONDUCTOR nææ නෑ no mahattea මහත්තයා sir nææ, mahattea. නෑ, මහත්තයා. No, sir. JOHN mee මේ this bas-ekə බස් - එක the bus yanne යන්නෙ is going kohaa Tə කොහා ට to where mee bas-ekə yanne kohaaTə də? මේ බස්-එක යන්නෙ කොහාට ද? Where is this bus going? CONDUCTOR meeka මේක this one kalutərəTə කලුතරට to Kalutara meekə yanne kalutərəTə. මේක යන්නෙ කලුතරට. This one is going to Kalutara. [page 2] JOHN kalutərə කලුතර Kalutara bas බස් buses tiyenəwa තියෙනව there are kalutərə in̆dəla koləm̆bəTə bas tiyenəwa də? කලුතර ඉඳල කොලඹට බස් තියෙනවා ද? Are there buses from Kalutara to Colombo? CONDUCTOR ow ඔව් yes nitərəmə නිතරම always ow, nitərəmə tiyenəwa. ඔව්, නිතරම තියෙනවා. Yes, (there are) always. meekeŋ මේකෙ න් by this one yannə යන්න go meekeŋ kalutərəTə yannə. මේකෙං කලුතරට යන්න. Go to Kalutara by this one. daŋ දන් now yanəwa යනව is going meekə dəŋ yanawa. මේක දන් යනව. This one is going now. koləm̆bə කොලඹ Colombo bas-ekəkiŋ බස් - එකකින් by a bus kalutərə in̆dəla koləm̆bə bas-ekəkiŋ yanne. කලුතර ඉඳල කොලඹ බස්-එකකින් යන්නෙ. From Kalutara, go by a Colombo bus. JOHN hon̆day හොඳයි fine hon̆day. හොඳයි Fine. kiiyə කීය how much kiiyə də kalutərəTə? කීය ද කලුතරට? How much to Kalutara? [page 3] CONDUCTOR rupiyal රුපියල් rupees dekay දෙකයි two rupiyal dekay. රුපියල් දෙකයි Two rupees. JOHN mennə මෙන්න here you are mennə මෙන්න Here you are. TikæT-ekak ටිකැට් - එකක් a ticket dennə දෙන්න give TikæT-ekak dennə. ටිකැට්- එකක් දෙන්න. Give (me) a ticket. Grammar 1. NOUN AND PRONOUN FORMS Sinhalese nouns and pronouns may appear in several forms. They may be DEFINITE or INDEFINITE, SINGULAR or PLURAL, and inflected for any one of four CASES. 2. THE SINGULAR THE DEFINITE AND INDEFINITE FORMS 2.1 The definite indefinite distinction occurs only in the singular. b as-ekə බස්- එක ‘the bus’ and TikaT-ekə ටිකට්- එක the ticket’ are singular definite forms. The singular Indefinite forms are bas-ekak බස්- එකක් and TikæT-ekak ටිකැට්- එකක්. This type of definite and indefinite, with - ekə -එක and ekak එකක්, is often found with nouns such as these, which have been borrowed from English. rupiyələ රුපියල ‘the rupee’ has the indefinite form rupiyəlak රුපියලක්. Notice that these forms are very similar to those above. The only difference is that there is no -ek- -එක්- before the a අ definite and ak අක් indefinite. Place names like koləm̆bə කොලඹ ‘Colombo’ and kalutərə කලුතර ‘Kalutara’ and pronouns like meeke මේකෙ ‘this one’ do not have indefinite forms. 2.2 In general, the definite form corresponds to English “the” with a noun, and the indefinite to English “a” with a noun. We say “in general” because this provides only a rough guide for the beginner: the forms do not always appear where the corresponding English translations would lead us to expect them. For example, the definite form appears after mee මේ ‘this’: mee bas-eke මේ බස්-එකෙ ‘this bus’. [page 4] 3. THE PLURAL The plural forms for bas-ekə බස්- එක and TikaT-eka ටිකට්- එක are bas බස් 'buses' and TikəT ටිකට් ‘tickets’. This “no ending” plural is the usual type for nouns with a definite form in - eke - එකෙ . The plural of rupiyələ රුපියල is rupiyal රුපියල් ‘rupees’. Notice that there is again no ending. Also, we have al before endings, but -al -අල් when final. This is a regular change in Sinhalese; where a occurs before a consonant when something else follows, it becomes a if that consonant becomes final. Place names like koləm̆bə කොලඹ and kalutərə කලුතර do not generally have plurals. The plurals of pronouns like meekə මේක will be taken up as they occur later. 4. CASES Three of the four Sinhalese cases will be introduced here, 4.1 The Direct Case The “basic” forms that have been given above and referred to simply as “singular definite,” “singular indefinite” or “plural” are in the DIRECT CASE. Thus, bas-ekə බස් - එක , bas-ekak බස්- එකක්, bas බස්; TikæT-ekə ටිකැට්- එක , TikæT-ekak ටිකැට්- එකක්, TikæT ටිකැට්; rupiyələ රුපියල, rupiyəlak රුපියලක්; kalutərə කලුතර, koləm̆bə කොලඹ and meekə මේක are all direct case forms, although some are singular, some plural, some definite and some indefinite. When new nouns occur, and when they are listed in the glossary, they are always listed under the direct singular definite form. The subject of most sentences is in the direct case: bas-ekak tiyenəwa. බස් - එකක් තියෙනවා . There is a bus. bas-ekə yanəwa. බස් - එක යනවා . The bus is going. meekə yanəwa. මේක යනවා . This one is going. 4.2 The Dative Case 4.21 The dative case form of a noun in the definite singular is formed by adding - Tə -ට to the direct case form. The dative definite forms of the nouns and pronouns in this lesson are thus: Direct Definite Dative Definite bas-ekə බස් - එක bas-ekəTə බස් - එකට TikæT-ekə ටිකැට් - එක TikæT-ekəTə ටිකැට් - එකට rupiyələ රුපියල rupiyələTə රුපියලට meekə මේක meekəTə මේකට kalutərə කලුතර kalutərəTə කලුතරට koləm̆bə කොලඹ koləm̆bəTə කොලඹට [page5] 4.22 The dative case form of a noun in the indefinite singular is formed by adding -əTə -අට to the direct case form. Notice here, too, we have -ek- -එක්- before endings but - ak -අක් where the consonant k ක් is final. For the nouns in this lesson that have an indefinite form, the dative indefinite form is as follows: Direct Indefinite Dative Indefinite bas-ekak බස් - එකක් bas-ekəkəTə බස් - එකකට TikæT-ekak ටිකැට් - එකක් TikæT-ekəkəTə ටිකැට් - එකකට rupiyəlak රුපියලක් rupiyələkəTə රුපියලකට 4.23 The dative case is used as an equivalent of the English “to a place.” kalutərəTə yannə. කලුතරට යන්න . Go to Kalutara. bas-ekəTə yannə. බස් - එකට යන්න . Go to the bus. bas-ekəkəTə yannə. බස් - එකකට යන්න . Go to a bus. In this connection we might note that the - Tə -ට on kohaaTə කොහාට ( də ද ) ‘where to’ is this same dative ending. 4.3 The Instrumental Case 4.31 The most frequent ending for definite nouns (and pronouns) in the instrumental case is - eŋ -එන්: Direct Definite Instrumental Definite bas-ekə බස් - එක bas ekeŋ බස් එකෙ න් TikaT-ekə ටිකට් - එක TikæT-ekeŋ ටිකැට් - එකෙ න් rupiyələ රුපියල rupiyələŋ රුපියල න් ??? < රුපියලෙන් ?> meekə මේක meekeŋ මේකෙ න් However, some nouns take -in - ඉන් : koləm̆bə කොලඹ kolam̆biŋ කොලඹි න් kalutərə කලුතර kalutəriŋ කලුතරි න් 4.32 In the indefinite, the instrumental ending is always in for the classes of nouns that we will meet for some time. It is added to the direct indefinite form and as always the rule for ə අ – a අ applies: Direct Indefinite Instrumental Indefinite bas-ekak බස් - එකක් bas-ekəkin බස් - එකකින් TikæT-ekak ටිකැට් - එකක් TikæT-ekəkin ටිකැට් - එකකින් rupiyəlak රුපියලක් rupiyələkin රුපියලකින් 4.33 The instrumental case is an equivalent of the English “with (a hammer)” or “by (a bus).” Thus: [page 6] meekeŋ kalutərəTə yannə. මේකෙන් කලුතරට යන්න . Go to Kalutara by this one. bas-ekeŋ koləm̆bəTə yannə. බස් - එකෙං කොලඹට යන්න . Go to Colombo by the bus. koləm̆bə bas-ekəkiŋ yannə. කොලඹ බස් - එකකින් යන්න . Go by a Colombo bus. 4.4. Plural Case Forms The case forms of the plural, except for the direct case forms given in paragraphs 3 and 4.1, will be dealt with in a later lesson. 5. NOUN CITATION Since the definite—indefinite distinction operates only in the singular, we need specify only: 1. case 2. definite, indefinite or plural in order to describe a noun form. That is, if we say that a noun form is either definite or indefinite it will automatically be singular as well. We will thus refer to nouns as being “dative definite” (automatically singular), “instrumental indefinite” (automatically singular), singular), “direct plural” (definite-indefinite does not apply), etc. 6. VERB FORMS 6.1 yanəwa යනවා and yanne යන්නේ are both present tense forms which we refer to as the SIMPLE PRESENT and EMPHATIC PRESENT respectively. yannə යන්න is the INFINITIVE form of the same verb. These forms all consist of a VERB STEM plus the endings -nəwa -නවා, -nne -න්නේ , or -nnə න්න. Whenever a new verb is given, whether in this book or a Sinhalese dictionary, it is given in the simple present form. The verb stem will be that part which precedes the -nəwa -නවා, so that the forms for the verbs that occur in this lesson are: Simple Present Verb Stem Emphatic Present Infinitive go yanəwa යන වා ya- ය - yanne යන් නේ yannə යන්න give denəwa දෙන වා də- දෙ - denne දෙන් නේ dennə දෙන්න be tiyenəwa තියෙන වා tiye- තියෙ - tiyenne තියෙන් නේ tiyennə තියෙන්න 6.2 Uses of the Forms 6.21 The simple and emphatic present forms are both used in forming present tense sentences. The most common difference between statements formed with these two forms is in emphasis. Generally non-emphatic statement sentences are formed by using the simple present form. [page 7] mee bas-ekə kalutərəTə yanəwa. මේ බස් - එක කලුතරට යනවා . This bus is going to Kalutara. meekə dæŋ yanǝwa. මේක දැං යනවා . This one is going now. Where special emphasis is to be given like that which might be indicated by translation such as: “It is to Kalutara that this one is going” or “This one is going to Kalutara,” the emphatic form is commonly used. Frequently, though not invariably, the empha-sized part is placed after the verb: mee bas-ekə yanne kalutərəTə මේ බස් - එක යන්නේ කලුතරට It is to Kalutara that bus is going. koləm̆bəTə yanne meekə කොලඹට යන්නේ මේක This one is going to Colombo. meekə yanne dæn də? මේක යන්නේ දැන් ද ? Is this one going now? Constructions with the simple form of the verb will be referred to as SIMPLE STATEMENTS; those with the emphatic form of the verb as EMPHATIC STATEMENTS. 6.22 One of the most common uses of the INFINITIVE is as an imperative, in giving directions or orders. It usually occurs last in the sentence when so used: meekeŋ kalutərəTə yannə. මේකෙං කලුතරට යන්න . Go to Kalutara by this one. TikæT-ekak dennə. ටිකැට් - එකක් දෙන්න . Give (me) a ticket. 6.3 Agreement Note that the verb forms above do not change to agree with the singular, plural, definite or indefinite status of nouns. For example: mehee bas tiyenəwa. මෙහේ බස් තියෙනවා . There are buses here. mehee bas-ekə tiyenəwa. මෙහේ බස් - එක තියෙනවා . Here is the bus -or- the bus is here. mehee bas-ekak tiyenəwa. මෙහේ බස් - එකක් තියෙනවා . There is a bus here. 7. POSTPOSITIONS indəla ඉන්දල ‘from’ is the first of an important class of POST-POSITIONS. Although these often have much the same function as English prepositions such as “from,” they appear after the word which depends on them. mehee in̆dəla මෙහේ ඉඳල from here koləm̆bə in̆dəla කොලඹ ඉඳල from Colombo [page 8] 8. THE QUESTION MARKER də ද də ද , THE QUESTION MARKER, may be added to any statement to change it to a question, but its placement varies with the kind of statement. 8.1 In a simple statement (i.e. one with the simple form of the verb), də ද always appears immediately after the verb: koləm̆bəTə bas-ekak tiyenəwa. කොලඹට බස් - එකක් තියෙනවා . There is a bus to Colombo. koləm̆bətə bas-ekak tiyenəwa də? කොලඹත බස් - එකක් තියෙනවා ද ? Is there a bus to Colombo? 8.2 In an emphatic statement (i.e. one with an emphatic form of the verb) də ද immediately follows the emphasized word, and cannot immediately follow the verb: mee bas-ekə yanne kalutərəTə මේ බස් - එක යන්නේ කලුතරට This bus is going to Kalutara mee bas-ekə yanne kalutərəTə də? මේ බස් - එක යන්නේ කලුතරට ද ? Is this bus going to Kalutara? 8.3 In all but a very few rare cases, then, following rule will hold for the position of də ද: də ද always follows a simple verb; it never directly follows an emphatic verb. 9. INTERROGATIVE EXPRESSIONS KohaaTə කොහාට ‘where to’ and kiiyə කීය ‘how much, how many’ are the first two of a set of interrogative words. In interrogative sentences, these appear with the question marker də ද. The də ද usually immediately follows the interrogative word, so that combinations such as kiiyə də කීය ද, kohaaTə də කොහාට ද are most easily learned as idiomatic idiomatic units. These interrogative expressions composed of interrogative plus an immediately following də ද never occur with a simple verb. kohaaTə də කොහාට ද may be used without the emphatic form of the verb if the context is sufficiently clear without it. meekə yanne kohaaTə də? මේක යන්නෙ කොහාට ද ? or meekə kohaaTə də? මේක කොහාට ද ? Where is this one going? kiiyə də කීය ද is the usual expression for asking the price of something: kalutərəTə kiiyə də? කලුතරට කීය ද ? How much to Kalutara? TikæT-ekə kiiyə də? ටිකැට් - එක කීය ද ? How much is the ticket? [page 9] Exercises A. Say in Sinhalese: 1. Is there a bus from here to Colombo? 2. No, sir. 3. Where is this bus going? 4. This one goes to Kalutara. 5. Is there a bus from Kalutara to Colombo? 6. Yes. 7. Yes, sir. 8. There are always (buses). 9. Go to Kalutara by this one. 10. This one is going now. 11. From Kalutara, go by a Colombo bus. 12. Fine. 13. How much to Kalutara? 14. Two rupees. 15. Here you are. 16. Give me a ticket. B. D. [page 4] 3. the plural the plural forms for bas-ekə බස- එක and tikat-eka ටකට- එක are bas බස 'buses' and tikət ටකට ‘tickets’. this “no ending” plural is the usual type for nouns with a definite form in - eke - එක . the plural of rupiyələ රපයල is rupiyal රපයල ‘rupees’. notice that there is again no ending. also, we have al before endings, but -al -අල when final. this is a regular change in sinhalese; where a occurs before a consonant when something else follows, it becomes a if that consonant becomes final. place names like koləm̆bə කලඹ and kalutərə කලතර do not generally have plurals. the plurals of pronouns like meekə මක will be taken up as they occur later. 4. cases three of the four sinhalese cases will be introduced here, 4.1 the direct case the “basic” forms that have been given above and referred to simply as “singular definite,” “singular indefinite” or “plural” are in the direct case. thus, bas-ekə බස - yanne යන න yannə යනන give denəwa දන ව də- ද - denne දන න dennə දනන be tiyenəwa තයන ව tiye- තය - tiyenne තයන න tiyennə තයනන 6.2 uses of the forms 6.21 the simple and emphatic present forms are both used in forming present tense sentences. the most common difference between statements formed with these two forms is in emphasis. generally non-emphatic statement sentences are formed by using the simple present form. [page 7] mee bas-ekə kalutərətə yanəwa. ම බස - එක කලතරට යනව . this bus is going to kalutara. meekə dæŋ yanǝwa. මක දං යනව . this one is going now. where special emphasis is to be given like that which might be indicated by translation such as: “it is to kalutara that this one is going” or “this one is going to kalutara,” the emphatic form is commonly used. frequently, though not invariably, the empha-sized part is placed after the verb: mee bas-ekə yanne kalutərətə ම බස - එක යනන කලතරට it is to kalutara that bus is going. koləm̆bətə yanne meekə කලඹට යනන මක this one is going to colombo. meekə yanne dæn də? මක යනන දන ද ? is this one going now? constructions with the simple form of the verb will be referred to as simple statements; those with the emphatic form of the verb as emphatic statements. 6.22 one of the most common uses of the infinitive is as an imperative, in giving directions or orders. it usually occurs last in the sentence when so used: meekeŋ kalutərətə yannə. මකං කලතරට යනන . go to kalutara by this one. tikæt-ekak dennə. ටකට - එකක දනන . give (me) a ticket. 6.3 agreement note that the verb forms above do not change to agree with the singular, plural, definite or indefinite status of nouns. for example: mehee bas tiyenəwa. මහ බස තයනව . there are buses here. mehee bas-ekə tiyenəwa. මහ බස - එක තයනව . here is the bus -or- the bus is here. mehee bas-ekak tiyenəwa. මහ බස - එකක තයනව . there is a bus here. 7. postpositions indəla ඉනදල ‘from’ is the first of an important class of post-positions. although these often have much the same function as english prepositions such as “from,” they appear after the word which depends on them. mehee in̆dəla මහ ඉඳල from here koləm̆bə in̆dəla කලඹ ඉඳල from colombo [page 8] 8. the question marker də ද də ද , the question marker, may be added to any statement to change it to a question, but its placement varies with the kind of statement. 8.1 in a simple statement (i.e. one with the simple form of the verb), də ද always appears immediately after the verb: koləm̆bətə bas-ekak tiyenəwa. කලඹට බස - එකක තයනව . there is a bus to colombo. koləm̆bətə bas-ekak tiyenəwa də? කලඹත බස - එකක තයනව ද ? is there a bus to colombo? 8.2 in an emphatic statement (i.e. one with an emphatic form of the verb) də ද immediately follows the emphasized word, and cannot immediately follow the verb: mee bas-ekə yanne kalutərətə ම බස - එක යනන කලතරට this bus is going to kalutara mee bas-ekə yanne kalutərətə də? ම බස - එක යනන කලතරට ද ? is this bus going to kalutara? 8.3 in all but a very few rare cases, then, following rule will hold for the position of də ද: də ද always follows a simple verb; it never directly follows an emphatic verb. 9. interrogative expressions kohaatə කහට ‘where to’ and kiiyə කය ‘how much, how many’ are the first two of a set of interrogative words. in interrogative sentences, these appear with the question marker də ද. the də ද usually immediately follows the interrogative word, so that combinations such as kiiyə də කය ද, kohaatə də කහට ද are most easily learned as idiomatic idiomatic units. these interrogative expressions composed of interrogative plus an immediately following də ද never occur with a simple verb. kohaatə də කහට ද may be used without the emphatic form of the verb if the context is sufficiently clear without it. meekə yanne kohaatə də? මක යනන කහට ද ? or meekə kohaatə də? මක කහට ද ? where is this one going? kiiyə də කය ද is the usual expression for asking the price of something: kalutərətə kiiyə də? කලතරට කය ද ? how much to kalutara? tikæt-ekə kiiyə də? ටකට - එක කය ද ? how much is the ticket? [page 9] exercises a. say in sinhalese: 1. is there a bus from here to colombo? 2. no, sir. 3. where is this bus going? 4. this one goes to kalutara. 5. is there a bus from kalutara to colombo? 6. yes. 7. yes, sir. 8. there are always (buses). 9. go to kalutara by this one. 10. this one is going now. 11. from kalutara, go by a colombo bus. 12. fine. 13. how much to kalutara? 14. two rupees. 15. here you are. 16. give me a ticket. b. substitute orally in the sentences below, the sinhalese equivalent of the english given: 1. __________ yanne kalutərətə . __________ යනන කලතරට this one buses this bus these buses 2. mehee in̆dəla __________ yannə. මහ ඉඳල __________ යනන . by a bus by this bus by the bus by this one 3. __________ tiyenəwa də? __________ තයනව ද? a ticket buses a bus tickets the bus 4. __________ yanawa. a bus this one buses the colombo bus this bus a colombo bus these buses colombo buses [page 10] 5. meekə __________ yanawa. always to kalutara to colombo from here from kalutara from colombo from here to colombo from here to kalutara from colombo to kalutara from kalutara to colombo 6.__________ yannə. by the bus by a bus by this bus by this one by colombo to kalutara by a bus to colombo by this one to colombo by the bus to kalutara by this bus to kalutara c. transform the following sentences into questions according to the model: model: meekə yanne kalutərətə → meekə yanne kalutərətə də? මක යනන කලතරට → මක යනන කලතරට ද? 1. mehee in̆dəla bas tiyenəwa. 2. mee bas-ekə koləm̆bətə yanəwa. 3. meekə dæŋ yanawa. 4. nitərəmə yanawa. 5. dæŋ bas-ekak tiyenəwa. 6. mee bas-ekə kalutərətə. 7. mehee in̆dəla bas-ekak dan yanawa. 8. mee bas-ekə yanne koləmbətə. 1. මහ ඉඳල බස තයනව. 2. ම බස-එක කලඹට යනව. 3. මක දන යනව. 4. නතරම යනව. 5. දන බස-එකක තයනව. 6. ම බස-එක කලතරට. 7. මහ ඉඳල බස-එකක දන යනව. 8. ම බස-එක යනන කලමබට. d. transform according to the model, changing each sentence into an emphatic sentence, emphasizing the underlined item: model: meekə koləm̆bətə yanəwa → koləm̆bətə yanne meekə. මක කලඹට යනව → කලඹට යනන මක. 1. mee bas-ekə kalutərətə yanəwa. 2. dæŋ bas-ekak tiyenəwa. 3. bas-ekə dæŋ yanəwa. 4. kalutərətə bas-ekak tiyenəwa. 5. mee bas koləm̆bətə yanəwa. 1. ම බස -එක කලතරට යනව. 2. ද න බස-එකක තයනව. 3. බස- එක ද න යනව. 4. කලතරට බස -එකක තයනව. 5. ම බස කලඹට යනව. [page 11] e. translate orally: 1. is this bus going to kalutara? 2. no, sir. 3. where is this one going? 4. this bus goes to colombo. 5. are there buses from colombo to kalutara? 6. yes, sir. 7. there are always buses. 8. how much to colombo? 9. two rupees. 10. fine, here you are. 11. give me a ticket. 12. here you are, sir.

JOHN laŋkaawe ලංකාවෙ of Ceylon, Ceylonese laŋkaawe suruTTu də? ලංකාවෙ සුරුත්තු ද? Ceylonese cigars? PROPRIETOR maatəlee මාතලේ Matale ow, maatəlee suruTTu. ඔව්, මාතෙලේ සුරුත්තු. Yes, Matale cigars. bohoma බොහොම very rasay රසයි tasty meekə bohomə rasay. මේක බොහොම රසයි. This one is very tasty. suwən̆də සුවඳ aroma. balannə බලන්න look, notice, see mennə, suwən̆də balanna. මෙන්න, සුවඳ බලන්න. Here you are. Notice the aroma [page 14] JOHN aa ආ oh særay සැරයි strong aa, meekə bohomə særay! ආ, මේක බොහොමෙ සැරයි! Oh, this one is very strong! maTə මට to me arə අර those pækæT-ekak පැකැට් - එකක් a pack maTə arə sigəræT pækæT-ekak dennə. මට අර සිගරැට් පැකැට්-එකක් දෙන්න. Give me a pack of those cigarettes. Grammar 1. ADDRESS mahattea මහත්තයා is used to address or refer to either (male) strangers 1 or superiors, excluding relations and clergy. Servants use mahattea මහත්තයා to refer to or address their employers, and thus it is generally translated (the) master'. Elsewhere, as when used for strangers, it means something like 'the gentleman' or ‘sir’, although there is no real English equivalent. It is the most commonly used polite form of address, and such terms are mandatory in Sinhalese in many situations in which a term of deference like “sir” would be optional or not used at all in English. Notice that in many situations where English would have the pro-noun "you" Sinhalese uses a form like mahattea මහත්තයා: e.g. mahattea suruTTu bonewa də? මහත්තයා සුරුට්ටු බොනෙවා ද? 'Do you smoke cigars? (Literally: Does the gentleman smoke cigars?). 2. NOUN CLASSES On the basis of the inflectional form of nouns, they may be grouped into four classes: 1. Those with a direct definite form in -ekə -එක 2. Those with a direct definite form in a and an instrumental definite in -en -එන් 3. Those with a direct definite in a and an instrumental in -i ŋ -ඉන් 4. Those with a direct definite form in -ee -ඒ or - e -එ These classes will be referred to as classes 1, 2, 3 and 4 respectively. 2.1 Class 1 Nouns of this class have an inflection identical with that of bas-eke බස්- එකෙ. Thus: Definite Indefinite Plural Direct p æ k æ T-ekə පැකැට් - එක p æ k æ T-ekak පැකැට් - එකක් pæk æ T පැකැට් Dative pæk æ T-ekəTə පැකැට් - එකට pæk æ T-ekəkəTə පැකැට් - එකකට Instrumental pækæT-eke ŋ පැකැට් - එකෙන් pækæT-ekəki ŋ පැකැට් - එකකින් The new nouns of this class that have occurred so far are: pæk æ T-ek ə පැකැට් - එක the pack, package n æ wik ə T-ekə නැවිකට් - එක the Navy Cut cigarette triiroos-eke ත්‍රීරෝස් - එකෙ the Three Roses cigarette sigəræ T -ekə සිගරැට් - එක the cigarette In future lessons, in the section for new nouns, nouns of this class will be cited only in the direct definite form, since all other forms are predictable from this one. 2.2 Class 2 Nouns of this class have an inflection in the singular that is identical with that of rupiyələ රුපියල. The plural form is not predictable from the direct definite and must be learned for each noun. Thus: Definite Indefinite Plural Direct suwən̆də සුවඳ suwən̆dak සුවඳක් suwən̆dəwal සුවඳවල් Dative suwən̆dəTə සුවඳට suwən̆dəkəTə සුවඳකට Instrumental suwen̆deŋ සුවෙඳෙන් suwən̆dəkiŋ සුවඳකින් Nouns of this type that have occurred so far are: Plural the aroma suwən̆də සුවඳ suwən̆dəwal සුවඳවල් the cigar suruTTuwə සුරුට්ටුව suruTTu සුරුට්ටු the kind, type jaatiyə ජාතිය jaati ජාති Ceylon laŋkaawa ලංකාව (no plural) [page 16] The form meekə මේක ‘this one’ has the same definite forms as nouns of this class, but does not have indefinite forms. Thus: Direct meekə මේක Dative meekəTə මේකට Definite meekeŋ මේකෙ න් 2.3 Class 3 Nouns of this class have an inflection in the definite singular that is identical with that of koləm̆bə කොලඹ. The plural form is not predictable from the direct definite and must be learned for each noun. Note that the direct and dative forms are like for Class 2 but the definite instrumental in this class has the ending -iŋ -ඉන්. The only nouns of this class that have occurred so far are koləm̆bə කොලඹ and kalutərə කලුතර, neither of which has indefinite or plural forms. The definite inflection is as follows: Direct koləm̆bə කොලඹ Dative koləm̆bəTə කොලඹට Instrumental koləm̆biŋ කොලඹින් 2.4 Class 4 The only noun of this class that has occurred so far is maatəlee මාතලේ ‘Matale’, which has neither an indefinite nor a plural form. Its definite forms are: Direct maatəlee මාතලේ Dative maatǝleeTə මාතලේට Instrumental maatəleŋ මාතලෙන් 3. THE GENITIVE CASE The fourth and last case of Sinhalese is the GENITIVE. 3.1 Class 1 Nouns of Class 1 have a genitive ending in -ekee -එකේ in the definite. The genitive indefinite adds -ə -අ to the direct indefinite with the regular change of ak අක් to ǝk අක්. The plural case form will be learned later for all classes. Definite Indefinite Direct bas-ekə බස් - එක bas-ekak බස් - එකක් Genitive bas-ekee බස් - එකේ bas-ekəkə බස් - එකක [page 17] 3.2 Class 2 Nouns of Class 2 have a genitive definite ending either in -ee -ඒ or in -e -එ . The genitive indefinite adds -ə -අ to the direct indefinite with the regular change of -ak -අක් to -ək -අක් : Definite Indefinite Direct rupiyələ රුපියල rupiyəlak රුපියලක් Genitive rupiyəlee රුපියලේ rupiyələkə රුපියලක Since it cannot be simply predicted from the direct definite whether the genitive definite will end in -ee -ඒ or -e -එ, the genitive will regularly be cited for nouns of this class. Thus: Direct Genitive (Definite) rupiyələ රුපියල rupiyəlee රුපියලේ suwən̆də සුවඳ suwən̆də සුවඳෙ suruTTuwə සුරුට්ටුව suruTTuwe සුරුට්ටුවෙ jaatiyə ජාතිය jaatiye ජාතියෙ laŋkaawə ලංකාව laŋkaawe ලංකාවෙ meekə මේක meeke මේකෙ 3.3 Class 3 Nouns of this class have a genitive definite ending in -ə -අ and hence identical with the direct definite. The genitive indefinite, like that of the classes above, adds -ə -අ to the direct indefinite with the regular change of - ak -අක් to - ǝk -අක් . However, the only nouns of this class that have occurred so far do not have an indefinite form. Direct Definite koləm̆bə කොලඹ Genitive Definite koləm̆bə කොලඹ The characteristics of this class as compared with Class 2 are: 1. The direct definite and the genitive definite both end in -ə -අ for Class 3, but for Class 2 the direct definite ends in -ə -අ, and the genitive is -ee -ඒ or -e -එ. 2. The instrumental definite for Class 3 ends in -iŋ -ඉන් , but for Class 2 in -eŋ -එන්. 3.4 Class 4 Nouns of this class have a genitive definite form identical with the direct definite. Thus: [page 18] Direct Definite maatəlee මාතලේ Genitive Definite maatəlee මාතලේ 3.5 Use of the Genitive 1. A noun or pronoun dependent on the postposition in̆dəla ඉඳල will always precede in̆dəla ඉඳල and will be in the genitive case: kalutərə in̆dəla කලුතර ඉඳල from Kalutara laŋkaawe in̆dəla ලංකාවෙ ඉඳල from Ceylon meeke in̆dəla මේකෙ ඉඳල from this one 2. The genitive case may be an equivalent of the English possessive -’s construction or “of” construction: mee suruTTuwe suwən̆də මේ සුරුට්ටුවෙ සුවඳ this cigar's aroma, or the aroma of this cigar With place names, it may equate with the English adjectival form of the place name: maatəlee suruTTu මාතලේ සුරුට්ටු Matale cigars laŋkaawe sigəræT ලංකාවෙ සිගරැට් Ceylonese cigarettes 4. FIRST PERSON PRONOUNS The pronouns of the first person are: Singular Plural Direct mamə I, me මම api we, us අපි Dative maTə මට apiTə අපිට The other case forms will be learned later. mamə kalutərəTə yanəwa. මම කලුතරට යනවා . I'm going to Kalutara, maTə pækæT-ekak dennə. මට පැකැට් - එකක් දෙන්න . Give me a pack. api kalutərəTə yanəwa. අපි කලුතරට යනවා . We are going to Kalutara. apiTə pækæT-ekak dennə. අපිට පැකැට් - එකක් දෙන්න . Give us a pack. Note that the dative form is used as indirect object of dennə දෙන්න ‘give’. [page 19] 5. NEW VERBS The three new verbs in Conversation 2 are: bonəwa බොන වා drink (with tobacco, smoke) balənəwa බලන වා look, observe, see kərənəwa කරන වා do, make The emphatic and infinitive forms are obtained, as stated in Lesson 1, by adding the ending - nne න්නෙ or -nnə -න්න to the verb stem obtained by removing -nəwa -න වා from the simple form. However, there is a general rule for verb stems ending in -ə -අ : whenever -nne -න්නෙ or -nnə -න්න are added, this stem-final -ə- -අ- becomes -a- - අ -. the three verbs above are thus: The forms for Simple Form Stem Emphatic Form Infinitive bonəwa බොන වා bo- බො - bonne බොන්නෙ bonnə බොන්න balənəwa බලන වා balə- බල - balanne බලන්නෙ balannə බලන්න kərənəwa කරන වා kərə- කර - kəranne කරන්නෙ kərannə කරන්න paawicci kərənəwa පාවිච්චි කරනව ‘(make) use (of)’ acts like a single verb, and may take both subject and object (both in the direct case) in the same way that a verb such as bon ə wa බොනවා does: mahattea suruTTu bon ə wa. මහත්තයා සුරුට්ටු බොනවා . The gentleman smokes cigars. hu ŋ̆ gak denaa triiroos paawicci kərənəwa. හුඟක් දෙනා ත්‍රීරෝස් පාවිච්චි කරනවා . Many people use Three Roses. Note that the two parts remain together, no matter what form kərənəwa කරනවා takes. For example: mahattea paawicci kəranne mee suruTTu. මහත්තයා පාවිච්චි කරන්නෙ මේ සුරුට්ටු . The gentleman smokes these cigars. 6. NEAR laŋ̆gə ලඟ ‘near, with by (location)’ is a postposition taking the noun or pronoun dependent on it in the direct case: api laŋ̆gə අපි ලඟ with us arə bas-ekə laŋ̆gə අර බස් - එක ලඟ by (near) that bus Note that a phrase with laŋ̆gə ලඟ together with the verb tiyenəwa තියෙනවා may have the English equivalent ‘have’. Thus: api laŋ̆gə hon̆də suruTTu tiyenəwa. අපි ලඟ හොඳෙ සුරුට්ටු තියෙනවා . We have good cigars (literally ‘By us there are good cigars’). [page 20] 7. EQUATIONAL SENTENCES In Equational sentences are those in which one thing is equated with another, e.g. English “x is y.” In such a sentence the x may be referred to as subject and y as predicate attribute. In Sinhalese, there is no equivalent of the English “is” and the structure of the sentence depends on whether the predicate attribute is an adjective or noun. 7.1 With an Adjective as Predicate Attribute Adjectives such as rasə රස ‘tasty’, særə සැර ‘strong (as of tobacco)’ and hon̆də හොඳ ‘good’, which end in a vowel, add -y - යි when they appear as predicate attributes (note that ə අ becomes a අ before final y යි): mee sigəræT hon̆day. මේ සිගරැට් හොඳයි These cigarettes are good. maatəlee suruTTu bohomə særay. මාතලේ සුරුට්ටු බොහොම සැරයි Matale cigars are very strong. suwən̆də සුවඳ ‘aroma, fragrance’, which is a noun in suwən̆də balannə සුවඳ බලන්න ‘notice the aroma’, is also an adjective of this type, with the meaning ‘aromatic, fragrant’: mee suruTTu suwən̆day. මේ සුරුට්ටු සුවඳයි. These cigars are aromatic. 7.2 With a Noun as Predicate Attribute When the predicate attribute is a noun, there is no y යි added. Both subject and predicate attribute are in the direct case: mee triiroos. මේ ත්‍රීරෝස් . These are Three Roses. mee bas-ekə koləm̆bə bas-ekak. මේ බස් - එක කොලඹ බස් - එකක් . This bus is a Colombo bus. 8. THE LOCATION SETS mee මේ ‘this’, ar ə අර ‘that’ and meek ə මේක ‘this one’ are representatives of two sets of items that are part of a large and important group of similar sets involving differences in location. Only the first two sets will be given here. 8.1 The ‘mee’ ‘මේ’ set The forms in this set are mee මේ, oyə ඔය, ar ə අර and ee ඒ. There are four distinctions in location where English has two, and these remain the same throughout the rest of the sets, so that this set should be learned thoroughly first. The first three forms in this set involve distinction in location with respect to speaker and hearer; the fourth refers to the topic being discussed. [page 21] 1. mee මේ ‘this, these’; near the speaker 2. oy ə ඔය ‘that, those’; near the hearer 3. ar ə අර ‘that, those’; away from both speaker and hearer, but in sight. This implies “pointing at” roughly ‘that (those) over there’ 4. ee ඒ ‘that, those’; away from both speaker and hearer, out of sight or with no “pointing at” implied; roughly, ‘that (those) we are talking about’ or ‘that (those) in question’ The The form mee මේ will be translated as “this” or “these”. Other forms will normally all equate with English “that” or those” ‘, but where it is important to indicate which form is meant, e.g. in exercises, oya ඔය will be translated as “that (those) near you”; ar ə අර as “that (those) over there’; and ee ඒ as “that (those) in question”. It is important to remember that this distinction is a necessary one in Sinhalese even though the last three forms will all equate with English “that, those”. The members of the mee මේ set never change form, regardless of the case or number of the nouns they precede. They may thus be “this (that)” or “these (those)” depending upon context: mee bas-ek ə මේ බස් - එක this bus ar ə bas-ekəTə අර බස් - එකට (to) that bus ee bas ඒ බස් those buses 8.2 The ‘meek ə ’ ‘මේක’ set The forms belonging to this set are meek ə මේක, ookə ඕක, arəkə අරක and eekə ඒක. The meanings exactly parallel those of the mee මේ set; thus meek ə මේක ‘this one’; ook ə ඕක that one near you’; arək ə අරක that one over there and eek ə ඒක ‘that one in question’. These forms are inflected for case in the singular as follows: Direct meekə මේක ookə ඕක arəkə අරක eekə ඒක Dative meekaTə මේකට ookəTə ඕකට arəkəTə අරකට eekəTə ඒකට Genitive meeke මේකෙ ooke ඕකෙ arǝke අරකෙ eeke ඒකෙ Instrumental meekeŋ මේකෙන් ookeŋ ඕකෙන් arəkeŋ අරකෙන් eekeŋ ඒකෙන් 8.3 The Uses of the Sets 8.31 The characteristic use of the mee මේ set is to qualify following nouns: [page 22] mee bas-ekə මේ බස් - එක this bus arə TikæT-ekə අර ටිකැට් - එක that ticket ee pækæT-ekə ඒ පැකැට් - එක that pack Notice that when the members of this set are used in this way, the noun qualified is always in the definite or the plural, never the indefinite. 8.32 The members of the meekə මේක set are pronouns that substitute for one of the mee මේ set plus definite noun: mee TikæT-ekə rupiyal dekay. මේ ටිකැට් - එක රුපියල් දෙකයි . This ticket is two rupees. meekə rupiyal dekay මේක රුපියල් දෙකයි This one is two rupees. ee bas-ekə maatəleeTə yanəwa. ඒ බස් - එක මාතලේට යනවා . That bus is going to Matale. eekə maatəleeTə yanəwa. ඒක මාතලේට යනවා . That one is going to Matale. 8.33 Members of the mee මේ set may also act as pronouns. As such, however, they may take the place only of a noun or pronoun in the direct case which is the subject of an equational sentence in which the predicate attribute is also a noun or pronoun in the direct case. Thus: mee ho n̆ də sigəræT jaatiyak. මේ හොඳ සිගරැට් ජාතියක් . This is (or these are) a good kind of cigarettes. or meekə hon̆də sigəræT jaatiyak. මේක හොඳ සිගරැට් ජාතියක් . This one is a good kind of cigarettes. mee bas-ekə. මේ බස් - එක . This is the bus. or meeke bas-ekə. මේකෙ බස් - එක . This one is the bus. but , in meekə koləm̆bəTə yanəwa මේක කොලඹට යනව, mee මේ cannot take the place of meekə මේක, since this is not an equational sentence of the required type. Notice that since mee මේ and the rest of the members of its set can be singular or plural in meaning, we may have: mee bas. මේ බස් . These are buses. mee bas-ekak. මේ බස් - එකක් . This is a bus. mee bas-ekə. මේ බස් - එක . This is the bus. While meekə මේක can only be singular: meekə bas-eka. මේක බස් - එක . This one is the bus. meekə bas-ekak. මේක බස් - එකක් . This one is a bus.

'do you smoke cigars? (literally: does the gentleman smoke cigars?). 2. noun classes on the basis of the inflectional form of nouns, they may be grouped into four classes: 1. those with a direct definite form in -ekə -එක 2. those with a direct definite form in a and an instrumental definite in -en -එන 3. those with a direct definite in a and an instrumental in -i ŋ -ඉන 4. those with a direct definite form in -ee -ඒ or - e -එ these classes will be referred to as classes 1, 2, 3 and 4 respectively. 2.1 class 1 nouns of this class have an inflection identical with that of bas-eke බස- එක. thus: definite indefinite plural direct p æ k æ t-ekə පකට - එක p æ k æ t-ekak පකට - එකක pæk æ t පකට dative pæk æ t-ekətə පකට - එකට pæk æ t-ekəkətə පකට - එකකට instrumental pækæt-eke ŋ පකට - එකන pækæt-ekəki ŋ පකට - එකකන the new nouns of this class that have occurred so far are: pæk æ t-ek ə පකට - එක the pack, package n æ wik ə t-ekə නවකට - එක the navy cut cigarette triiroos-eke ත‍රරස - එක the three roses cigarette sigəræ t -ekə සගරට - එක the cigarette in future lessons, in the section for new nouns, nouns of this class will be cited only in the direct definite form, since all other forms are predictable from this one. 2.2 class 2 nouns of this class have an inflection in the singular that is identical with that of rupiyələ රපයල. the plural form is not predictable from the direct definite and must be learned for each noun. thus: definite indefinite plural direct suwən̆də සවඳ suwən̆dak සවඳක suwən̆dəwal සවඳවල dative suwən̆dətə සවඳට suwən̆dəkətə සවඳකට instrumental suwen̆deŋ සවඳන suwən̆dəkiŋ සවඳකන nouns of this type that have occurred so far are: plural the aroma suwən̆də සවඳ suwən̆dəwal සවඳවල the cigar suruttuwə සරටටව suruttu සරටට the kind, type jaatiyə ජතය jaati ජත ceylon laŋkaawa ලංකව (no plural) [page 16] the form meekə මක ‘this one’ has the same definite forms as nouns of this class, but does not have indefinite forms. thus: direct meekə මක dative meekətə මකට definite meekeŋ මක න 2.3 class 3 nouns of this class have an inflection in the definite singular that is identical with that of koləm̆bə කලඹ. the plural form is not predictable from the direct definite and must be learned for each noun. note that the direct and dative forms are like for class 2 but the definite instrumental in this class has the ending -iŋ -ඉන. the only nouns of this class that have occurred so far are koləm̆bə කලඹ and kalutərə කලතර, neither of which has indefinite or plural forms. the definite inflection is as follows: direct koləm̆bə කලඹ dative koləm̆bətə කලඹට instrumental koləm̆biŋ කලඹන 2.4 class 4 the only noun of this class that has occurred so far is maatəlee මතල ‘matale’, which has neither an indefinite nor a plural form. its definite forms are: direct maatəlee මතල dative maatǝleetə මතලට instrumental maatəleŋ මතලන 3. the genitive case the fourth and last case of sinhalese is the genitive. 3.1 class 1 nouns of class 1 have a genitive ending in -ekee -එක in the definite. the genitive indefinite adds -ə -අ to the direct indefinite with the regular change of ak අක to ǝk අක. the plural case form will be learned later for all classes. definite indefinite direct bas-ekə බස - එක bas-ekak බස - එකක genitive bas-ekee බස - එක bas-ekəkə බස - එකක [page 17] 3.2 class 2 nouns of class 2 have a genitive definite ending either in -ee -ඒ or in -e -එ . the genitive indefinite adds -ə -අ to the direct indefinite with the regular change of -ak -අක to -ək -අක : definite indefinite direct rupiyələ රපයල rupiyəlak රපයලක genitive rupiyəlee රපයල rupiyələkə රපයලක since it cannot be simply predicted from the direct definite whether the genitive definite will end in -ee -ඒ or -e -එ, the genitive will regularly be cited for nouns of this class. thus: direct genitive (definite) rupiyələ රපයල rupiyəlee රපයල suwən̆də සවඳ suwən̆də සවඳ suruttuwə සරටටව suruttuwe සරටටව jaatiyə ජතය jaatiye ජතය laŋkaawə ලංකව laŋkaawe ලංකව meekə මක meeke මක 3.3 class 3 nouns of this class have a genitive definite ending in -ə -අ and hence identical with the direct definite. the genitive indefinite, like that of the classes above, adds -ə -අ to the direct indefinite with the regular change of - ak -අක to - ǝk -අක . however, the only nouns of this class that have occurred so far do not have an indefinite form. direct definite koləm̆bə කලඹ genitive definite koləm̆bə කලඹ the characteristics of this class as compared with class 2 are: 1. the direct definite and the genitive definite both end in -ə -අ for class 3, but for class 2 the direct definite ends in -ə -අ, and the genitive is -ee -ඒ or -e -එ. 2. the instrumental definite for class 3 ends in -iŋ -ඉන , but for class 2 in -eŋ -එන. 3.4 class 4 nouns of this class have a genitive definite form identical with the direct definite. thus: [page 18] direct definite maatəlee මතල genitive definite maatəlee මතල 3.5 use of the genitive 1. a noun or pronoun dependent on the postposition in̆dəla ඉඳල will always precede in̆dəla ඉඳල and will be in the genitive case: kalutərə in̆dəla කලතර ඉඳල from kalutara laŋkaawe in̆dəla ලංකව ඉඳල from ceylon meeke in̆dəla මක ඉඳල from this one 2. the genitive case may be an equivalent of the english possessive -’s construction or “of” construction: mee suruttuwe suwən̆də ම සරටටව සවඳ this cigar's aroma, or the aroma of this cigar with place names, it may equate with the english adjectival form of the place name: maatəlee suruttu මතල සරටට matale cigars laŋkaawe sigəræt ලංකව සගරට ceylonese cigarettes 4. first person pronouns the pronouns of the first person are: singular plural direct mamə i, me මම api we, us අප dative matə මට apitə අපට the other case forms will be learned later. mamə kalutərətə yanəwa. මම කලතරට යනව . i'm going to kalutara, matə pækæt-ekak dennə. මට පකට - එකක දනන . give me a pack. api kalutərətə yanəwa. අප කලතරට යනව . we are going to kalutara. apitə pækæt-ekak dennə. අපට පකට - එකක දනන . give us a pack. note that the dative form is used as indirect object of dennə දනන ‘give’. [page 19] 5. new verbs the three new verbs in conversation 2 are: bonəwa බන ව drink (with tobacco, smoke) balənəwa බලන ව look, observe, see kərənəwa කරන ව do, make the emphatic and infinitive forms are obtained, as stated in lesson 1, by adding the ending - nne නන or -nnə -නන to the verb stem obtained by removing -nəwa -න ව from the simple form. however, there is a general rule for verb stems ending in -ə -අ : whenever -nne -නන or -nnə -නන are added, this stem-final -ə- -අ- becomes -a- - අ -. the three verbs above are thus: the forms for simple form stem emphatic form infinitive bonəwa බන ව bo- බ - bonne බනන bonnə බනන balənəwa බලන ව balə- බල - balanne බලනන balannə බලනන kərənəwa කරන ව kərə- කර - kəranne කරනන kərannə කරනන paawicci kərənəwa පවචච කරනව ‘(make) use (of)’ acts like a single verb, and may take both subject and object (both in the direct case) in the same way that a verb such as bon ə wa බනව does: mahattea suruttu bon ə wa. මහතතය සරටට බනව . the gentleman smokes cigars. hu ŋ̆ gak denaa triiroos paawicci kərənəwa. හඟක දන ත‍රරස පවචච කරනව . many people use three roses. note that the two parts remain together, no matter what form kərənəwa කරනව takes. for example: mahattea paawicci kəranne mee suruttu. මහතතය පවචච කරනන ම සරටට . the gentleman smokes these cigars. 6. near laŋ̆gə ලඟ ‘near, with by (location)’ is a postposition taking the noun or pronoun dependent on it in the direct case: api laŋ̆gə අප ලඟ with us arə bas-ekə laŋ̆gə අර බස - එක ලඟ by (near) that bus note that a phrase with laŋ̆gə ලඟ together with the verb tiyenəwa තයනව may have the english equivalent ‘have’. thus: api laŋ̆gə hon̆də suruttu tiyenəwa. අප ලඟ හඳ සරටට තයනව . we have good cigars (literally ‘by us there are good cigars’). [page 20] 7. equational sentences in equational sentences are those in which one thing is equated with another, e.g. english “x is y.” in such a sentence the x may be referred to as subject and y as predicate attribute. in sinhalese, there is no equivalent of the english “is” and the structure of the sentence depends on whether the predicate attribute is an adjective or noun. 7.1 with an adjective as predicate attribute adjectives such as rasə රස ‘tasty’, særə සර ‘strong (as of tobacco)’ and hon̆də හඳ ‘good’, which end in a vowel, add -y - ය when they appear as predicate attributes (note that ə අ becomes a අ before final y ය): mee sigəræt hon̆day. ම සගරට හඳය these cigarettes are good. maatəlee suruttu bohomə særay. මතල සරටට බහම සරය matale cigars are very strong. suwən̆də සවඳ ‘aroma, fragrance’, which is a noun in suwən̆də balannə සවඳ බලනන ‘notice the aroma’, is also an adjective of this type, with the meaning ‘aromatic, fragrant’: mee suruttu suwən̆day. ම සරටට සවඳය. these cigars are aromatic. 7.2 with a noun as predicate attribute when the predicate attribute is a noun, there is no y ය added. both subject and predicate attribute are in the direct case: mee triiroos. ම ත‍රරස . these are three roses. mee bas-ekə koləm̆bə bas-ekak. ම බස - එක කලඹ බස - එකක . this bus is a colombo bus. 8. the location sets mee ම ‘this’, ar ə අර ‘that’ and meek ə මක ‘this one’ are representatives of two sets of items that are part of a large and important group of similar sets involving differences in location. only the first two sets will be given here. 8.1 the ‘mee’ ‘ම’ set the forms in this set are mee ම, oyə ඔය, ar ə අර and ee ඒ. there are four distinctions in location where english has two, and these remain the same throughout the rest of the sets, so that this set should be learned thoroughly first. the first three forms in this set involve distinction in location with respect to speaker and hearer; the fourth refers to the topic being discussed. [page 21] 1. mee ම ‘this, these’; near the speaker 2. oy ə ඔය ‘that, those’; near the hearer 3. ar ə අර ‘that, those’; away from both speaker and hearer, but in sight. this implies “pointing at” roughly ‘that (those) over there’ 4. ee ඒ ‘that, those’; away from both speaker and hearer, out of sight or with no “pointing at” implied; roughly, ‘that (those) we are talking about’ or ‘that (those) in question’ the the form mee ම will be translated as “this” or “these”. other forms will normally all equate with english “that” or those” ‘, but where it is important to indicate which form is meant, e.g. in exercises, oya ඔය will be translated as “that (those) near you”; ar ə අර as “that (those) over there’; and ee ඒ as “that (those) in question”. it is important to remember that this distinction is a necessary one in sinhalese even though the last three forms will all equate with english “that, those”. the members of the mee ම set never change form, regardless of the case or number of the nouns they precede. they may thus be “this (that)” or “these (those)” depending upon context: mee bas-ek ə ම බස - එක this bus ar ə bas-ekətə අර බස - එකට (to) that bus ee bas ඒ බස those buses 8.2 the ‘meek ə ’ ‘මක’ set the forms belonging to this set are meek ə මක, ookə ඕක, arəkə අරක and eekə ඒක. the meanings exactly parallel those of the mee ම set; thus meek ə මක ‘this one’; ook ə ඕක that one near you’; arək ə අරක that one over there and eek ə ඒක ‘that one in question’. these forms are inflected for case in the singular as follows: direct meekə මක ookə ඕක arəkə අරක eekə ඒක dative meekatə මකට ookətə ඕකට arəkətə අරකට eekətə ඒකට genitive meeke මක ooke ඕක arǝke අරක eeke ඒක instrumental meekeŋ මකන ookeŋ ඕකන arəkeŋ අරකන eekeŋ ඒකන 8.3 the uses of the sets 8.31 the characteristic use of the mee ම set is to qualify following nouns: [page 22] mee bas-ekə ම බස - එක this bus arə tikæt-ekə අර ටකට - එක that ticket ee pækæt-ekə ඒ පකට - එක that pack notice that when the members of this set are used in this way, the noun qualified is always in the definite or the plural, never the indefinite. 8.32 the members of the meekə මක set are pronouns that substitute for one of the mee ම set plus definite noun: mee tikæt-ekə rupiyal dekay. ම ටකට - එක රපයල දකය . this ticket is two rupees. meekə rupiyal dekay මක රපයල දකය this one is two rupees. ee bas-ekə maatəleetə yanəwa. ඒ බස - එක මතලට යනව . that bus is going to matale. eekə maatəleetə yanəwa. ඒක මතලට යනව . that one is going to matale. 8.33 members of the mee ම set may also act as pronouns. as such, however, they may take the place only of a noun or pronoun in the direct case which is the subject of an equational sentence in which the predicate attribute is also a noun or pronoun in the direct case. thus: mee ho n̆ də sigəræt jaatiyak. ම හඳ සගරට ජතයක . this is (or these are) a good kind of cigarettes. or meekə hon̆də sigəræt jaatiyak. මක හඳ සගරට ජතයක . this one is a good kind of cigarettes. mee bas-ekə. ම බස - එක . this is the bus. or meeke bas-ekə. මක බස - එක . this one is the bus. but , in meekə koləm̆bətə yanəwa මක කලඹට යනව, mee ම cannot take the place of meekə මක, since this is not an equational sentence of the required type. notice that since mee ම and the rest of the members of its set can be singular or plural in meaning, we may have: mee bas. ම බස . these are buses. mee bas-ekak. ම බස - එකක . this is a bus. mee bas-ekə. ම බස - එක . this is the bus. while meekə මක can only be singular: meekə bas-eka. මක බස - එක . this one is the bus. meekə bas-ekak. මක බස - එකක . this one is a bus.

title: Lesson 3
text: Lesson 3 Lesson 3 [page 27] Conversation: Buying Fruit Mrs. Perera goes into a shop to buy some fruit. She is then directed to another one. In the First Shop: MRS. PERERA lamea ලමයා child, boy, girl pal ə turu පලතුරු fruit lamea mehee paləturu tiyenəwa də? ලමයා මෙහේ පලතුරු තියෙනවා ද? Boy, do you have (is there) fruit here? SHOPKEEPER noona mahattea නෝන මහත්තයා madam, you allapu අල්ලපු next, adjoining kaDee කඩේ the shop nææ, noona mahattea. නෑ, නෝන මහත්තයා. No, madam. paləturu tiyenne allapu kaDee. පලතුරු තියෙන්නෙ අල්ලපු කඩේ. Fruit is in the adjoining shop. MRS. PERERA eloolu එලෝලු vegetables witərə විතර only mehee tiyenne eloolu witərə də? මෙහේ තියෙන්නෙ එලෝලු විතර දෙ? Are there only vegetables here? SHOPKEEPER ow, eloolu witəray. ඔව්, එලෝලු විතෙරයි. Yes, only vegetables. [page 28] In the second shop: MRS PERERA Tikak ටිකක් some, a few gann ə wa ගන්නව buy, get oon ə ඕනෙ want maTə paləturu Tikak gannə oonə. මට පලතුරු ටිකක් ගන්න ඕන. I want to buy some fruit SECOND SHOPKEEPER noona mahatteaTə නෝන මහත්තයට madam, you (dative) (respectful feminine) hon̆day. noona mahatteaTə monǝwa də oonə? හොඳයි, නෝන මහත්තයට මොනව ද ඕන? Fine. What do you want, madam? MRS. PERERA keselgeDiyə කෙසෙල්ගෙඩිය the banana hon̆də keselgeDi tiyenəwa də? හොඳ කෙසෙල්ගෙඩි තියෙනවා ද? Do you have good bananas? SECOND SHOPKEEPER noona නෝන madam, you kehelgeDiyə කෙහෙල්ගෙඩිය the banana (alternate) tiyenəwa, noona. තියෙනවා, නෝන. Yes we have, madam. noona mahatteaTə kehelgeDi oonə də? නෝන මහත්තයට කෙහෙල්ගෙඩි ඕන ද? NEW NOUNS Class 2 keselgeDiya කෙසෙල්ගෙඩිය ‘the banana’; gen. keselgeDiye කෙසෙල්ගෙඩියෙ; pl. keselgeDi කෙසෙල්ගෙඩි. Class 4 kaDee කඩේ ‘the shop’; pl. kaDə කඩ or kaDəwal කඩවල් satee සතේ ‘the cent’; pl. satə සත Some nouns of this class may have a direct form ending in -ее -ее, and some a direct form ending in -e -එ. The genitive is always identical with the direct. The dative will have -ee -ඒ or -e -එ before the -Tə -ට in agreement with the direct. always have the ending -eŋ -එන්. Thus the The instrumental will definite forms of kaDee කඩේ are: [page 30] Direct kaDee කඩේ Dative kaDeeTə කඩේට Genitive kaDee කඩේ Instrumental kaDeŋ කඩෙන් Note that the definite forms of kaDee කඩේ are just like those for maatəlee මාතලේ, the only other noun of this class to occur so far. kaDee කඩේ and satee සතේ are the first nouns of this class to occur that have indefinite and plural forms. The indefinite forms of kaDee කඩේ are: Direct kaDeak කඩයක් Dative kaDeekəTə කඩේකට Genitive kaDeekə කඩේක Instrumental kaDeekiŋ කඩේකින් The direct indefinite of nouns of this class always ends in -eak -අයක්, and the other case forms will have either -ee- -ඒ- or -e- -එ- before the -k- -ක්- in agreement with the direct definite. The plural is not predictable from the direct definite, and will be cited for each new noun of Class 4 in future lessons. Other Nouns: The nouns paləturu පලතුරු ‘fruit’, eloolu එලෝලු ‘vegetables’ and æpəl ඇපල් ‘apples’ are all plural forms. These nouns rarely occur in the singular, and hence the singular forms are not given here. Dative case forms for mahattea මහත්තයා ‘sir, you’, noona mahattea නෝන මහත්තයා ‘madam, you’, noona නෝන ‘madam, you’ and lamea ලමයා, child, boy, girl’, may be formed, as with other nouns, by adding -Tə -ට: mahatteaTə මහත්තයට noonaTə නෝනට noona mahatteaTə නෝන මහත්තයට lameaTə ලමයට These nouns belong to a separate class, distinct from the four already discussed, and their other forms will be given in a later lesson. 2. NEW VERBS gannəwa ගන්නවා ‘get, buy’; gan- ගන්-; ganne ගන්නෙ; gannə ගන්න Note that when the ending -nəwa -නවා is taken from the form gannəwa ගන්නවා, the stem that is left is gan- ගන්-. When an ending beginning with two n's, such as -nne -න්නෙ or -nnə -න්න , is added to a stem like this one, ending in -n -න්, the result is only two n's. [page 31] 3. ‘MADAM’ noona නෝන and noona mahattea නෝන මහත්තයා, like mahattea ,මහත්තයා are used either as a term of address or as an equivalent of English ‘you’, but for women rather than men. Both noona නෝනand noona mahattea නෝන මහත්තයා are respectful terms, and one of them would almost always be used by a servant, shopkeeper, a bus conductor in addressing a lady. However, noona mahattea නෝන මහත්තයා implies greater respect than just noona නෝන , and so would scarcely ever be used where the person addressed was considered to be of equal or inferior status. Simple noona නෝන, however, like mahattea මහත්තයා, may be used for equals and, if desired, inferiors when they are strangers. In circumstances where greater familiarity exists, equals and inferiors are generally addressed by their proper names. noona mahatteaTə paləturu oonə də? නෝන මහත්තයට පලතුරු ඕන ද ? Do you want fruit, madam? noona mee bas-ekeŋ yanəwa də? නෝන මේ බස් - එකෙන් යනවා ද ? Are you going by this bus? 4. THE GENITIVE OF PLACE One of the characteristic uses of nouns in the genitive case in Sinhalese is adverbial, to indicate location. The sense is generally ‘in’ or ‘at’ whatever is referred to by the noun (or pronoun) in the genitive. Thus, in the sentence paləturu tiyenne allǝpu kaDee. පලතුරු තියෙන්නෙ අල්ලපු කඩේ . Fruit is in the adjoining shop kaDee කඩේ is in the genitive case, although with this noun (as with maatəlee මාතලේ) the genitive and direct are the same in form. Compare the following: sigəræT tiyenne p æ k æ T-ekee. සිගරැට් තියෙන්නෙ පැකැට් - එකේ . The cigarettes are in the packet. bas-ek ə arəke tiyenəwa. බස් - එක අරකෙ තියෙනවා . The bus is in that one (such as a building). ee kaDee tiyenne kalutərə. ඒ කඩේ තියෙන්නෙ කලුතර . That shop is in Kalutara (genitive). mahattea pal ə turu ganne ee kaDee. මහත්තයා පලතුරු ගන්නෙ ඒ කඩේ . The master buys fruit at that shop (genitive). [page 32] 5. THE ASSERTION MARKER -y -යි They that appears on adjectives used as predicate attributes is the assertion marker. It has a number of important functions; those that have appeared so far are listed here. 1. It appears (as pointed out in Lesson 2) on adjectives used as predicate attributes in equational sentences, provided the adjective ends, as all have so far, in a vowel: meekə bohomə hon̆day. මේක බොහොම හොඳයි . This one is very good. mee keselgeDi rasay. මේ කෙසෙල්ගෙඩි රසයි . These bananas are tasty. Compare hon̆day හොඳයි and rasay රසයි, above, which are predicative, with the forms of the same adjectives in the following sentences, in which they modify a following noun: mehee hon̆də eloolu tiyenawə. මෙහේ හොඳ එලෝලු තියෙනවා . Here there are good vegetables. mee bohomə rasə suruTTu. මේ බොහොම රස සුරුට්ටු . These are very tasty cigars. 2. When vowel-final adjectives are used alone, without a subject, the -y -ය් also appears. Thus hon̆day හොඳයි ‘good, fine, all right’, as well as bohomə rasay. බොහොම රසයි . Very tasty. aa, særay! ආ , සැරයි ! Oh, (this one is) strong! 3. The assertion marker is used with numerals in counting and quoting prices. Thus: rupiyal dekay රුපියල් දෙකයි two rupees compare dekə දෙක two satə tunay සත තුනයි three cents compare tunə තුන three satə hatəray සත හතරයි four cents compare hatərə හතර four 4. The assertion marker also forms sentences with witərə විතර ‘only’. Thus: eloolu witəray එලෝලු විතරයි vegetables only or only vegetables 6. -y -යි and -də -දෙ : When the question marker də ද is added to the sentences that take the assertion marker -y -ය්, the latter does not appear. Thus we have the corresponding question for each of the types of assertion discussed in the preceding section: [page 33] Assertion Question mehee eloolu hon̆day. මෙහේ එලෝලු හොඳ්‍යි . Vegetables are good here. mehee eloolu hon̆də də? මෙහේ එලෝලු හොඳ ද ? Are vegetables good here? hon̆day. හොඳ්‍යි . Good, fine. hon̆də də? හොඳ ද ? Good? All right? rupiyal dekay රුපියල් දෙකයි Two rupees. rupiyal dekə də? රුපියල් දෙක ද ? Two rupees? eloolu witəray එලෝලු විතරයි Only vegetables. eloolu witərə də? එලෝලු විතර ද ? Only vegetables? 7. ekak එකක් ‘each’ (literally ‘a one’) The numeral ‘one’ is eka එක. The indefinite form of eka එක ‘one’ is ekak එකක්, literally ‘a one’. It is used to mean ‘each’, as in: meekə ekak sata tunay. මේක එකක් සත තුනයි . This one (i.e. ‘This bunch’) is three cents each. The indefinite forms of the other numerals may be used in the same way, with the meaning ‘for two’, ‘for three’, etc. Thus: meekə dekak satə tunay. මේක දෙකක් සත තුනයි . This one (i.e. This bunch’) is three cents for two. meekə tunak satə tunay. මේක තුනක් සත තුනයි . This one is three cents for three. meekə hatərak satə tunay. මේක හතරක් සත තුනයි . This one is three cents for four. 8. THE ‘WANT’ CONSTRUCTION The Sinhalese word onnə ඔන්න is an equivalent of English ‘want’. The person who wants something is in the dative case: maTə … onnə මට … ඔන්න I want … mahatteaTə … onnə මහත්තයට … ඔන්න The gentleman wants … Like English ‘want’, onnə ඔන්න may occur with a dependent noun or verb. 1. A dependent noun is in the direct case: mahatteaTə keselgeDi oona. මහත්තයට කෙසෙල්ගෙඩි ඕන . The gentleman wants bananas. [page 34] maTə paləturu onnə. මට පලතුරු ඔන්න . I want fruit. 2. A dependent verb is always in the infinitive form: mahatteaTə yannə onnə. මහත්තයට යන්න ඔන්න . The gentleman wants to go. The infinitive may in turn have its own object or modifiers (as may the equivalent English infinitive). Note the order: maTə paləturu gannə onnə. මට පලතුරු ගන්න ඔන්න . I want to buy fruit. mahatteaTə kalutərəTə yannə onnə. මහත්තයට කලුතරට යන්න ඔන්න . The gentleman wants to go to Kalutara. 9. SOME NEGATIVE FORMATIONS: nææ නෑ and epaa එපා 9.1 The negative of tiyen ə wa තියෙනවා ‘there is’ is nææ නෑ, substituted for tiyen ə wa තියෙනවා. mehee æ pel tiyen ə wa. මෙහේ ඇපෙල් තියෙනව . There are apples here. mehee æ pəl n ææ . මෙහේ ඇපල් නෑ . There aren't any (or 'are not') apples here. 9.2 -Tə … onnə ට … ඔන්න sentences, with either a noun or a verb, may be negated by adding n ææ නෑ. maTə keselgeDi onnə. මට කෙසෙල්ගෙඩි ඔන්න . I want bananas. maTə keselgeDi onnə n ææ . මට කෙසෙල්ගෙඩි ඔන්න නෑ . I don't want bananas. maTə paləturu gannə onnə. මට පලතුරු ගන්න ඔන්න . I want to buy fruit. maTə paləturu gann ə onnə n ææ . මට පලතුරු ගන්න ඔන්න නෑ . I don't want to buy fruit. 9.3 If the Tə … onnə ට … ඔන්න sentence has a dependent noun, it may also be negated in an alternate way: epaa එපා is substituted for onnə ඔන්න: maTə keselgeDi oon ə . මට කෙසෙල්ගෙඩි ඕන . I want bananas. maTə keselgeDi oon ə n ææ. or මට කෙසෙල්ගෙඩි ඕන නෑ . maTə keselgeDi epaa. මට කෙසෙල්ගෙඩි එපා . I don't want bananas. However, T ə … onnə ට … ඔන්න sentences with a dependent infinitive cannot be negated with epaa එපා, but only by adding n ææ නෑ.

[page 28] in the second shop: mrs perera tikak ටකක some, a few gann ə wa ගනනව buy, get oon ə ඕන want matə paləturu tikak gannə oonə. මට පලතර ටකක ගනන ඕන. i want to buy some fruit second shopkeeper noona mahatteatə නන මහතතයට madam, you (dative) (respectful feminine) hon̆day. noona mahatteatə monǝwa də oonə? හඳය, නන මහතතයට මනව ද ඕන? fine. what do you want, madam? mrs. perera keselgediyə කසලගඩය the banana hon̆də keselgedi tiyenəwa də? හඳ කසලගඩ තයනව ද? do you have good bananas? second shopkeeper noona නන madam, you kehelgediyə කහලගඩය the banana (alternate) tiyenəwa, noona. තයනව, නන. yes we have, madam. noona mahatteatə kehelgedi oonə də? නන මහතතයට කහලගඩ ඕන ද? do you want bananas? ekak එකක a one/each satee සත the cent tun ə තන three meekeŋ ekak satə tunay මකන එකක සත තනය from this one (the bunch), each is three cents. hatərə හතර four arǝkeŋ ekak satə hatəray. අරකන එකක සත හතරය from that one, each is four cents. kehelgedi කහලගඩ and keselgeli කසලගල are alternate forms, and kehelgedi කහලගඩ is now probably more common. many sinhala words have an alternation between h හ and s ස. when there are alternate forms, the one with s ස is often more formal. [page 29] mrs. perera tunak තනක three, a quantity of three meekeŋ tunak dennə. මකන තනක දනන. give me three from this one. æpəl ඇපල apples æpəl tiyenəwa də? ඇපල තයනව ද? do you have (any) apples? second shopkeeper æpəl nææ. ඇපල න.. no apples. wenǝ වන else noona mahatteatə wenə monəwa də oonə? නන මහතතයට වන මනව ද ඕන? what else do you want, madam? mrs. perera mokut මකත anything, some-thing epaa එප don't want wenə mokut epaa. වන මකත එප. i don't want anything else. grammar l3 1. new nouns class 2 keselgediya කසලගඩය ‘the banana’; gen. keselgediye කසලගඩය; pl. keselgedi කසලගඩ. class 4 kadee කඩ ‘the shop’; pl. kadə කඩ or kadəwal කඩවල satee සත ‘the cent’; pl. satə සත some nouns of this class may have a direct form ending in -ее -ее, and some a direct form ending in -e -එ. the genitive is always identical with the direct. the dative will have -ee -ඒ or -e -එ before the -tə -ට in agreement with the direct. always have the ending -eŋ -එන. thus the the instrumental will definite forms of kadee කඩ are: [page 30] direct kadee කඩ dative kadeetə කඩට genitive kadee කඩ instrumental kadeŋ කඩන note that the definite forms of kadee කඩ are just like those for maatəlee මතල, the only other noun of this class to occur so far. kadee කඩ and satee සත are the first nouns of this class to occur that have indefinite and plural forms. the indefinite forms of kadee කඩ are: direct kadeak කඩයක dative kadeekətə කඩකට genitive kadeekə කඩක instrumental kadeekiŋ කඩකන the direct indefinite of nouns of this class always ends in -eak -අයක, and the other case forms will have either -ee- -ඒ- or -e- -එ- before the -k- -ක- in agreement with the direct definite. the plural is not predictable from the direct definite, and will be cited for each new noun of class 4 in future lessons. other nouns: the nouns paləturu පලතර ‘fruit’, eloolu එලල ‘vegetables’ and æpəl ඇපල ‘apples’ are all plural forms. these nouns rarely occur in the singular, and hence the singular forms are not given here. dative case forms for mahattea මහතතය ‘sir, you’, noona mahattea නන මහතතය ‘madam, you’, noona නන ‘madam, you’ and lamea ලමය, child, boy, girl’, may be formed, as with other nouns, by adding -tə -ට: mahatteatə මහතතයට noonatə නනට noona mahatteatə නන මහතතයට lameatə ලමයට these nouns belong to a separate class, distinct from the four already discussed, and their other forms will be given in a later lesson. 2. new verbs gannəwa ගනනව ‘get, buy’; gan- ගන-; ganne ගනන; gannə ගනන note that when the ending -nəwa -නව is taken from the form gannəwa ගනනව, the stem that is left is gan- ගන-. when an ending beginning with two n's, such as -nne -නන or -nnə -නන , is added to a stem like this one, ending in -n -න, the result is only two n's. [page 31] 3. ‘madam’ noona නන and noona mahattea නන මහතතය, like mahattea ,මහතතය are used either as a term of address or as an equivalent of english ‘you’, but for women rather than men. both noona නනand noona mahattea නන මහතතය are respectful terms, and one of them would almost always be used by a servant, shopkeeper, a bus conductor in addressing a lady. however, noona mahattea නන මහතතය implies greater respect than just noona නන , and so would scarcely ever be used where the person addressed was considered to be of equal or inferior status. simple noona නන, however, like mahattea මහතතය, may be used for equals and, if desired, inferiors when they are strangers. in circumstances where greater familiarity exists, equals and inferiors are generally addressed by their proper names. noona mahatteatə paləturu oonə də? නන මහතතයට පලතර ඕන ද ? do you want fruit, madam? noona mee bas-ekeŋ yanəwa də? නන ම බස - එකන යනව ද ? are you going by this bus? 4. the genitive of place one of the characteristic uses of nouns in the genitive case in sinhalese is adverbial, to indicate location. the sense is generally ‘in’ or ‘at’ whatever is referred to by the noun (or pronoun) in the genitive. thus, in the sentence paləturu tiyenne allǝpu kadee. පලතර තයනන අලලප කඩ . fruit is in the adjoining shop kadee කඩ is in the genitive case, although with this noun (as with maatəlee මතල) the genitive and direct are the same in form. compare the following: sigəræt tiyenne p æ k æ t-ekee. සගරට තයනන පකට - එක . the cigarettes are in the packet. bas-ek ə arəke tiyenəwa. බස - එක අරක තයනව . the bus is in that one (such as a building). ee kadee tiyenne kalutərə. ඒ කඩ තයනන කලතර . that shop is in kalutara (genitive). mahattea pal ə turu ganne ee kadee. මහතතය පලතර ගනන ඒ කඩ . the master buys fruit at that shop (genitive). [page 32] 5. the assertion marker -y -ය they that appears on adjectives used as predicate attributes is the assertion marker. it has a number of important functions; those that have appeared so far are listed here. 1. it appears (as pointed out in lesson 2) on adjectives used as predicate attributes in equational sentences, provided the adjective ends, as all have so far, in a vowel: meekə bohomə hon̆day. මක බහම හඳය . this one is very good. mee keselgedi rasay. ම කසලගඩ රසය . these bananas are tasty. compare hon̆day හඳය and rasay රසය, above, which are predicative, with the forms of the same adjectives in the following sentences, in which they modify a following noun: mehee hon̆də eloolu tiyenawə. මහ හඳ එලල තයනව . here there are good vegetables. mee bohomə rasə suruttu. ම බහම රස සරටට . these are very tasty cigars. 2. when vowel-final adjectives are used alone, without a subject, the -y -ය also appears. thus hon̆day හඳය ‘good, fine, all right’, as well as bohomə rasay. බහම රසය . very tasty. aa, særay! ආ , සරය ! oh, (this one is) strong! 3. the assertion marker is used with numerals in counting and quoting prices. thus: rupiyal dekay රපයල දකය two rupees compare dekə දක two satə tunay සත තනය three cents compare tunə තන three satə hatəray සත හතරය four cents compare hatərə හතර four 4. the assertion marker also forms sentences with witərə වතර ‘only’. thus: eloolu witəray එලල වතරය vegetables only or only vegetables 6. -y -ය and -də -ද : when the question marker də ද is added to the sentences that take the assertion marker -y -ය, the latter does not appear. thus we have the corresponding question for each of the types of assertion discussed in the preceding section: [page 33] assertion question mehee eloolu hon̆day. මහ එලල හඳ‍ය . vegetables are good here. mehee eloolu hon̆də də? මහ එලල හඳ ද ? are vegetables good here? hon̆day. හඳ‍ය . good, fine. hon̆də də? හඳ ද ? good? all right? rupiyal dekay රපයල දකය two rupees. rupiyal dekə də? රපයල දක ද ? two rupees? eloolu witəray එලල වතරය only vegetables. eloolu witərə də? එලල වතර ද ? only vegetables? 7. ekak එකක ‘each’ (literally ‘a one’) the numeral ‘one’ is eka එක. the indefinite form of eka එක ‘one’ is ekak එකක, literally ‘a one’. it is used to mean ‘each’, as in: meekə ekak sata tunay. මක එකක සත තනය . this one (i.e. ‘this bunch’) is three cents each. the indefinite forms of the other numerals may be used in the same way, with the meaning ‘for two’, ‘for three’, etc. thus: meekə dekak satə tunay. මක දකක සත තනය . this one (i.e. this bunch’) is three cents for two. meekə tunak satə tunay. මක තනක සත තනය . this one is three cents for three. meekə hatərak satə tunay. මක හතරක සත තනය . this one is three cents for four. 8. the ‘want’ construction the sinhalese word onnə ඔනන is an equivalent of english ‘want’. the person who wants something is in the dative case: matə … onnə මට … ඔනන i want … mahatteatə … onnə මහතතයට … ඔනන the gentleman wants … like english ‘want’, onnə ඔනන may occur with a dependent noun or verb. 1. a dependent noun is in the direct case: mahatteatə keselgedi oona. මහතතයට කසලගඩ ඕන . the gentleman wants bananas. [page 34] matə paləturu onnə. මට පලතර ඔනන . i want fruit. 2. a dependent verb is always in the infinitive form: mahatteatə yannə onnə. මහතතයට යනන ඔනන . the gentleman wants to go. the infinitive may in turn have its own object or modifiers (as may the equivalent english infinitive). note the order: matə paləturu gannə onnə. මට පලතර ගනන ඔනන . i want to buy fruit. mahatteatə kalutərətə yannə onnə. මහතතයට කලතරට යනන ඔනන . the gentleman wants to go to kalutara. 9. some negative formations: nææ න and epaa එප 9.1 the negative of tiyen ə wa තයනව ‘there is’ is nææ න, substituted for tiyen ə wa තයනව. mehee æ pel tiyen ə wa. මහ ඇපල තයනව . there are apples here. mehee æ pəl n ææ . මහ ඇපල න . there aren't any (or 'are not') apples here. 9.2 -tə … onnə ට … ඔනන sentences, with either a noun or a verb, may be negated by adding n ææ න. matə keselgedi onnə. මට කසලගඩ ඔනන . i want bananas. matə keselgedi onnə n ææ . මට කසලගඩ ඔනන න . i don't want bananas. matə paləturu gannə onnə. මට පලතර ගනන ඔනන . i want to buy fruit. matə paləturu gann ə onnə n ææ . මට පලතර ගනන ඔනන න . i don't want to buy fruit. 9.3 if the tə … onnə ට … ඔනන sentence has a dependent noun, it may also be negated in an alternate way: epaa එප is substituted for onnə ඔනන: matə keselgedi oon ə . මට කසලගඩ ඕන . i want bananas. matə keselgedi oon ə n ææ. or මට කසලගඩ ඕන න . matə keselgedi epaa. මට කසලගඩ එප . i don't want bananas. however, t ə … onnə ට … ඔනන sentences with a dependent infinitive cannot be negated with epaa එප, but only by adding n ææ න.

text: Lesson 4 Lesson 4 [page 38] Conversation: Getting Directions John stops a passerby to find the way to the Galle-Face Hotel. JOHN gool-fees ගෝල් - ෆේස් Galle-Face hooTəlee හෝටලේ The hotel durə දුර far gool-fees hooTəlee huŋ̆gak durə də? ගෝල්- ෆේස් හෝටලේ හුඟක් දුර ද? Is the Galle-Face very far? PASSERBY Tikak duray. ටිකක් දුරය්. Some distance. JOHN hætæpmə හැතැප්ම the mile kiiyak කීයක් how many hætæpmə kiiyak tiyenəwa də? හැතැප්ම කීයක් තියෙනවා ද? How many miles is it? PASSERBY metənə මෙතන here metənə in̆dəla hætæpmə tunak tiyenəwa. මෙතන ඉඳල හැතැප්ම තුනක් තියෙනවා. It is three miles from here. Tæksiyə ටැක්සිය the taxi onnə ඔන්න must Tæksiyəkiŋ yannə oonǝ. ටැක්සියකින් යන්න ඕන. (You) must go by taxi. [page 39] JOHN teerune nææ තේරුනෙ නෑ didn't understand maTə teerune nææ. මට තේරුනෙ නෑ. I didn't understand. aayet ආයෙත් again kiyənəwa කියනව say aayet kiyannə. ආයෙත් කියන්න. Say (it) again. PASSERBY metəne in̆dəla hætæpmə tunak tiyenəwa. මෙතනෙ ඉඳල හැතැප්ම තුනක් තියෙනවා. It is three miles from here. Tæksiyəkiŋ yannə oonə. ටැක්සියකින් යන්න ඕන. (You) must go by a taxi. teeruna තේරුන Understood teeruna də? තේරුන ද? Did you understanmd? JOHN ow teeruna. ඔව් තේරුන. Yes (I) understood. kohomə කොහොම how Tæksiyak ganne kohomə də kiyannə. ටැක්සියක් ගන්නෙ කොහොම ද කියන්න. Tell me how to get a taxi. PASSERBY paarə පාර the road, street arə paarətə yannə. අර පාරත යන්න. THE ‘MUST’ OR ‘HAVE TO CONSTRUCTION: direct case… onnə ඔන්න 3.1 In the previous conversation, onnə ඔන්න appeared with the equivalent of the English subject in the dative case and the meaning ‘want In one of the sentences in the present conversation, onnə ඔන්න appears in a construction in which it means ‘must, have to’: Tæksiyəkiŋ yannə oonə ටැක්සියකින් යන්න ඕන You must go by a taxi. This construction differs from the ‘want’ construction in two principal ways: 1. It occurs with the infinitive of a verb only, never with a dependent noun. Here a comparison with English may help. Tə … onnə ට … ඔන්න ‘want’, like English ‘want (to)’ may take either a noun or a verb. oonə ඕන ‘must’ may take only a verb, like English ‘must’ or ‘have to’. 2. When the equivalent of the English subject is expressed, it is in the direct case, not in the dative. Compare the following pairs: maTə yannə oonǝ. මට යන්න ඕන . I want to go. mamə yannə oonə මම යන්න ඕන I must go! mahatteaTə paləturu gannə oonǝ. මහත්තයට පලතුරු ගන්න ඕන . The gentleman wants to buy fruit. mahattea paləturu gannə oonǝ. මහත්තයා පලතුරු ගන්න ඕන . The gentleman must buy fruit. 3.2 In either of the two constructions with onnə ඔන්න, the equivalent of the English subject may be omitted when the situation makes the meaning clear. Thus Tæksiyəkin yannə oonə ටැක්සියකින් යන්න ඕන could mean either ‘(I, you, he, she, they) must go by taxi.’ or ‘(I, you, he, she, they) want to go by taxi’, depending on the context or situation. 4. THE CAN CONSTRUCTION - puluwa ŋ පුලුවන් 4.1 puluwaŋ පුලුවන් ‘can’ takes the form puluwəni පුලුවනි when the assertion marker is added. Either form may occur, optionally, at the end of statement sentences. Thus either [page 42] maTə puluwaŋ or මට පුලුවන් maTə puluwəni මට පුලුවනි I can As with other forms that take the assertion marker, -y -යි is never present when də ද is added to form a question. Thus only maTə puluwaŋ də? මට පුලුවන් ද ? Can I? 4.2 The puluwaŋ පුලුවන් ‘can’ construction, except for the possible occurrence of the assertion marker, is parallel in form to the onnə ඔන්න ‘want’ construction: A. The equivalent of the English subject, when expressed, is in the dative case: maTə Tæksiyak nawattannə puluwəni ( or puluwaŋ). මට ටැක්සියක් නවත්තන්න පුලුවනි ( or පුලුවන් ). I can stop a taxi. mahatteaTə yannə puluwani ( or puluwaŋ). මහත්තයට යන්න පුලුවනි ( or පුලුවන් ). The gentleman can go! B. It may occur with a verb in the infinitive, which may have its own object and modifiers: mahatteaTə sigəræT bonnə puluwəni. මහත්තයට සිගරැට් බොන්න පුලුවනි . It may occur with a dependent noun in the direct case, although the nouns that may occur in this fashion are relatively few in number, such as siŋhələ සිංහල ‘Sinhalese’: maTə siŋhələ puluwəni. මට සිංහල පුලුවනි . I know (literally ‘can’) Sinhalese. 5. THE QUESTION MARKER də ද WITH DIFFERENT SENTENCE TYPES 5.1 As pointed out before, də ද may be added to a simple statement converting it to a question. The simple statement always has the simple form of the verb, commonly occurring at the end, and the də ද is added immediately after the verb form. Emphatic sentences use the emphatic form of a verb. In this case, də ද occurs immediately after the emphasized item in the sentence. [page 43] Most interrogatives will always be the emphasized word in any question in which they appear, and will therefore occur with the emphatic form of the verb and with də ද immediately following the interrogative. QUANTITY PHRASES 6.1 hætæpmə tunak (tiyenəwa) හැතැප්ම තුනක් ( තියෙනවා ) (It is) three miles sigəræ pækæT-ekak සිගරැ පැකැට් - එකක් a pack of cigarettes sigeraT jaatiyak සිගෙරට් ජාතියක් a kind of cigarettes. all illustrate the QUANTITY PHRASE construction, with this structure: PLURAL NOUN plus QUANTITY WORD “Quantity words” include numerals, nouns of measure like pækæT-ek ə පැකැට්- එක, and jaatiy ə ජාතිය ‘the kind’. The quantity word carries the number, definiteness, and case endings for the entire phrase: sigəræ pækæT-ek ə සිගරැ පැකැට් - එක the pack of cigarettes sigəræT pækæT-ekak සිගරැට් පැකැට් - එකක් a pack of cigarettes sigeræt pækæT සිගෙරැත් පැකැට් packs of cigarettes sigəræT pækæT-ekə Tə සිගරැට් පැකැට් - එක ට to the pack of cigarettes mee sigəræt pækæT-eka මේ සිගරැත් පැකැට් - එක this pack of cigarettes A plural quantity phrase may be followed by another word, usually a numeral, to form a new phrase in which the whole first phrase becomes the “plural noun.” sigəræT pækæT සිගරැට් පැකැට් packs of cigarettes sigeræT pækæT dekə සිගෙරැට් පැකැට් දෙක The two packs of cigarettes keselgeDi jaati කෙසෙල්ගෙඩි ජාති kinds of bananas keselge Di jaati tunə කෙසෙල්ගෙ ඩි ජාති තුන the three kinds of bananas 6.2 In quantity phrases, there is a general agreement between the use of the Sinhalese definite form and the English definite article, and the use of the Sinhalese indefinite form and the English form without any article: hætæpmə tunak හැතැප්ම තුනක් three miles hætæpmə tunə හැතැප්ම තුන the three miles 1. When a quantity expression is modified by a form like ‘this, that’, then the definite form is used: mee sigəræT tunə මේ සිගරැට් තුන these three cigarettes mahattea arə sigəræT pækæT tunə gannawa. මහත්තයා අර සිගරැට් පැකැට් තුන ගන්නවා . The gentleman is buying those three packs of cigarettes. [page 46] 2. Quantity phrases as subjects or objects of simple sentences use the definite form where English uses the definite ‘the’ and the indefinite form where English uses no article: bas hatərə yanəwa. බස් හතර යනව . The four buses are going. bas hatǝrak yanəwa. බස් හතරක් යනවා . Four buses are going. mahattea pækæT tunə gannawa. මහත්තයා පැකැට් තුන ගන්නවා . In emphatic sentences, the definite form of quantity phrases is used where the English would use the definite form: bas hatərə yanne kalutərəTə. බස් හතර යන්නෙ කලුතරට . The four buses are going to Kalutara. kalutərəTə yanne bas hatərə. කලුතරට යන්නෙ බස් හතර . It is the four buses that are going to Kalutara. However, where English would use the form without an article, in Sinhala the indefinite is used if it is not the emphasized word, but the definite with -y -යි if it is the emphasized word in final position. In the latter case, since the form in final position is emphasized, it is likely to equate with English ‘ only such and such’: bas hatǝrak yanne kalutərəTə. බස් හතරක් යන්නෙ කලුතරට . Four buses are going to Kalutara. kalutərəTə yanne bas hatǝray. කලුතරට යන්නෙ බස් හතරයි . (Only) four buses are going to Kalutara. 4.
