Four buses are going. bas hatǝrak yanəwa də? බස් හතරක් යනවා ද ? Are four buses going? 7. kiiyak කීයක් The interrogative word kiiyak කීයක් ‘how many’ behaves like a quantity word. Note that the form kiiyak කීයක් is the indefinite form of kiiyə කීය ‘how much, how many’. It is also special in that it is one of the few interrogatives, characteristically expressing quantity, which will not necessarily occur as the emphasized word immediately followed by də ද: [page 47] hætəpmə kiiyak tiyenəwa də? හැතප්ම කීයක් තියෙනවා ද ? How many miles is it? æpəl kiiyak oonə də? ඇපල් කීයක් ඕන ද ? How many apples do you want? 8. Tikak ටිකක් and hu ŋ̆ gak හුඟක් A. Tikak ටිකක් is actually an indefinite form. The definite is Tikə ටික. When it is used as a quantity word, meaning ‘some, (a) little, (a) small amount’, it acts like a numeral, and takes the same endings: paləturu Tikak gann ə onnə. පලතුරු ටිකක් ගන්න ඔන්න . I want to buy a little (some) fruit. mee pal ə turu Tikə denn ə . මේ පලතුරු ටික දෙන්න . Give me this small amount of fruit. mehee tiyenne paləturu Tikay. මෙහේ තියෙන්නෙ පලතුරු ටිකයයි . Here there is (only) a little fruit. (When the assertion marker is used with Tika ටික, ‘only’ is usually implied.) B. huŋ̆gak හුන්ගක් ‘a lot, much’ is also used as a quantity word: mehee pal ə turu hu ŋ̆ gak tiyenəwa. මෙහේ පලතුරු හුඟක් තියෙනවා . There is a lot of fruit here. However, the definite hu ŋ̆ g ə හුඟ is not used in sentences parallel to those above where the definite form Tika ටික is used. C. Both indefinite forms, Tikak ටිකක් and huŋ̆gak හුඟක්, are used to qualify following adjectives to mean ‘somewhat, a little, a bit’ and ‘very, quite’ respectively. Thus: huŋ̆gak durə də? හුඟක් දුර ද ? (Is it) very far? Tikak duray. ටිකක් දුරය් . Somewhat distant. D. huŋ̆gak හුඟක් and bohomə බොහොම Notice that bohomə බොහොම and huŋ̆gak හුඟක් are commonly used inter-changeably to qualify adjectives. bohomə rasə keselgeDi or බොහොම රස කෙසෙල්ගෙඩි or huŋ̆gak rasə keselgeDi හුඟක් රස කෙසෙල්ගෙඩි very tasty bananas mee suruTTu bohomə særay. or මේ සුරුට්ටු බොහොම සැරයි . mee suruTTu huŋ̆gak særay. මේ සුරුට්ටු හුඟක් සැරයි . These cigars are very strong. [page 48] 9. INDIRECT QUESTIONS An indirect question can be formed from a direct question by the addition of kiyann ə කියන්න ‘tell me.’ Direct Tæksiyak ganne kohomə də? ටැක්සියක් ගන්නෙ කොහොම ද ? How does one get a taxi? Indirect Tæksiyak ganne kohomə də kiyannə. ටැක්සියක් ගන්නෙ කොහොම ද කියන්න . Tell me how to get a taxi. Direct mahattea yanne kohaaTə də? මහත්තයා යන්නෙ කොහාට ද ? Where is the gentleman going? Indirect mahattea yanne kohaaTə də kiyann ə . මහත්තයා යන්නෙ කොහාට ද කියන්න . Tell me where the gentleman is going. 10. THE mehee මෙහේ and met ə n ə මෙතන SETS mehee මෙහේ ‘here’ and metənə මෙතන ‘here’ represent two more subsets of location words. Both sets are inflected for the four case forms, and the same four distinctions of location that were found in the mee set exist: 10.1 The mehee මෙහේ set here there (by you) (over there) there (the place in question) Direct mehee මෙහේ ohee ඔහේ arəhe අරහෙ ehee එහේ Dative meheeTa මෙහේට meheTə මෙහෙට mehaaTe මෙහාටෙ oheeTə ඔහේට oheTə ඔහෙට ohaaTə ඔහාට arəheTə අරහෙට arəhəTə අරහට arəhaTə අරහට eheeTə එහේට eheTə එහෙට ehaaTə එහාට Genitive mehee මෙහේ ohee ඔහේ arəhe අරහෙ ehe e එහේ Instrumental meheŋ මෙහෙ න් oheŋ ඔහෙ න් arəheŋ අරහෙ න් eheŋ එහෙ න් Notice that these have the same endings as Class 4 nouns and that there are alternate dative case forms. [page 49] 10.2 The met ə n ə මෙතන set here there (by you) (over) there there (the place in question Direct metənə මෙතන otənə ඔතන atənə අතන etənə එතන Dative met ə nT ə මෙතන්ට otenT ə ඔතෙන්ට at ə nT ə අතන්ට et ə nT ə එතන්ට Genitive metənə මෙතන otənə ඔතන atənə අතන etənə එතන Instrumental met ə ni ŋ මෙතනින් oteni ŋ ඔතෙනින් at ə ni ŋ අතනින් et ə ni ŋ එතනින් Notice that these all have -e- -එ- before the -n- -න්- in the dative, but - ə- -අ - in all other cases, and that the endings are the same as those for Class 3 nouns. 10.3 Use of the sets Both mehee මෙහේ and metənə මෙතන specify location. The difference between them is one of specificity of location, metənə මෙතන indicating a more specific or smaller area than mehee මෙහේ. The difference does not normally show up in translation, although metənə මෙතන may sometimes be translated as ‘this spot’: mehee i n ̆dələ koləm̆bəTə bas tiyenəwa də? මෙහේ ඉඳල කොලඹට බස් තියෙනව ද ? Is there a bus from here to Colombo? metənə in̆dələ hætæpmə tunak tiyenəwə. මෙතන ඉඳල හැතැප්ම තුනක් තියෙනව . It is three miles from here (this spot). Exercises A. [page 41] 3. the ‘must’ or ‘have to construction: direct case… onnə ඔනන 3.1 in the previous conversation, onnə ඔනන appeared with the equivalent of the english subject in the dative case and the meaning ‘want in one of the sentences in the present conversation, onnə ඔනන appears in a construction in which it means ‘must, have to’: tæksiyəkiŋ yannə oonə ටකසයකන යනන ඕන you must go by a taxi. this construction differs from the ‘want’ construction in two principal ways: 1. it occurs with the infinitive of a verb only, never with a dependent noun. here a comparison with english may help. tə … onnə ට … ඔනන ‘want’, like english ‘want (to)’ may take either a noun or a verb. oonə ඕන ‘must’ may take only a verb, like english ‘must’ or ‘have to’. 2. when the equivalent of the english subject is expressed, it is in the direct case, not in the dative. compare the following pairs: matə yannə oonǝ. මට යනන ඕන . i want to go. mamə yannə oonə මම යනන ඕන i must go! mahatteatə paləturu gannə oonǝ. මහතතයට පලතර ගනන ඕන . the gentleman wants to buy fruit. mahattea paləturu gannə oonǝ. මහතතය පලතර ගනන ඕන . the gentleman must buy fruit. 3.2 in either of the two constructions with onnə ඔනන, the equivalent of the english subject may be omitted when the situation makes the meaning clear. thus tæksiyəkin yannə oonə ටකසයකන යනන ඕන could mean either ‘(i, you, he, she, they) must go by taxi.’ or ‘(i, you, he, she, they) want to go by taxi’, depending on the context or situation. 4. the can construction - puluwa ŋ පලවන 4.1 puluwaŋ පලවන ‘can’ takes the form puluwəni පලවන when the assertion marker is added. either form may occur, optionally, at the end of statement sentences. thus either [page 42] matə puluwaŋ or මට පලවන matə puluwəni මට පලවන i can as with other forms that take the assertion marker, -y -ය is never present when də ද is added to form a question. thus only matə puluwaŋ də? මට පලවන ද ? can i? 4.2 the puluwaŋ පලවන ‘can’ construction, except for the possible occurrence of the assertion marker, is parallel in form to the onnə ඔනන ‘want’ construction: a. the equivalent of the english subject, when expressed, is in the dative case: matə tæksiyak nawattannə puluwəni ( or puluwaŋ). මට ටකසයක නවතතනන පලවන ( or පලවන ). i can stop a taxi. mahatteatə yannə puluwani ( or puluwaŋ). මහතතයට යනන පලවන ( or පලවන ). the gentleman can go! b. it may occur with a verb in the infinitive, which may have its own object and modifiers: mahatteatə sigəræt bonnə puluwəni. මහතතයට සගරට බනන පලවන . the gentleman can smoke cigarettes. matə kalutərətə yannə puluwəni. මට කලතරට යනන පලවන . i can go to kalutara. c. it may occur with a dependent noun in the direct case, although the nouns that may occur in this fashion are relatively few in number, such as siŋhələ සංහල ‘sinhalese’: matə siŋhələ puluwəni. මට සංහල පලවන . i know (literally ‘can’) sinhalese. 5. the question marker də ද with different sentence types 5.1 as pointed out before, də ද may be added to a simple statement converting it to a question. the simple statement always has the simple form of the verb, commonly occurring at the end, and the də ද is added immediately after the verb form. emphatic sentences use the emphatic form of a verb. in this case, də ද occurs immediately after the emphasized item in the sentence. [page 43] most interrogatives will always be the emphasized word in any question in which they appear, and will therefore occur with the emphatic form of the verb and with də ද immediately following the interrogative. simple sentences statement: mahattea kalutərətə yanawa. මහතතය කලතරට යනව . the gentleman is going to kalutara. question: mahattea kalutərətə yanawa də? මහතතය කලතරට යනව ද ? is the gentleman going to kalutara? emphatic sentences statement: mahattea yanne kalut ə r ə t ə . or මහතතය යනන කලතරට . mahattea kalutərətə yanne. මහතතය කලතරට යනන . the gentleman is going to kalutara. question: mahattea yanne kalutərətə də? or මහතතය යනන කලතරට ද ? mahattea kalutərətə də yanne? මහතතය කලතරට ද යනන ? is the gentleman going to kalutara? questions with interrogatives mahattea yanne kohaatə də? or මහතතය යනන කහට ද ? mahattea kohaatə də yanne? මහතතය කහට ද යනන ? where is the gentleman going? mahattea ganne mon ə wa də? or මහතතය ගනන මනව ද ? mahattea mon ə wa də ganne? මහතතය මනව ද ගනන ? what is the gentleman buying? 5.2 statements with onnə ඔනන and puluwaŋ පලවන may be either simple or emphatic without any change in form except that the emphasized item is likely to occur after onnə ඔනන or puluwaŋ පලවන. questions with onnə ඔනන or puluwaŋ පලවන will have də ද in the expected position: i.e. the simple question will have də ද after onnə ඔනන or puluwaŋ පලවන and the emphatic question will have də ද after the emphasized item: [page 44] simple sentences statement: mahatteatə eloolu onnə. මහතතයට එලල ඔනන . the gentleman wants vegetables. question: mahatteatə eloolu oonə də? මහතතයට එලල ඕන ද ? does the gentleman want vegetables? emphatic sentences statement: mahatteatə eloolu onnə. or මහතතයට එලල ඔනන . mahatteatə oona eloolu. මහතතයට ඕන එලල . the gentleman wants vegetables. question: mahatteatə eloolu də oonə? or මහතතයට එලල ද ඕන ? mahatteatə onnə eloolu də? මහතතයට ඔනන එලල ද ? does the gentleman want vegetables? question with an interrogative mahatteatə monəwa də oonǝ? මහතතයට මනව ද ඕන ? what does the gentleman want? 5.3 in emphatic sentences or questions, puluwaŋ පලවන will never occur with the assertion marker: emphatic sentence: mahatteatə siŋhələ puluwaŋ. or මහතතයට සංහල පලවන . mahatteatə puluwaŋ siŋhələ. මහතතයට පලවන සංහල . it is sinhalese that you can speak. emphatic question: mahatteatə siŋhələ də puluwaŋ? or මහතතයට සංහල ද පලවන ? mahatteatə puluwaŋ siŋhələ də? මහතතයට පලවන සංහල ද ? is it sinhalese that you can speak? question with an interrogative: mahatteatə monəwa də puluwaŋ? මහතතයට මනව ද පලවන ? what can you do? [page 45] 6. quantity phrases 6.1 hætæpmə tunak (tiyenəwa) හතපම තනක ( තයනව ) (it is) three miles sigəræ pækæt-ekak සගර පකට - එකක a pack of cigarettes sigerat jaatiyak සගරට ජතයක a kind of cigarettes. all illustrate the quantity phrase construction, with this structure: plural noun plus quantity word “quantity words” include numerals, nouns of measure like pækæt-ek ə පකට- එක, and jaatiy ə ජතය ‘the kind’. the quantity word carries the number, definiteness, and case endings for the entire phrase: sigəræ pækæt-ek ə සගර පකට - එක the pack of cigarettes sigəræt pækæt-ekak සගරට පකට - එකක a pack of cigarettes sigeræt pækæt සගරත පකට packs of cigarettes sigəræt pækæt-ekə tə සගරට පකට - එක ට to the pack of cigarettes mee sigəræt pækæt-eka ම සගරත පකට - එක this pack of cigarettes a plural quantity phrase may be followed by another word, usually a numeral, to form a new phrase in which the whole first phrase becomes the “plural noun.” sigəræt pækæt සගරට පකට packs of cigarettes sigeræt pækæt dekə සගරට පකට දක the two packs of cigarettes keselgedi jaati කසලගඩ ජත kinds of bananas keselge di jaati tunə කසලග ඩ ජත තන the three kinds of bananas 6.2 in quantity phrases, there is a general agreement between the use of the sinhalese definite form and the english definite article, and the use of the sinhalese indefinite form and the english form without any article: hætæpmə tunak හතපම තනක three miles hætæpmə tunə හතපම තන the three miles 1. when a quantity expression is modified by a form like ‘this, that’, then the definite form is used: mee sigəræt tunə ම සගරට තන these three cigarettes mahattea arə sigəræt pækæt tunə gannawa. මහතතය අර සගරට පකට තන ගනනව . the gentleman is buying those three packs of cigarettes. [page 46] 2. quantity phrases as subjects or objects of simple sentences use the definite form where english uses the definite ‘the’ and the indefinite form where english uses no article: bas hatərə yanəwa. බස හතර යනව . the four buses are going. bas hatǝrak yanəwa. බස හතරක යනව . four buses are going. mahattea pækæt tunə gannawa. මහතතය පකට තන ගනනව . the gentleman is buying the three packs. mahattea pækæt tunak gannəwa. මහතතය පකට තනක ගනනව . the gentleman is buying three packs. 3. in emphatic sentences, the definite form of quantity phrases is used where the english would use the definite form: bas hatərə yanne kalutərətə. බස හතර යනන කලතරට . the four buses are going to kalutara. kalutərətə yanne bas hatərə. කලතරට යනන බස හතර . it is the four buses that are going to kalutara. however, where english would use the form without an article, in sinhala the indefinite is used if it is not the emphasized word, but the definite with -y -ය if it is the emphasized word in final position. in the latter case, since the form in final position is emphasized, it is likely to equate with english ‘ only such and such’: bas hatǝrak yanne kalutərətə. බස හතරක යනන කලතරට . four buses are going to kalutara. kalutərətə yanne bas hatǝray. කලතරට යනන බස හතරය . (only) four buses are going to kalutara. 4. each of the types of corresponding question, with rules: sentences above has its də ද following the regular bas hatǝrak yan ə wa. බස හතරක යනව . four buses are going. bas hatǝrak yanəwa də? බස හතරක යනව ද ? are four buses going? 7. kiiyak කයක the interrogative word kiiyak කයක ‘how many’ behaves like a quantity word. note that the form kiiyak කයක is the indefinite form of kiiyə කය ‘how much, how many’. it is also special in that it is one of the few interrogatives, characteristically expressing quantity, which will not necessarily occur as the emphasized word immediately followed by də ද: [page 47] hætəpmə kiiyak tiyenəwa də? හතපම කයක තයනව ද ? how many miles is it? æpəl kiiyak oonə də? ඇපල කයක ඕන ද ? how many apples do you want? 8. tikak ටකක and hu ŋ̆ gak හඟක a. tikak ටකක is actually an indefinite form. the definite is tikə ටක. when it is used as a quantity word, meaning ‘some, (a) little, (a) small amount’, it acts like a numeral, and takes the same endings: paləturu tikak gann ə onnə. පලතර ටකක ගනන ඔනන . i want to buy a little (some) fruit. mee pal ə turu tikə denn ə . ම පලතර ටක දනන . give me this small amount of fruit. mehee tiyenne paləturu tikay. මහ තයනන පලතර ටකයය . here there is (only) a little fruit. (when the assertion marker is used with tika ටක, ‘only’ is usually implied.) b. huŋ̆gak හනගක ‘a lot, much’ is also used as a quantity word: mehee pal ə turu hu ŋ̆ gak tiyenəwa. මහ පලතර හඟක තයනව . there is a lot of fruit here. however, the definite hu ŋ̆ g ə හඟ is not used in sentences parallel to those above where the definite form tika ටක is used. c. both indefinite forms, tikak ටකක and huŋ̆gak හඟක, are used to qualify following adjectives to mean ‘somewhat, a little, a bit’ and ‘very, quite’ respectively. thus: huŋ̆gak durə də? හඟක දර ද ? (is it) very far? tikak duray. ටකක දරය . somewhat distant. d. huŋ̆gak හඟක and bohomə බහම notice that bohomə බහම and huŋ̆gak හඟක are commonly used inter-changeably to qualify adjectives. bohomə rasə keselgedi or බහම රස කසලගඩ or huŋ̆gak rasə keselgedi හඟක රස කසලගඩ very tasty bananas mee suruttu bohomə særay. or ම සරටට බහම සරය . mee suruttu huŋ̆gak særay. ම සරටට හඟක සරය . these cigars are very strong. [page 48] 9. indirect questions an indirect question can be formed from a direct question by the addition of kiyann ə කයනන ‘tell me.’ direct tæksiyak ganne kohomə də? ටකසයක ගනන කහම ද ? how does one get a taxi? indirect tæksiyak ganne kohomə də kiyannə. ටකසයක ගනන කහම ද කයනන . tell me how to get a taxi. direct mahattea yanne kohaatə də? මහතතය යනන කහට ද ? where is the gentleman going? indirect mahattea yanne kohaatə də kiyann ə . මහතතය යනන කහට ද කයනන . tell me where the gentleman is going. 10. the mehee මහ and met ə n ə මතන sets mehee මහ ‘here’ and metənə මතන ‘here’ represent two more subsets of location words. both sets are inflected for the four case forms, and the same four distinctions of location that were found in the mee set exist: 10.1 the mehee මහ set here there (by you) (over there) there (the place in question) direct mehee මහ ohee ඔහ arəhe අරහ ehee එහ dative meheeta මහට mehetə මහට mehaate මහට oheetə ඔහට ohetə ඔහට ohaatə ඔහට arəhetə අරහට arəhətə අරහට arəhatə අරහට eheetə එහට ehetə එහට ehaatə එහට genitive mehee මහ ohee ඔහ arəhe අරහ ehe e එහ instrumental meheŋ මහ න oheŋ ඔහ න arəheŋ අරහ න eheŋ එහ න notice that these have the same endings as class 4 nouns and that there are alternate dative case forms. [page 49] 10.2 the met ə n ə මතන set here there (by you) (over) there there (the place in question direct metənə මතන otənə ඔතන atənə අතන etənə එතන dative met ə nt ə මතනට otent ə ඔතනට at ə nt ə අතනට et ə nt ə එතනට genitive metənə මතන otənə ඔතන atənə අතන etənə එතන instrumental met ə ni ŋ මතනන oteni ŋ ඔතනන at ə ni ŋ අතනන et ə ni ŋ එතනන notice that these all have -e- -එ- before the -n- -න- in the dative, but - ə- -අ - in all other cases, and that the endings are the same as those for class 3 nouns. 10.3 use of the sets both mehee මහ and metənə මතන specify location. the difference between them is one of specificity of location, metənə මතන indicating a more specific or smaller area than mehee මහ. the difference does not normally show up in translation, although metənə මතන may sometimes be translated as ‘this spot’: mehee i n ̆dələ koləm̆bətə bas tiyenəwa də? මහ ඉඳල කලඹට බස තයනව ද ? is there a bus from here to colombo? metənə in̆dələ hætæpmə tunak tiyenəwə. මතන ඉඳල හතපම තනක තයනව . it is three miles from here (this spot). exercises a. substitute orally: 1. mehee in̆dələ koləm̆bətə two miles three miles tiyenawə. four miles a mile 2. mata three bananas denne. the four apples some fruit these three apples. two tickets a pack of navy cuts that (by you) pack of three roses a good kind of cigarettes two packs of cigars three kinds of bananas those (over there) cigarettes this kind of bananas [page 50]

title: Lesson 5
text: Lesson 5 Lesson 5 [page 57] Conversation: Information about a journey John wants to visit the ancient ruins in the North Central Province of Ceylon. He wants to find out something about the area from his servant Banda who comes from that region. JOHN anuraadəpuree අනුරාදපුරේ Anuradhapura wæsse වැස්සෙ (the) rain dan anuraadəpuree wæssə tiyenəwa də? දන් අනුරාදපුරේ වැස්ස තියෙනවා ද? Is there rain in Anuradhapura now? BANDA pættə පැත්ත the area, locality nææ, dæŋ ee pætte wæssə nææ. නෑ, දැන් ඒ පැත්තෙ වැස්ස නෑ. No, there is no rain in that area now. æy ඇය් why æy, mahatteaTə anuraadəpureeTə yanne oonə də? ඇය්, මහත්තයට අනුරාදපුරේට යන්නෙ ඕන ද? Why, do you want to go to Anuradhapura? JOHN palaatə පලාත the province, part of the country ow, maTə ee palaate balannə onnə. ඔව්, මට ඒ පලාතෙ බලන්න ඔන්න. Yes, I want to see that part of the country. koocciyə කෝච්චිය the train anuraadəpureeTə koocci tiyenəwa də? අනුරාදපුරේට කෝච්චි තියෙනවා ද? Are there trains to Anuradhapura? [page 58] BANDA ow, koocciyeŋ yannə puluwəni. ඔව්, කෝච්චියෙන් යන්න පුලුවනි. Yes, (you) can go by train. kaar-ekə කාර් - එක the car anuraadəpuree in̆dəla kaar-ekak gannə oonə. අනුරාදපුරේ ඉඳල කාර්- එකක් ගන්න ඕන. From Anuradhapura, (you) must get a car. JOHN dawəsə දවස the day nawətinəwa නවතිනව stop (intransitive), stay anuraadəpuree dawas kiiyak nawatinnə oonə də? අනුරාදපුරේ දවස් කීයක් නවතින්න ඕන ද? How many days should one stay in Anauradhapura? BANDA dawas dekak nawətinnə. දවස් දෙකක් නවතින්න. Stay two days. tænə තැන the place balannə tæŋ huŋ̆gak tiyenawə. බලන්න තැන් හුඟක් තියෙනවා. There are many places to see. JOHN anuraadəpuree kaar-ekak gannə puluwaŋ də? අනුරාදපුරේ කාර්-එකක් ගන්න පුලුවන් ද? Can one get a car in Anuradhapura? BANDA puluwani. ehee Tæksi tiyenawa. පුලුවනි. එහේ ටැක්සි තියෙනව. One can. There are taxis there. isTeesəmə ඉස්ටේසම the (train) station anuraadəpuree isTeesəmə laŋ̆gə hooTəleak tiyenəwa. අනුරාදපුරේ ඉස්ටේසම ලඟ හෝටලයක් තියෙනවා. The rest house is near Sigiriya Rock. } Notes on the Conversation Anuradhapura was the first capital of the Sinhala kings, and the period of Sri Lankan culture up to about the 10th century A.D. is known as the “Anuradhapura Period.” The ruins of many ancient structures, both secular and religious, remain from this period and demonstrate the remarkable engineering and organizational skill of those who constructed them. Although many of these structures remain in ruins, some of the religious edifices, ancient shrines, and great irrigation works have been restored. Today, some of the latter are again in use, and the restoration work continues steadily. [page 60] Sigiriya is situated about 50 miles to the south of Anuradhapura. There, a large rock was transformed into a royal palace during the 5th century. Originally, entrance to the palace was gained by means of a stairway cut inside the rock, and the stairway was entered through the mouth of a large sculptured lion hence the name Sigiriya ‘Lion Rock’. The most famous feature for visitors to Sigiriya today are the magnificent frescoes depicting beautiful women in a gallery on the rock face. These date from the 5th century, and there are a number of poems commenting upon them which were written on a wall below by admiring visitors of the 8th through 10th centuries: the famous “Sigiri Graffiti”. taanaayəmə තානායම ‘resthouse’: Rest houses are maintained either by the Government Tourist Bureau or by the government of the area in which they are located. They provide food and lodging at a moderate rate, and are found in almost any important town. One may go to a rest house for a meal or for tea without taking a room. Increasingly, these are going “upscale” or being replaced by tourist hotels, however. hooTələ හෝටල ‘hotel’: In Sinhala or Sri Lankan English, a hotel is not necessarily a place to stay. The term is extended as well to restaurants of almost any type. Grammar L5 1. NEW NOUNS Class 1 kaar-ekə කාර්- එක ‘the car, automobile’ Class 2 isTeesəmə ඉස්ටේසම ‘the (train) station’; gen. isTeesəmee ඉස්ටේසමේ; pl. isTeesaŋ ඉස්ටේසන් koocciyə කෝච්චිය ‘the train’; gen. koocciye කෝච්චියෙ; pl. koocci කෝච්චි taanaayəmə තානායම ‘the rest house gen. taanaayəmee තානායමේ; pl. taanaayaŋ තානායන් dawəsə දවස ‘the day’; gen. dawəse දවසෙ; pl. dawas දවස් palaatə පලාත ‘the province, region’; gen. palaate පලාතෙ; pl. palaat පලාත් pætte පැත්තෙ ‘the area, locality, side’; gen. pætte පැත්තෙ; pl. pæti පැති wæssə වැස්ස ‘(the) rain’; gen. wæsse වැස්සෙ; pl. wæhi වැහි (Note the change of -ss- -ස්ස්- to -h- -හ්-.) [page 61] Note: Usually the definite is used when English has ‘rain’. The indefinite is used for a single instance: wæssak වැස්සක් ‘a shower, rainstorm’. Similarly, in the plural, wæhi වැහි ‘showers, rainstorms’. siigiriyə සීගිරිය 'Sigiriya'; gen. siigiriye සීගිරියෙ; (no plural) galə ගල 'the rock'; gen. galee ගලේ; pl. gal ගල් siigiri galə සීගිරි ගල 'Sigiriya Rock'; gen. siigiri galee සීගිරි ගලේ; (no plural) Note that many nouns of this class have a plural formed by dropping the final -ə -අ of the direct definite. When this -ə -අ is lost an -ə -අ in the final syllable becomes a -අ. Thus rupiyələ රුපියල, rupiyal රුපියල්; dawəsə දවස, dawas දවස්. Also a final -m -ම් or -n -න් becomes -ŋ -න් ; thus isteesəmə ඉස්තේසම, isteesan ඉස්තේසන්. Class 3 tænə තැන ‘the place, spot’; pl. tæŋ තැන් Note that here again a final -n -න් becomes - ŋ -න් . This is the first noun of this class to occur that has indefinite forms (the rest have been place names or pronouns). The forms are just like those for Class 2. Thus: Direct tænak තැනක් Dative tænəkəTə තැනකට Genitive tænəkə තැනක Instrumental tænekiŋ තැනෙකිං Class 4 anuraadəpuree අනුරාදපුරේ ‘Anuradhapura’; (no plural) 2. NEW VERBS nawətinəwa නවතිනවා ‘to stay, stop’ (intransitive) 3. THE INDEFINITE IN TIME PHRASES In expressions of periods of time, just as in expressions of distance, price or other quantities, Sinhalese commonly uses the indefinite of a quantity phrase unless a particular stretch of time is referred to, or the form of the sentence is such that the assertion marker is required: [page 62] anuraadəpuree dawas kiiyak naw ə tinne oonə də? අනුරාදපුරේ දවස් කීයක් නවතින්නෙ ඕන ද ? How many days should (one) stay in Anuradhapura? dawas dekak nawətinn ə . දවස් දෙකක් නවතින්න . Stay two days. or the answer could be: dawas dekay. දවස් දෙකය් . Two days. 4. INFINITIVES WITH NOUNS In Sinhalese an infinitive form may modify a noun just as an infinitive with ‘to’ may in English, but the Sinhalese infinitive precedes the noun: balann ə tæn බලන්න තැන් places to see nawətinn ə hooT ə leak නවතින්න හෝටලයක් a hotel (in which) to stay Like any other noun, a noun so modified may be used in the plural as part of a quantity phrase: balann ə taa ŋ huŋ̆gak බලන්න තාං හුඟක් many places to see nawətinnə hooTələ tunak නවතින්න හෝටල තුනක් three hotels to stay in 5. THE SINHALESE WRITING SYSTEM The Sinhalese writing system, known as the siŋhələ hooDiyə සිංහල හෝඩිය, ‘the Sinhalese alphabet’ has 54 basic symbols used in the literary tradition. These 54 include 18 vowel symbols and 36 consonant symbols. For writing spoken Sirihalese, however, only 36 symbols are necessary. These include 24 basic consonant symbols and 12 vowel symbols. Each symbol is called akurə අකුර ‘the letter’, pl. akuru අකුරු. There is no modern language other than Sinhalese for which the sinhələ hooDiyə සින්හල හෝඩිය is used. 5.1 Consonants In the Sinhalese writing system, a consonant symbol by itself represents a consonant plus a following vowel, which will be called THE INHERENT VOWEL. This inherent vowel will be ə අ or a අ depending upon position within the word. The first symbols to be learned are the following: ක k ə (or ka) ද də (or da) හ h ə (or ha) ට T ə (or Ta) ම m ə (or ma) ර r ə (or ra) ද D ə (or Da) ස s ə (or sa) ල l ə (or la) ත t ə (or ta) ග g ə (or ga) ව wə (or wa) Note that some symbols are quite different in form while others such as ට, ම and ව or ග and හ are similar in their basic shape. The following rules for the inherent vowel will apply in almost all cases: 1. In words written with a single consonant symbol, the inherent vowel will be ə අ. Thus the question marker is ද. 2. A consonant symbol at the beginning of a word will have the inherent vowel a අ. 3. A consonant symbol at the end of a word will have the inherent vowel ə අ. For the two-syllable words written with two consonant symbols, then the effect of rules 2 and 3 together is that the first vowel will be a අ, the second ə අ. රස rasə ‘tasty’ මට maTə ‘I, me’, (dat.) මම mamə ‘I’ කඩ kaDə ‘shops’ 4. In the middle of words longer than two syllables, the inherent vowel will be a except under certain regular conditions to be learned later and in some irregular cases: දවස dawəsə ‘the day’ දවසක dawəsəkə ‘on a day’ හතර hatərə ‘four’ Exercises Substitute Orally A. 1. nawətinnə oonə də? how many days a day two days three days three days 2. mehee tiyenəwa də? a hotel to stay (in) some fruit to buy hotels to stay (in) cigarettes to smoke a place to see a place to go places to see a place to stay fruit to buy

tænəkətə තනකට genitive tænəkə තනක instrumental tænekiŋ තනකං class 4 anuraadəpuree අනරදපර ‘anuradhapura’; (no plural) 2. new verbs nawətinəwa නවතනව ‘to stay, stop’ (intransitive) 3. the indefinite in time phrases in expressions of periods of time, just as in expressions of distance, price or other quantities, sinhalese commonly uses the indefinite of a quantity phrase unless a particular stretch of time is referred to, or the form of the sentence is such that the assertion marker is required: [page 62] anuraadəpuree dawas kiiyak naw ə tinne oonə də? අනරදපර දවස කයක නවතනන ඕන ද ? how many days should (one) stay in anuradhapura? dawas dekak nawətinn ə . දවස දකක නවතනන . stay two days. or the answer could be: dawas dekay. දවස දකය . two days. 4. infinitives with nouns in sinhalese an infinitive form may modify a noun just as an infinitive with ‘to’ may in english, but the sinhalese infinitive precedes the noun: balann ə tæn බලනන තන places to see nawətinn ə hoot ə leak නවතනන හටලයක a hotel (in which) to stay like any other noun, a noun so modified may be used in the plural as part of a quantity phrase: balann ə taa ŋ huŋ̆gak බලනන තං හඟක many places to see nawətinnə hootələ tunak නවතනන හටල තනක three hotels to stay in 5. the sinhalese writing system the sinhalese writing system, known as the siŋhələ hoodiyə සංහල හඩය, ‘the sinhalese alphabet’ has 54 basic symbols used in the literary tradition. these 54 include 18 vowel symbols and 36 consonant symbols. for writing spoken sirihalese, however, only 36 symbols are necessary. these include 24 basic consonant symbols and 12 vowel symbols. each symbol is called akurə අකර ‘the letter’, pl. akuru අකර. there is no modern language other than sinhalese for which the sinhələ hoodiyə සනහල හඩය is used. 5.1 consonants in the sinhalese writing system, a consonant symbol by itself represents a consonant plus a following vowel, which will be called the inherent vowel. this inherent vowel will be ə අ or a අ depending upon position within the word. the first symbols to be learned are the following: ක k ə (or ka) ද də (or da) හ h ə (or ha) ට t ə (or ta) ම m ə (or ma) ර r ə (or ra) ද d ə (or da) ස s ə (or sa) ල l ə (or la) ත t ə (or ta) ග g ə (or ga) ව wə (or wa) note that some symbols are quite different in form while others such as ට, ම and ව or ග and හ are similar in their basic shape. the following rules for the inherent vowel will apply in almost all cases: 1. in words written with a single consonant symbol, the inherent vowel will be ə අ. thus the question marker is ද. 2. a consonant symbol at the beginning of a word will have the inherent vowel a අ. 3. a consonant symbol at the end of a word will have the inherent vowel ə අ. for the two-syllable words written with two consonant symbols, then the effect of rules 2 and 3 together is that the first vowel will be a අ, the second ə අ. රස rasə ‘tasty’ මට matə ‘i, me’, (dat.) මම mamə ‘i’ කඩ kadə ‘shops’ 4. in the middle of words longer than two syllables, the inherent vowel will be a except under certain regular conditions to be learned later and in some irregular cases: දවස dawəsə ‘the day’ දවසක dawəsəkə ‘on a day’ හතර hatərə ‘four’ exercises substitute orally a. 1. nawətinnə oonə də? how many days a day two days three days three days 2. mehee tiyenəwa də? a hotel to stay (in) some fruit to buy hotels to stay (in) cigarettes to smoke a place to see a place to go places to see a place to stay fruit to buy

title: Lesson 6
text: Lesson 6 Lesson 6 [page 67] Conversation: Offering a Job Mr. Perera, an estate owner, meets Banda, a young man from the village whom he hasn't seen for some time. PERERA oheege ඔහේගෙ your næddə නැද්ද isn’t there dæŋ oheege kaDee næddə? දැන් ඔහේගෙ කඩේ නැද්ද? Don't you have your shop these days? (Literally: Isn't there your shop now?) BANDA kaDee kərənəwa කඩේ කරනව tend shop, keep shop maama මාම maternal uncle næ mahattea. dæŋ kaDee kəranne maama. නැ මහත්තයා. දැන් කඩේ කරන්නෙ මාම. No, sir. (My) uncle is tending the shop now. PERERA ohee ඔහේ you ohee? ඔහේ? And you? BANDA uDeraTə උඩෙරට the up-country poDi පොඩි small, little rassaawə රස්සාව the position, job mamə uDeraTə poDi rassaawak kərənəwa. මම උඩෙරට පොඩි රස්සාවක් කරනව. I am working at (literally: doing) a little job in the up-country. [page 68] pawlə පව්ල the family pawlə inne uDaraTə də? පව්ල ඉන්නෙ උඩරට ද? Is (your) family in the up-country? BANDA gamə ගම at home nææ. gamə. නෑ. ගම. No. At home. balaagannəwa බලාගන්නව tend, take care of taatta තාත්ත father pawlə balaaganne taatta. පව්ල බලාගන්නෙ තාත්ත. Father is taking care of the family. PERERA lamay ලමය් children kiidenek කීදෙනෙක් how many innəwa ඉන්නව there is, there are lamay kildenek innəwa də? ලමය් කිල්දෙනෙක් ඉන්නව ද? How many children have you (literally: ‘are there’)? BANDA tuŋ denek තුන් දෙනෙක් three tun denek innəwa, mahattea. තුන් දෙනෙක් ඉන්නව, මහත්තයා . I have three, sir. PERERA iskoole ඉස්කෝලෙ the school iskoole yanəwa ඉස්කෝලෙ යනව go to school iskoole yanne næddə? ඉස්කෝලෙ යන්නෙ නැද්ද? Aren't they going to school? duwə දුව the daughter BANDA iskoole yanne duwə witəray. ඉස්කෝලෙ යන්නෙ දුව විතරය්. Only (my) daughter is going to school. [page 69] putaa පුතා the son puttu පුත්තු sons dennə දෙන්න two puttu dennə yanne nææ. පුත්තු දෙන්න යන්නෙ නෑ. The two sons are not going. PERERA oheeTə ඔහේට you (dative) gamə ගම the village raksaawǝ රක්සාව alternate for rassaawə රස්සාව oheeTə gamee raksaawak kərannə puluwaŋ də? ඔහේට ගමේ රක්සාවක් කරන්න පුලුවන් ද? Could you work at a job in the village? BANDA puluwəni mahattea rassaawak tiyenəwa də? පුලුවනි මහත්තයා රස්සාවක් තියෙනව ද? I can, sir. Is there a job? PERERA waDuwæDə වඩුවැඩ carpentry oheeTǝ waDuwæDə puluwaŋ də? ඔහේට වඩුවැඩ පුලුවන් ද? Can you (do) carpentry? BANDA puluwəni. mamə dæŋ kəranne waDuwæDe. පුලුවනි. මම දැන් කරන්නෙ වඩුවැඩෙ. Yes, I can. I am doing carpentry now. PERERA ehenaŋ එහෙනන් then magee මගේ my wattə වත්ත the estate ehanaŋ magee watte raksaawak dennə puluwəni. එහනන් මගේ වත්තෙ රක්සාවක් දෙන්න පුලුවනි. If so, I can give you a job in my estate. waDuwa වඩුව the carpenter waDuwek වඩුවෙක් a carpenter watte waDuwek innəwa. වත්තෙ වඩුවෙක් ඉන්නව. There is a carpenter in the estate. namut නමුත් but miniha මිනිහ the man minihage මිනිහගෙ the man's wæDee වැඩේ the work, the job wæDə වැඩ work namut ee minihage wæDə hon̆də nææ. නමුත් ඒ මිනිහගෙ වැඩ හොඳ නෑ. But that man's work is not good. [page 70] BANDA bohomə istutiy, mahattea. බොහොම ඉස්තුතිය්, මහත්තයා . ??? Thank you very much, sir. heTə හෙට tomorrow maTə heTə in̆dəla ennə puluwəni. මට හෙට ඉඳල එන්න පුලුවනි. I can come from tomorrow on. PERERA hon̆day, ehenaŋ hetə ennə. හොඳ්‍ය, එහෙනන් හෙත එන්න. Fine. Then come tomorrow. wæDəpələ වැඩපල the workshop arə tiyenne wæDəpələ. අර තියෙන්නෙ වැඩපල. There is the workshop udee උදේ the morning udee etenTə ennə. උදේ එතෙන්ට එන්න. Come there in the morning BANDA hon̆day mahattea. හොඳ්‍ය මහත්තයා. Fine, sir. Grammar L6 1. NEW NOUNS Class 2 gamə ගම ‘the village’; gen. gamee ගමේ; pl. gaŋ ගන් rassaawə/raksaawe රස්සාව /රක්සාවෙ ‘the position, job’; gen. rassaawe/raksaawe රස්සාවෙ/ රක්සාවෙ; pl. rassaawal/raksaawal රස්සාවල්/ රක්සාවල් wattə වත්ත ‘the estate’; gen. watte වත්තෙ; pl. watu වතු waDuwæDə වඩුවැඩ ’carpentry’; gen. waDuwæDee වඩුවැඩේ; (no plural) pawlə පව්ල ‘the family’; gen. pawle පව්ලෙ; pl. pawl/pawul පව්ල්/ පවුල් Class 3 uDaraTə උඩරට 'the up-country' (no plural) heTə හෙට 'tomorrow' (no plural) [page 71] Class 4 waDee වඩේ 'the work' (see notes on meaning below); pl. wæDə වැඩ udee උදේ 'the morning'; pl. udee උදේ iskoole ඉස්කෝලෙ 'the school'; pl. iskoolə ඉස්කෝල Nouns of Class 4, as mentioned in Lesson 3, with a direct form in short -e -එ have this -e -එ throughout the definite and indefinite forms, while those with a direct in long -ee - ඒ have long -ee -ඒ everywhere except in the instrumental definite and the direct indefinite. Thus: Definite: with -e - එ with -ee - ඒ Direct iskoole ඉස්කෝලෙ kaDee කඩේ Dative iskooleTə ඉස්කෝලෙට kaDeeTa කඩේට Genitive iskoole ඉස්කෝලෙ kaDee කඩේ Instrumental iskooleŋ ඉස්කෝලෙන් kaDen කඩෙන් Indefinite: with -e - එ with -ee - ඒ Direct iskooleak ඉස්කෝලයක් kaDeak කඩයක් Dative iskoolekəTə ඉස්කෝලෙකට kaDeekəTə කඩේකට Genitive iskoolekə ඉස්කෝලෙක kaDeekə කඩේක Instrumental iskoolekin ඉස්කෝලෙකින් kaDeekin කඩේකින් Notes on the New Nouns: The noun wæDee වැඩේ ‘the work’ has the usual forms of a Class 4 noun, but it also has an irregular direct case indefinite form wæDak වැඩක්. This form commonly appears in the expression wæDak nææ වැඩක් නෑ meaning roughly ‘(of) no use.’ If the subject appears it will be in the direct case, or it may be an infinitive: eekə wæDak nææ. ඒක වැඩක් නෑ. That’s no use; There’s no use in that.’ ee bas ekeŋ yannə wæDak nææ. ඒ බස් එකෙන් යන්න වැඩක් නෑ. There’s no use in going on that bus’ The noun waDee වඩේ and the noun rassaawə/ raksaawə රස්සාව/ රක්සාව may be both be the equivalent of the English term ‘job’. waDee වඩේ refers to a job or task generally lasting for a short period of time, whereas rassaawə රස්සාව is likely to equate with the English term occupation or ‘position’. The plural of wæDee වැඩේ may often equate with the English term ‘work as in: ee minihage wædə hon̆də nææ. ඒ මිනිහගෙ වැද හොඳ නෑ . [page 72] a Sinhala has number of occupational terms like waDuw æ D ə වඩුවැඩ carpentry, which end in wæDǝ වැඩ. This is the noun wæDee වැඩේ, but note that the direct definite ends in -a -අ. Nouns compounded with wæD ə වැඩ are all regular members of Class 2 but have no plurals. The indefinite form waDuwæDak වඩුවැඩක් means ‘a carpentry job’ and the indefinites of other similar compounds have similar meanings. 2. CLASS 5 NOUNS 2.1 All nouns in Sinhala fall into two large divisions: ANIMATE and INANIMATE. Which division a given noun belongs to may be predicted almost without exception from its meaning. 1. INANIMATE: places, non-living things, plants 2. ANIMATE: persons, animals, living things (excluding plants) There are a very few nouns, most of them referring to such things as groups or organizations of living things, which do not fit neatly into this classification. The first four classes of Sinhala nouns (1-4) belong to the inanimate division whereas Class 5 belongs to the thematanimate division. The inflection of Class 5 nouns is illustrated by the following: Definite Indefinite Plural Direct mahattea මහත්තයා mahatteek මහත්තේක් mahatturu මහත්තුරු Dative mahatteaTə මහත්තයට mahattekuTə මහත්තෙකුට Genitive mahatteage මහත්තයගෙ mahatteekuge මහත්තේකුගෙ Instrum. mahatteagen මහත්තයගෙන් mahatteekugen මහත්තේකුගෙන් The dative ending for this class, as for all other the classes, is -T ə -ට . The genitive ending in -ge -ගෙ and instrumental is -gen -ගෙන්. Nouns of this class, in the definite, add the case endings directly to the direct definite. The direct indefinite is formed by replacing the last vowel a අ, aa ආ or ə අ of the direct definite by -ek -එක්. Thus mahattea මහත්තයා, mahatteek මහත්තේක් ???; duwe දුවෙ, duwek දුවෙක්. The other forms of the indefinite are formed by adding the regular case ending with preceding -u- -උ - to the direct indefinite. The plural is not predictable from the direct definite, and will be given with lists of new nouns. A number of Class 5 nouns, including many kin and Western occupational terms, have plurals in -la -ල. Note that if the singular ends in (short) -a -අ, that -a -අ changes to ə අ before the -la -ල . [page 73] The Class 5 nouns that have occurred so far are: mahattea මහත්තයා ‘the gentleman, master’; pl. mahatturu මහත්තුරු or mahatteəla මහත්තෙඅල ??? lamea ලමයා ‘the child’; pl. lamay ලමය් maama මාම ‘the (maternal) uncle’; pl. maaməla මාමල taatta තාත්ත ‘the father’; pl. taattəla තාත්තල noona නෝන ‘the lady’; pl. noonəla නෝනල miniha මිනිහ ‘the man’; pl. minissu මිනිස්සු waDuwa වඩුව ‘the carpenter’; waDuwo වඩුවො duwə දුව ‘the daughter’; pl. duwəla දුවල or duula දූල. 2.2 The Respectful Indefinite Kinship terms specifying older relatives and certain nouns denoting superiors are respectful terms, and take a special indefinite. PRONOUNS 5.1 First Person Pronouns The direct and dative case forms of mamə මම ‘I’ and api අපි ‘we’ were given in Lesson 2. The complete set of case forms for these pronouns is as follows: Direct mam ə මම ‘ I’ api අපි ‘ we’ Dative maTə මට apiTə, apəTə අපිට , අපට Genitive magee, mage මගේ , මගෙ apee අපේ Instrumental mageŋ මගෙන් apeŋ අපෙන් Note that the forms for mamə මම are like those of a Class 5 noun, those of api අපි like a Class 2 noun. The two dative case forms of api අපි may be used interchangeably. 5.2 ohee ඔහේ The second person pronoun ohee ඔහේ which occurs in this lesson is used in some areas, areas, especially the South, to address equals or, as a polite form, to inferiors. However, the use of such pronouns may vary with the area of Sri Lanka. Thus ohee ඔහේ is not used in this way the up-country, and in some areas it may imply coldness, impersonality, or excessive distancing. Thus, it is better to avoid ohee ඔහේ as a second person pronoun, unless one knows the usage in the particular place of speaking. In many areas, oyaa ඔයා, pl. oyaala ඔයාල, is coming into use as a kind of general, informal, second person pronoun for acquaintances, but again, it is best to be sure before using it. On the whole, the best strategy is to follow the common Sri Lankan usage, and use (1) nothing (a “zero” pronoun), (2) the person’s name, or (3) a title if appropriate. Thus, one could ask: banDaTə heTǝ ennə puluwaŋ də? බන්ඩට හෙට එන්න පුලුවන් ද?, mahatteaTə heTə ennə puluwaŋ də? මහත්තයට හෙට එන්න පුලුවන් ද? or, if the context will allow, simply: heTə ennə puluwaŋ də? හෙට එන්න පුලුවන් ද? In any event, the use of pronouns is much less in Sinhala than in English, though doing without is sometimes a hard habit to acquire for English speakers. The case forms of ohee ඔහේ and oyaa ඔයා are those of a Class 5 noun, The plurals are oheela ඔහේල and oyaala ඔයාල. 6. gamə ගම The form game ගමෙ is used as an adverb of place equating with the English expression ‘at home’ when the latter means one’s native village or town, but not when it means ‘in one’s own house. There is a small estate. mee watt ə poDii. මේ වත්ත පොඩී . This estate is small. 8. ‘FROM...ON’ Note that in̆dələ ඉඳල may be used with time to mean ‘from … on’: maTə heTə in̆dəla ennə puluwəni. මට හෙට ඉඳල එන්න පුලුවනි . THE mee මේ SET AS ADVERBS OF PLACE The forms mee මේ, oya ඔය, ara අර, ee ඒ can be used adverbially referring to place: ‘here, there, over there, there (in question)’. This is mostly restricted to emphatic sentences, especially those with inn ə wa ඉන්නවා or tiyenəwa තියෙනවා which single out or identify something or someone: arə tiyenne wæDapələ. අර තියෙන්නෙ වැඩපල . THE SINHALESE WRITING SYSTEM II 12.1 More Consonant Symbols The following consonant symbols should be added to those already learned. (In giving new consonant symbols from now on, the inherent vowel will be symbolized simply as a, and the rules given in the preceding lesson will apply): බ bə ය yə ප pə න nə Note the difference between ය yə , ස s ə ; and න n ə , ත t ə . 12.2 Removing the Inherent Vowel The inherent vowel is removed by adding ් or } to a consonant symbol depending on the shape of that symbol: } is added to ට , බ, ම, and other consonants yet to be learned of that general (”circular”) shape: ට් T ම් m බ් b ඩ් D [page 80] ් is added to all other consonant symbols: ක් k ද් d ර් r ග් g ස් s ල් l ත් t ය් y ප් p න් n හ් h When the inherent vowel is removed, the consonant symbol represents the consonant alone. Thus if a word ends in a consonant, the symbol representing that consonant must have the inherent vowel removed: බස් bas (compare රස rasə) ගල් gal (compare ගල galə) Double consonants are indicated by writing a consonant symbol twice and removing the inherent vowel from the first one. The second retains the inherent vowel: වත්ත watte ගන්න gannə 12.3 Another rule for the inherent vowel may now be given: (5) Before a final consonant, a double consonant, or a consonant combination, the vowel -a- -අ- may occur but not the vowel - ə - -අ-. This implies that the inherent vowel of a consonant symbol that precedes another consonant symbol from which the inherent vowel is removed will always be -a- -අ - and not - ə - -අ -: බස් bas කඩවල් kaDəwal වත්තක් wattak නවත්තන්න nawattannə 12.4 The Symbol ා The symbol ා following a consonant symbol represents either a or aa instead of the inherent vowel as follows: 1. If the consonant symbol is at the beginning or in the middle of a word, the vowel represented by ා is aa ආ: පාර paarə පලාත palaatə රස්සාව rassaawe තානායම taanaayəmə 2. At the end of a word, ා will represent either a අ or aa ආ as follows: If the word has two syllables, and the first syllable has a short vowel followed by a single consonant, ා will represent aa ආ: [page 81] බලා balaa Otherwise, it will represent a අ, regardless of the number of syllables: යනවා yanewa මාමා maama තාත්තා taatta 3. When case or plural endings are added to Class 5 nouns spelled with a final ා , that sound that ා will represent the same it did when final. Note that this leads to exceptions to rule #1: තාත්තාට taattaTə මාමාට maamaTə මාමාලා maamalə 12.5 The verb kərənəwa is spelled කරනවා. This is an exception to the rule that a consonant symbol at the beginning of a word has the inherent vowel a අ, and is true for all forms of that verb: කරන්න kərənnə Exercises A. inanimate in agreement 3.1 tiyenawə තයනව - innəwa ඉනනව tiyenəwa තයනව and its various forms may be used only with inanimate objects. with animate subjects, the verb innəwa ඉනනව must be used in the same constructions: [page 74] bas tiyenawə. බස තයනව . there are buses. lamay innəwa. ලමය ඉනනව . there are children. sigəræt tiyenne kadee. සගරට තයනන කඩ . cigarettes are in the shop. lamea inne kadee. ලමය ඉනන කඩ . the child is in the shop. pawla පවල ‘the family’ is one of the few words that were mentioned in 3.1 as not falling neatly into the animate-inanimate classification. it is a regular class 2 noun, and hence inanimate in inflection, but it takes innəwa ඉනනව: magee pawlə inne gamee. මග පවල ඉනන ගම . my family is in the village. when such nouns occur, the fact that they are inanimate but take innəwa ඉනනව will be stated. 3.2 agreement of numerals numerals have different forms depending on whether they occur with animate or inanimate nouns. for the numbers 14 the forms are: inanimate definite inanimate indefinite animate definite animate indefinite one ekə එක ekak එකක ekkenaa එකකන ekkenek එකකනක two dekə දක dekak දකක denna දනන dennek දනනක three tunə තන tunak තනක tuŋ denaa තන දන tuŋ denek තන දනක four hatərə හතර hatərak හතරක hatərə denaa හතර දන hatərə denek හතර දනක the definite and indefinite of the animate numbers ‘two’, ‘three’ and ‘four’ are used with animate nouns in the same way that the equivalent forms of the inanimate numbers are used with inanimate nouns, as stated in lesson 4 (section 6). thus: sigeræt tunə metənə tiyenewa. සගරට තන මතන තයනව . the three cigarettes are here. lamay tu ŋ denaa iskoole innəawa . ලමය තන දන ඉසකල ඉනනඅව . the three children are in the school. sigəræt tunak metənə tiyenəwa. සගරට තනක මතන තයනව . there are three cigarettes here. lamay tun denek iskoole inn ə wa. ලමය තන දනක ඉසකල ඉනනව . there are three children in the school. sigəræt tunə tiyenne metənə. සගරට තන තයනන මතන . the three cigarettes are here. lamay tu ŋ denaa inne iskoole. ලමය තන දන ඉනන ඉසකල . the three children are in the school. [page 75] sigəræt tunak tiyenne metənə. සගරට තනක තයනන මතන . three cigarettes are here. lamay tuŋ denek inne iskoole. ලමය තන දනක ඉනන ඉසකල . three children are in the school. metənə tiyenne sig ə ræt tun ə . මතන තයනන සගරට තන . the three cigarettes are here. iskoole inne lamay tun denaa. ඉසකල ඉනන ලමය තන දන . the three children are in the school. metənə tiyenne sigəræt tunay. මතන තයනන සගරට තනය . there are only three cigar-ettes here. iskoole inne lamay tu ŋ denay. ඉසකල ඉනන ලමය තන දනය . there are only three children. in the school. the main use of the numeral ‘one’ is pronominal; that is, it is used without a dependent noun: hetə ekkenek w æ da karannə en ə wa. හට එකකනක වඩ කරනන එනව . tomorrow one person is coming to work. ehena ŋ matə ekak oon ə . එහනං මට එකක ඕන . in that case, i want one. 3.3 kiiyak කයක - kiidenek කදනක the animate equivalent of kiiyak කයක ‘how many’ is kiidenek කදනක. thus: h æ t æ pm ə kiiyak tiyenəwa də? හතපම කයක තයනව ද ? how many miles are there (is it)? lamay kiidenek innəwa də? ලමය කදනක ඉනනව ද ? how many children are there? similarly, in speaking of children: kiidenek iskoole yan ə wa də? කදනක ඉසකල යනව ද ? how many are going to school? but of buses: ki i yak kalutərətə yanawa də? කයක කලතරට යනව ද ? how many are going to kalutara? 4. new verbs balaagannəwa බලගනනව ‘tend, take care of, look after’ innewa ඉනනව ‘be’ (animate) kadee kərənəwa කඩ කරනව ‘tend shop, keep shop’ [page 76] 5. pronouns 5.1 first person pronouns the direct and dative case forms of mamə මම ‘i’ and api අප ‘we’ were given in lesson 2. the complete set of case forms for these pronouns is as follows: direct mam ə මම ‘ i’ api අප ‘ we’ dative matə මට apitə, apətə අපට , අපට genitive magee, mage මග , මග apee අප instrumental mageŋ මගන apeŋ අපන note that the forms for mamə මම are like those of a class 5 noun, those of api අප like a class 2 noun. the two dative case forms of api අප may be used interchangeably. 5.2 ohee ඔහ the second person pronoun ohee ඔහ which occurs in this lesson is used in some areas, areas, especially the south, to address equals or, as a polite form, to inferiors. however, the use of such pronouns may vary with the area of sri lanka. thus ohee ඔහ is not used in this way the up-country, and in some areas it may imply coldness, impersonality, or excessive distancing. thus, it is better to avoid ohee ඔහ as a second person pronoun, unless one knows the usage in the particular place of speaking. in many areas, oyaa ඔය, pl. oyaala ඔයල, is coming into use as a kind of general, informal, second person pronoun for acquaintances, but again, it is best to be sure before using it. on the whole, the best strategy is to follow the common sri lankan usage, and use (1) nothing (a “zero” pronoun), (2) the person’s name, or (3) a title if appropriate. thus, one could ask: bandatə hetǝ ennə puluwaŋ də? බනඩට හට එනන පලවන ද?, mahatteatə hetə ennə puluwaŋ də? මහතතයට හට එනන පලවන ද? or, if the context will allow, simply: hetə ennə puluwaŋ də? හට එනන පලවන ද? in any event, the use of pronouns is much less in sinhala than in english, though doing without is sometimes a hard habit to acquire for english speakers. the case forms of ohee ඔහ and oyaa ඔය are those of a class 5 noun, the plurals are oheela ඔහල and oyaala ඔයල. 6. gamə ගම the form game ගම is used as an adverb of place equating with the english expression ‘at home’ when the latter means one’s native village or town, but not when it means ‘in one’s own house. it thus serves the same function as a genitive of place. compare: [page 77] taatta inne gamə. තතත ඉනන ගම . father is at home (in his native village or town). taatta inne gamee. තතත ඉනන ගම . father is in the village (not necessarily his own) 7. assertion marker when adjectives like podi පඩ, ending in -i -ඉ, take the assertion marker, - y -ය , the pronunciation is - ii ඊ. podi wattak tiyenəwa. පඩ වතතක තයනව . there is a small estate. mee watt ə podii. ම වතත පඩ . this estate is small. 8. ‘from...on’ note that in̆dələ ඉඳල may be used with time to mean ‘from … on’: matə hetə in̆dəla ennə puluwəni. මට හට ඉඳල එනන පලවන . i can come from tomorrow on. udee in̆dələ mamə gamee inn ə wa. උද ඉඳල මම ගම ඉනනව . from the morning on, i am (will be) in the village. note also that where a particular time is mentioned, or made clear from the context, the present tense may have a future meaning, so that innəwa ඉනනව in the sentence above can be translated as ‘will be’. similarly: hetə udee mamə koləm̆bətə yanawa. හට උද මම කලඹට යනව . tomorrow morning i am going (or ‘will go’) to colombo 9. the mee ම set as adverbs of place the forms mee ම, oya ඔය, ara අර, ee ඒ can be used adverbially referring to place: ‘here, there, over there, there (in question)’. this is mostly restricted to emphatic sentences, especially those with inn ə wa ඉනනව or tiyenəwa තයනව which single out or identify something or someone: arə tiyenne wædapələ. අර තයනන වඩපල . there is the workshop (over there). ar ə enne tæksiyak. අර එනන ටකසයක . there comes a taxi. mee inne magee putaa. ම ඉනන මග පත . here is my son. or: this is my son here. 10. more negative formations 10.1 the form nææ න serves as the negative of inn ə wa ඉනනව ‘there is, here are’ as well as the negative of tiyenəwa තයනව ‘there is, there are’: mehee eloolu tiyenəwa. මහ එලල තයනව . there are vegetables here. mehee eloolu nææ. මහ එලල න . there are no (or 'aren't any) vegetables here. [page 78] mehee lamay inn ə wa. මහ ලමය ඉනනව . there are children here. mehee lamay n ææ . මහ ලමය න . there are no (or 'aren't any') children here. 10.2 the negative of a simple sentence with a verb other than inn ə wa ඉනනව or tiyenəwa තයනව is formed by changing the verb to the emphatic form and adding n ææ න: puttu denna iskoole yan ə wa. පතත දනන ඉසකල යනව . the two boys are going to school. puttu denna iskoole yanne n ææ . පතත දනන ඉසකල යනන න . the two boys don't go to school (or 'aren't going to school'). mamə anuraadəpuree in̆dəla kaar-ekak gannəwa. මම අනරදපර ඉඳල කර - එකක ගනනව . i'm taking a car from anuradhapura on. mamə anuraadəpuree in̆dəla kaar-ekak ganne nææ. මම අනරදපර ඉඳල කර - එකක ගනන න . i'm not taking a car from anuradhapura (on). 10.3 equational sentences with adjectives as predicate attributes may be negated by dropping the assertion marker and adding nææ න: ee minihage wædə hon̆day. ඒ මනහග වඩ හඳ‍ය . that man’s work is good ee minihage wædə hon̆də nææ. ඒ මනහග වද හඳ න . that man’s work isn’t good 11. næddə නදද any negative sentence formed with nææ න may be made into a question by adding də ද, but when də ද is added to nææ න, the result is nædda නදද. observe the following series: mehee eloolu tiyenəwa. මහ එලල තයනව . there are vegetables here. mehee eloolu tiyenəwa də? මහ එලල තයනව ද ? are there vegetables here? mehee eloolu nææ. මහ එලල න . there are no vegetables here. mehee eloolu næddə? මහ එලල නදද ? aren't there (any) vegetables here? mehee lamay inn ə wa. මහ ලමය ඉනනව . there are children here. mehee lamay innewa də? මහ ලමය ඉනනව ද ? are there children here? mehee lamay n ææ . මහ ලමය න . there are no children here. mehee lamay n æ ddə? මහ ලමය නදද ? aren't there (any) children here? [page 79] magee putaatə siigiriyətə yannə onnə. මග පතට සගරයට යනන ඔනන . my son wants to go to sigiriya. magee putaatə siigiriyətə yannə oonə də? මග පතට සගරයට යනන ඕන ද ? does my son want to go to sigiriya? magee putaatə siigiriyətə yanne onnə nææ. මග පතට සගරයට යනන ඔනන න . my son doesn't want to go to sigiriya. magee putaatə siigiriyətə yanne oonə næddə? මග පතට සගරයට යනන ඕන නදද ? doesn't my son want to go to sigiriya? mahattea kalutərətə kaar-ekak gannawa. මහතතය කලතරට කර - එකක ගනනව the gentleman is taking a car to kalutara. mahattea kalutərətə kaar-ekak gann ə wa d ə ? මහතතය කලතරට කර - එකක ගනනව ද ? is the gentleman taking a car to kalutara? mahattea kalutərətə kaar-ekak ganne n ææ . මහතතය කලතරට කර - එකක ගනන න . the gentleman isn't taking a car to kalutara. mahattea kalutərətə kaar-ekak ganne nædd ə ? මහතතය කලතරට කර - එකක ගනන නදද ? isn't the gentleman taking a car to kalutara? 12. the sinhalese writing system ii 12.1 more consonant symbols the following consonant symbols should be added to those already learned. (in giving new consonant symbols from now on, the inherent vowel will be symbolized simply as a, and the rules given in the preceding lesson will apply): බ bə ය yə ප pə න nə note the difference between ය yə , ස s ə ; and න n ə , ත t ə . 12.2 removing the inherent vowel the inherent vowel is removed by adding  or } to a consonant symbol depending on the shape of that symbol: } is added to ට , බ, ම, and other consonants yet to be learned of that general (”circular”) shape: ට t ම m බ b ඩ d [page 80]  is added to all other consonant symbols: ක k ද d ර r ග g ස s ල l ත t ය y ප p න n හ h when the inherent vowel is removed, the consonant symbol represents the consonant alone. thus if a word ends in a consonant, the symbol representing that consonant must have the inherent vowel removed: බස bas (compare රස rasə) ගල gal (compare ගල galə) double consonants are indicated by writing a consonant symbol twice and removing the inherent vowel from the first one. the second retains the inherent vowel: වතත watte ගනන gannə 12.3 another rule for the inherent vowel may now be given: (5) before a final consonant, a double consonant, or a consonant combination, the vowel -a- -අ- may occur but not the vowel - ə - -අ-. this implies that the inherent vowel of a consonant symbol that precedes another consonant symbol from which the inherent vowel is removed will always be -a- -අ - and not - ə - -අ -: බස bas කඩවල kadəwal වතතක wattak නවතතනන nawattannə 12.4 the symbol  the symbol  following a consonant symbol represents either a or aa instead of the inherent vowel as follows: 1. if the consonant symbol is at the beginning or in the middle of a word, the vowel represented by  is aa ආ: පර paarə පලත palaatə රසසව rassaawe තනයම taanaayəmə 2. at the end of a word,  will represent either a අ or aa ආ as follows: if the word has two syllables, and the first syllable has a short vowel followed by a single consonant,  will represent aa ආ: [page 81] බල balaa otherwise, it will represent a අ, regardless of the number of syllables: යනව yanewa මම maama තතත taatta 3. when case or plural endings are added to class 5 nouns spelled with a final  , that sound that  will represent the same it did when final. note that this leads to exceptions to rule #1: තතතට taattatə මමට maamatə මමල maamalə 12.5 the verb kərənəwa is spelled කරනව. this is an exception to the rule that a consonant symbol at the beginning of a word has the inherent vowel a අ, and is true for all forms of that verb: කරනන kərənnə exercises a. substitute orally: 1. a gentleman the child my son the two sons gamee innawa. two daughters three children two men four uncles 2. ennə puluwəni. tomorrow from tomorrow on from the morning on in the morning. tomorrow morning from the up-country by the colombo bus by a taxi from the village to my estate always to the workshop

title: Lesson 7
text: Lesson 7 Lesson 7 [page 86] Conversation: Hiring a Driver Mr. Perera, needing someone to drive and take care of his car while he is away for a time, speaks to Gunapala, a villager known to him. PERERA dæŋ gunəpaalə* gamə də? දැන් ගුනපාල ගම ද? Are you at home these days? GUNAPALA ow, mahattea. dæn wæDak nææ. ඔව්, මහත්තයා. දැන් වැඩක් නෑ. Yes, sir. I am not working now. oyə lamea ඔය ලමයා you (literally: 'the boy by you') eləwənəwa එලවනව drive nee də නේ ද isn't it oyə lameaTə kaar eləwannə puluwaŋ, nee dǝ? ඔය ලමයට කාර් එලවන්න පුලුවන්, නේ ද? You can drive a car (literally: 'drive cars) can't you? GUNAPALA puluwəni, mahattea පුලුවනි, මහත්තයා I can, sir. The nouns koliijiyə කොලීජිය and widyaale විද්‍යාලෙ may be roughly translated as ‘high school’, in that they refer to the school immediately preceding the university. The word iskoole ඉස්කෝලෙ generally refers to the elementary school, attended for seven years, approximately from age five to age twelve, and the koliijiyə කොලීජිය or widyaale විද්‍යාලෙ is attended for seven years after the iskoole ඉස්කෝලෙ. koliijiyə කොලීජිය is the normal colloquial term and widyaale is more literary, although it may be used in a proper name like wisaaka widyaale විසාක විද්‍යාලෙ, ‘Visaka High School’. 2. daruwa දරුව generally means ‘one’s own child’, lamea ලමයා, in addition to being a term of address (see below), means ‘child’ in general. 3. THE SINHALESE WRITING SYSTEM III 9.1 VOWELS FOLLOWING CONSONANTS Vowels other than the inherent vowel following consonants are written by adding symbols as follows: 9.11 æ ඇ, ææ ඈ The short vowel æ ඇ following a consonant is written by ැ after the consonant symbol: The long vowel ææ ඈ following a consonant is written by ෑ after the consonant symbol: [page 93] කෑ kææ සෑ sææ ටෑ Tææ දෑ dææ නෑ nææ The only exceptions are: æ ඇ and ææ ඈ following r ර් written with ැ and ෑ respectively joined to the tip of ර: රැ ræ රෑ ææ 9.12 i ඉ, ii ඊ The short vowel i ඉ following a consonant is written with ‍ ‍ ි over the consonant symbol: කි ki සි si ටි Ti දි di නි ni Note that ‍ ‍ි is joined to the tip of letters that have a shape like ට . Thus: බි bi, වි wi, ඩි Di, etc. The long vowel ii ඊ following a consonant is written with ී over the consonant symbol: කී ki i සී sii ටී Tii දී dii නී nii 9.13 u උ, uu ඌ u උ and uu ඌ after consonants are each written in three ways depend-ing upon the consonant as follows: 1. With ක, ග, ත, short u උ is written with } and long uu ඌ with } attached to the consonant symbol. Thus: කු ku ගු gu තු tu කූ kuu ගූ guu තූ tuu 2. With ර, u උ is written with ැ and uu ඌ with ෑ: රු ru රූ ruu Note that these are the same symbols used to write æ ඇ and ææ ඈ with other consonants, and ræ රැ and r ææ රෑ are distinguished from ru රු, ruu රූ by the way the symbols are added: ræ රැ, ræ æ රෑ, but රු ru , රූ ruu . 3. With all other consonants, short u උ is written with ු and long uu ඌ with attached ූ below the consonant as follows: ටු Tu මු mu සු su නු nu හු hu ටූ T uu මූ muu සූ suu නූ nuu හූ huu Note that when these symbols are added to ද the lower part of ද is not written: දු du දූ duu . [page 94] 9.2 CONSONANT COMBINATIONS Consonant combinations may be written in the same manner as double consonants, i.e. with the inherent vowel removed from the first consonant symbol: ක්ස ksə න්ද ndə Vowel symbols are added to the second consonant symbol: ක්සි ks ඉ න්දි nd ඉ Combinations with w Where the first consonant in a combination is w ව්, it will sometimes be treated like any other consonant and written ව් , but it will also be found written as wu වු, i.e. වු. For many words, these will be alternated. For example, pawl ə පව්ල may be written පව්ල or පවුල In other cases, however, one of these spellings will be regularly used, so that spellings of words with these combinations should be learned as they occur. 9.3 FINAL -y -ය් -y -ය් at the end of a word is written as yi යි, i.e. යි: ලමයි lamay Thus both the assertion marker and the conjunction y … y යි … යි written යි: තුනයි tunay රුපියලයි rupiyəlay රසයි rasay මාමයි මමයි maamay mamay Note that a preceding consonant symbol will have the inherent vowel a අ. 9.4 FINAL ea AND eak Class 5 nouns such as mahattea මහත්තයා, lamea ලමයා which end in -ee -ඒ are written as if they ended in - ə ya අයා. Hence: මහත්තයා mahattea ලමයා lamea The direct case indefinite of Class 4 nouns, -eak is written as -əyak: සුමානයක් sumaaneak කඩයත් kaDeak [page 99]

[page 87] kenek කනක a person etəkotə matə kaar-ekee wæde kərannə kenek oonə. එතකට මත කර-එක වඩ කරනන කනක ඕන. then i need a man to take care of (literally: ‘a person to work in the car’) my car for a week. gunapala ennə puluwəni, mahattea. එනන පලවන, මහතතය . i can come, sir. geniyənəwa ගනයනව take kaar-ekə yaapaneetə geniyənəwa da? කර- එක යපනට ගනයනව ද? are you taking the car to jaffna? perera nææ. kaar-ekə gamə tiyenne onnə. න. කර- එක ගම තයනන ඔනන. no. the car must remain at home. lamay iskoole yanne kaar-ekeŋ. ලමය ඉසකල යනන කර-එකන. the children go to school in the car. gunapala nee න isn’t it ehenaŋ yaapəneetə yanne mahattea witeray, nee. එහනන යපනට යනන මහතතය වතරය, න. then only you are going to jaffna, eh? perera ow, mamə witeray ඔව, මම වතරය yes. only me. noona නන the lady, wife daruwa දරව the child noonay daruwoy නනය දරවය the wife and children noonay daruwoy gamə nawətinəwa. නනය දරවය ගම නවතනව. (my) wife and children are staying at home. [page 88] gunapala lamay iskoole yanne koləm̆bə də? ලමය ඉසකල යනන කලඹ ද? are the children going to school in colombo? perera rooyəl koliijiyə රයල කලජය royal college ow, puttu denna yanne rooyəl koliijiyətə ඔව, පතත දනන යනන රයල කලජයට yes, (my) two boys go to royal college. wisaaka widyaale වසක වද‍යල visaka college duwə wisaaka widyaaletə. දව වසක වද‍යලට. (my) daughter (goes) to visaka college. gunapala ostin-ekə ඔසටන - එක the austin mahatteage kaar-ekə ostin-ekak, nee də? මහතතයග කර-එක ඔසටන-එකක, න ද? your car is an austin, isn't it? perera ow, gunepaalətə ostin eləwannə puluwaŋ, nee? ඔව, ගනපලත ඔසටන එලවනන පලවන, න? yes, you can drive austins, can't you? gunapala ow, puluwəni, mahattea. ඔව, පලවන, මහතතය. yes, i can, sir. perera wædətə enawa වඩට එනව come to work hetə udee in̆dəla wædətə ennə puluwaŋ də? හට උද ඉඳල වඩට එනන පලවන ද? can you come to work from tomorrow on? gunapala puluwəni. mahattea. පලවන. මහතතය. i can, sir. perera hon̆day, ehenan udee ennə. හඳ‍ය, එහනන උද එනන. fine. then come in the morning. * here the name is being used in direct address rather than a pronoun. see the note on ohee ඔහ in lesson 6, 5.2. [page 89] grammar 1. new nouns class 1 ostin-ekə ඔසටන- එක ‘the austin’ class 2 koliijiyə කලජය ‘the high school’; gen. koliijiye කලජය; pl. koliiji කලජ class 4 sumaane සමන ‘the week’; pl. sumaanə සමන yaapǝnee යපන ‘jaffna’; (no plural) widyaale වද‍යල ‘the (high) school’; pl. widyaalə වද‍යල class 5 daruwa දරව ‘the child, offspring’; pl. daruwo දරව noona නන ‘the wife, lady’; indefinite: noona kenek නන කනක; pl. noonəla නනල kenaa කන ‘the person’; (no plural) notes on new nouns 1. the nouns koliijiyə කලජය and widyaale වද‍යල may be roughly translated as ‘high school’, in that they refer to the school immediately preceding the university. the word iskoole ඉසකල generally refers to the elementary school, attended for seven years, approximately from age five to age twelve, and the koliijiyə කලජය or widyaale වද‍යල is attended for seven years after the iskoole ඉසකල. koliijiyə කලජය is the normal colloquial term and widyaale is more literary, although it may be used in a proper name like wisaaka widyaale වසක වද‍යල, ‘visaka high school’. 2. daruwa දරව generally means ‘one’s own child’, lamea ලමය, in addition to being a term of address (see below), means ‘child’ in general. 3. note that although wadee වඩ ‘the job, work’ has the regular dative form wædeete වඩට, the form for to work as in come to work’ is wædətə වඩට. 4. kenek කනක ‘a person’ is the same item that forms the respectful indefinite, but as ‘a person, someone’, it has no special connotations of respect. 2. new verbs eləwənəwa එලවනව ‘drive’ note: without kaar කර, eləwənəwa එලවනව generally means ‘drive’ as in english ‘drive out’ or ‘drive cattle.’ geniyənəwa ගනයනව ‘take (away) [page 90] 3. lamea ලමය the form lamea ලමය may be used referring to a person of either sex who is a younger relative or an unrelated younger person of inferior status. the term lamea ලමය or oya lamea ඔය ලමය may be used as an equivalent of english ‘you’ as follows: oyə lameatə kaar eləwannə puluwaŋ, nee dǝ? or ඔය ලමයත කර එලවනන පලවන , න ද ? lameatə kaar eləwannə puluwaŋ, nee dǝ? ලමයට කර එලවනන පලවන , න ද ? ‘you can drive a car, can’t you?’ note that the use of lamea ලමය in referring to a younger person is similar to the use of mahattea මහතතය in referring to an equal or superior, although oya ඔය is less frequently used with mahattea මහතතය. as we have seen (lesson 3), lamea ලමය may be used as a term. of direct address (calling someone), in which case oyǝ ඔය cannot be used with it. in this usage it very clearly implies that the speaker is is of superior status or that the one addressed very young, so that one should be cautious in using it. lamea mehee paləturu tiyenəwa də? ලමය මහ පලතර තයනව ද ? boy (or girl), is there fruit here? 4. ‘remain, stay’ innawa ඉනනව and tiyenəwa තයනව may mean ‘stay, remain’ as well as ‘be.’ sumaaneak yaapǝnee innə oonə සමනයක යපන ඉනන ඕන i must be (or ‘stay’) in jaffna a week. kaar-ekə gamə tiyennə oon ə . කර - එක ගම තයනන ඕන . the car must remain at home. 5. infinitives infinitives may modify verbs as well as nouns (lesson 5,4) and again the infinitíve precedes the word it modifies. balannə yannə. බලනන යනන . go to see (or ‘go see’). the modifying infinitive may have its own object preceding it: magee kaar-ekə eləwannə ennə. මග කර - එක එලවනන එනන . come (to) drive my car. mahattea waduwek balannə etentə yanawa. මහතතය වඩවක බලනන එතනට යනව . the master is going there to look for a carpenter. [page 91] 6. the conjunction y … y ය … ය in the sentence noonay daruwoy gamə nawətinəwa. නනය දරවය ගම නවතනව . (my) wife and children are staying home. the y ’s ය’s are not assertion but together form a conjunction ‘and’ joining noona නන ‘wife’ and daruwo දරව ‘children’. when two or more items are joined thus or in a longer series, y ය is added to each of them. when this y ය is added to an item ending in a vowel final ə අ or aa ආ become a අ, ee ඒ becomes e එ, and other vowels remain unchanged (as with the assertion marker, -i -ඉplus y ය is pronounced -ii -ඊ). the y ’s ය’s are added after any other endings that may be present. markers, keselgediy elooluy gannə onnə. කසලගඩය එලලය ගනන ඔනන . i want to buy bananas and vegetables. mamay, lameay, mahatteay koləm̆bətə yanawa. මමය , ලමයය , මහතතයය කලඹට යනව . i, the child, and the master are going to colombo. mamə sumaaneak kolam̆bay, siigiriyay, anuraadəpurey, yaapəney balannə yanəwa. මම සමනයක කලඹය, සගරයය, අනරදපරය , යපනය බලනන යනව. i am going for a week to see colombo, sigiriya, anuradhapura, and jaffna. mehee in̆dala kalutərətay, koləm̆bətay bas tiyenəwa. මහ ඉඳල කලතරටය, කලඹටය බස තයනව. there are buses from here to kalutara and colombo. mahatteagey, magey tikæt dekə matə denna. මහතතයගය , මගය ටකට දක මට දනන. give me the two tickets belong-ing to the master and me. (literally: the master's and my two tickets.) 7. sentences with an adverbial expression sentences in english that are composed of subject plus verb ‘to be’ plus an adverbial expression may have an equivalent in sinhalese either with or without the verb tiyenəwa තයනව or innawa ඉනනව. taatta gam ə . තතත ගම . father is at home. taatta gamə innəwa. තතත ගම ඉනනව . father is (stays, lives, remains) at home. taatta inne gam ə . තතත ඉනන ගම . father is at home. the sentence with the verb innəwa ඉනනව or tiyen ə w a තයනව indicates a more permanent state of things, and the verb may equate with an english ‘stay, remain, live’, whereas the sentence without the verb indicates a temporary state of affairs: [page 92] pal ə turu tiyenne all ə pu kadee. පලතර තයනන අලලප කඩ . fruit is in the next shop (where it generally is). paləturu allapu kadee. පලතර අලලප කඩ . fruit is in the next shop (at the moment, but this is not the ordinary state of affairs). 8. nee න and nee də න ද the forms nee න and nee də න ද may be added to the end of a sinhalese sentence to form a question where the expected answer is a confirmation of the original statement. it equates with the english ‘isn’t it, aren’t you, doesn’t he’, etc. mahattea kalutərətə yanawa, nee (də)? මහතතය කලතරට යනව , න ( ද )? the gentleman is going to kalutara, isn’t he? or you are going to kalutara, aren’t you? mehee æpəl tiyenəwa, nee (də)? මහ ඇපල තයනව , න ( ද )? there are apples here, aren’t there? mehee æpəl nææ, nee (də)? මහ ඇපල න , න ( ද )? there are no apples here, are there? mahattea eloolu ganne arə kadee, nee (də)? මහතතය එලල ගනන අර කඩ , න ( ද )? you buy vegetables at that shop, don’t you? or the gentleman buys vegetables at that shop, doesn't he? 9. the sinhalese writing system iii 9.1 vowels following consonants vowels other than the inherent vowel following consonants are written by adding symbols as follows: 9.11 æ ඇ, ææ ඈ the short vowel æ ඇ following a consonant is written by  after the consonant symbol: the long vowel ææ ඈ following a consonant is written by  after the consonant symbol: [page 93] ක kææ ස sææ ට tææ ද dææ න nææ the only exceptions are: æ ඇ and ææ ඈ following r ර written with  and  respectively joined to the tip of ර: ර ræ ර ææ 9.12 i ඉ, ii ඊ the short vowel i ඉ following a consonant is written with ‍ ‍  over the consonant symbol: ක ki ස si ට ti ද di න ni note that ‍ ‍ is joined to the tip of letters that have a shape like ට . thus: බ bi, ව wi, ඩ di, etc. the long vowel ii ඊ following a consonant is written with  over the consonant symbol: ක ki i ස sii ට tii ද dii න nii 9.13 u උ, uu ඌ u උ and uu ඌ after consonants are each written in three ways depend-ing upon the consonant as follows: 1. with ක, ග, ත, short u උ is written with } and long uu ඌ with } attached to the consonant symbol. thus: ක ku ග gu ත tu ක kuu ග guu ත tuu 2. with ර, u උ is written with  and uu ඌ with : ර ru ර ruu note that these are the same symbols used to write æ ඇ and ææ ඈ with other consonants, and ræ ර and r ææ ර are distinguished from ru ර, ruu ර by the way the symbols are added: ræ ර, ræ æ ර, but ර ru , ර ruu . 3. with all other consonants, short u උ is written with  and long uu ඌ with attached  below the consonant as follows: ට tu ම mu ස su න nu හ hu ට t uu ම muu ස suu න nuu හ huu note that when these symbols are added to ද the lower part of ද is not written: ද du ද duu . [page 94] 9.2 consonant combinations consonant combinations may be written in the same manner as double consonants, i.e. with the inherent vowel removed from the first consonant symbol: කස ksə නද ndə vowel symbols are added to the second consonant symbol: කස ks ඉ නද nd ඉ combinations with w where the first consonant in a combination is w ව, it will sometimes be treated like any other consonant and written ව , but it will also be found written as wu ව, i.e. ව. for many words, these will be alternated. for example, pawl ə පවල may be written පවල or පවල in other cases, however, one of these spellings will be regularly used, so that spellings of words with these combinations should be learned as they occur. 9.3 final -y -ය -y -ය at the end of a word is written as yi ය, i.e. ය: ලමය lamay thus both the assertion marker and the conjunction y … y ය … ය written ය: තනය tunay රපයලය rupiyəlay රසය rasay මමය මමය maamay mamay note that a preceding consonant symbol will have the inherent vowel a අ. 9.4 final ea and eak class 5 nouns such as mahattea මහතතය, lamea ලමය which end in -ee -ඒ are written as if they ended in - ə ya අය. hence: මහතතය mahattea ලමය lamea the direct case indefinite of class 4 nouns, -eak is written as -əyak: සමනයක sumaaneak කඩයත kadeak [page 99]

text: Lesson 8 Lesson 8 Conversation: The Mailman Comes John comes to the door to meet the mallman. JOHN adə අද today liyumə ලියුම the letter maTə adə liyuŋ nædda? මට අද ලියුම් නැද්ද? Aren't there any letters for me today?
