ADDITIONAL VOCABULARY DAYS OF THE WEEK Monday සඳුදා san̆duda Tuesday අඟහරුවාදා an̆gəharuwaada Wednesday බදාදා badaada Thursday බ්‍රහස්පතින්දා brahaspətinda Friday සිකුරාදා sikuraada Saturday සෙනසුරාදා senəsuraada Sunday ඉරිදා irida Grammar 1. NEW NOUNS Class 1 pooskaaT-ekə පෝස්කාට් -එක ‘the postcard’ Class 2 liyumə ලියුම ‘the letter’; gen, liyume ලියුමෙ; pl. liyuŋ ලියුම් rejisTər liyuma රෙජිස්ටර් ලියුම ‘the registered letter’; gen. rejistər liyume රෙජිස්තර් ලියුමෙ; pl. rejistər liyuŋ රෙජිස්තර් ලියුම් balaaporottuwə බලාපොරොත්තුව ‘the expectation’; gen. balaaporottuwe බලාපොරොත්තුවෙ; pl. balaaporottu බලාපොරොත්තු Class 3 adə අද ‘today’ (no plural) [page 102] Some nouns of Class 3 have a direct form in -a -අ instead of the usual - ə -අ. Like other nouns of this class, the genitive is identical with the direct (in the definite). The dative and the instrumental add -Tə -ට and - iŋ -ඉන් respectively to the direct, but unlike the of the other Class 3 noun, the -a -අ of these nouns is not lost before the - iŋ -ඉන් of the instrumental. The names of the days of the week are all of this type. Thus: Direct san̆duda සඳු දා ‘ Monday’ Dative san̆dudaTə සඳුදට Genitive san̆duda සඳුද Instrumental san̆dudain සඳුදඉන් These nouns do not have indefinite or plural forms Class 4 muddǝree මුද්දරේ ‘the stamp’; pl. muddərə මුද්දර paarsǝlee පාර්සලේ ‘the parcel’; pl. paarsal පාර්සල් (some people may have a plural paarsələ පාර්සල) salli සල්ලි ‘the money’, like eloolu එලෝලු and paləturu පලතුරු appears in the plural. 2. VERBS 2.1 NEW VERBS: geenǝwa ගේනව ‘bring’ nætiwenǝwa නැතිවෙනව ‘get lost, not exist’ bedənəwa බෙදනව ‘distribute, deliver (mail)’ 2.2 PASSIVE EQUIVALENT: ‘THEY DO’ bedənəwa බෙදනවා is a transitive verb, though bedanne nææ බෙදන්නෙ නෑ in the conversation is translated as the passive ‘aren’t delivered.’ Colloquial Sinhala has no real passive equivalent for the English passive (‘is done’, etc.). Instead, it commonly uses the ordinary verb with no subject expressed, as in this example. This is actually a kind of equivalent for English sentences with a non-specific ‘they’ as in ‘They (people in general) do that a lot now’. However, Sinhala never expresses the ‘they’ in this construction, but uses a “zero pronoun”. Thus: mee wæDəpəlee huŋ̆gak wæDə kərənəwa, nee da? මේ වැඩපලේ හුඟක් වැඩ කරනවා , නේ ද ? ‘They (people) do a lot of work in this workshop, don’t they.’ OR ‘A lot of work is done in this workshop, isn’t it?’ 3. ‘HAVE, HAS’ 3.1 The Sinhala construction for ‘have, has’ (possession) is formed with the dative case of the possessor, the direct case of the thing possessed, and the verb tiyenəwa තියෙනවා or innəwa ඉන්නවා. Thus, maTə sigəræt tiyenəwa. මට සිගරැත් තියෙනවා . I have cigarettes. Literally, this is To/for me there are cigarettes’. mahatteaTə kaar-ekak tiyenəwa මහත්තයට කාර් - එකක් තියෙනවා The gentleman has a car. arə noonaTə putek innəwa. අර නෝනට පුතෙක් ඉන්නවා . That lady has a son. [page 103] Notice that the choice of inn ə wa ඉන්නවා or tiyenəwa තියෙනවා depends upon whether the thing possessed is animate or inanimate, regardless of the possessor. As with other constructions with these verbs, the negative is næ æ නෑ substituted for the simple form: maTə sigəræT n ææ . මට සිගරැට් නෑ . I don't have cigarettes. mahatteaTə kaar-ekak nææ. මහත්තයට කාර් - එකක් නෑ . The gentleman does not have a car. arə noonaTə putek nææ. අර නෝනට පුතෙක් නෑ . That lady doesn't have a son. This ‘have’ construction may have its literal meaning also, depending upon context, so that maTə liyuŋ tiyenawa. මට ලියුම් තියෙනව . maTə liyuŋ nææ. මට ලියුම් නෑ . may mean either ‘I have letters’, ‘I don’t have letters’, or ‘There are letters for me’, ‘There are no letters for me.’ Hence, maTə adə liyun nædda? මට අද ලියුම් නැද්ද ? Aren't there any letters for me today? may also mean ‘Haven’t I any letters today?’ 3.2 Instead of the construction with the dative case and tiyenəwa තියෙනවා or innawa ඉන්නවා, Sinhalese may use the construction with la ŋ̆ ge ලඟ that was met in Lesson 2. This is likely to equate with an English ‘with one’, ‘on one’, ‘at my place’, ‘here’: mamə la ŋ̆ ga sigəræT tiyen ə w a . මම ලඟ සිගරැට් තියෙනවා . I have cigarettes on me. api la ŋ̆ g ə hon̆də suruTTu tiyen ə w a . අපි ලඟ හොඳ සුරුට්ටු තියෙනවා . We have good cigarettes here (i.e. with us, at our place, at our shop). 4. æti ඇති ‘MIGHT BE, MIGHT HAVE’ There are in Sinhalese constructions identical to those in Section 3, or to ‘there is, there are’, constructions, but with æti ඇති replacing innəwa ඉන්නවා, tiyenəwa තියෙනවා. These constructions imply ‘might be, might have, but with the implication that the situation discussed is fairly likely to be true or to come about. [page 104] saməharəwiTə heTə æti. සමහරවිට හෙට ඇති . Perhaps there might be some tomorrow. dæ ŋ bas æti. දැන් බස් ඇති . There might be buses now. maTə sigəræT æti. මට සිගරැට් ඇති . I might have cigarettes. mahatteaTə kaar-ekak æti. මහත්තයට කාර් - එකක් ඇති . The gentleman might have a car. arə noonaTə putek æti. අර නෝනට පුතෙක් ඇති . That lady might have a son. api la ŋ̆ ge sigeræT æti. අපි ලඟෙ සිගෙරැට් ඇති . We might have cigarettes (on us). 5. THE VERBAL ADJECTIVE FORM OF THE VERB A new verb form occurs in Conversation 8—the VERBAL ADJECTIVE. This is made by adding -nə -න to the stem of the verb. Stem-final -ə - අ is not changed before this ending, although it becomes -a- -අ- before the -nnə -න්න of the infinitive. This means that the verbal adjective will differ from the infinitive in these ways: 1. The verbal adjective adds -nə -න and the infinitive adds -nnə -න්න. 2. Stem-final -ə- -අ - is not changed before the -nə -න ending, but it becomes a අ before -nnə -න්න . However, note that when the verb stem ends in -n- -න්-, the verbal adjective and the infinitive will be identical. Examples: Verb Stem Infinitive Verbal Adjective enəwa එනවා e- එ - ennə එන්න enə එන yanəwa යනවා ya- ය - yannə යන්න yanə යන bonəwa බොනවා bo- බො - bonnə බොන්න bonə බොන tiyenəwa තියෙනවා tiye- තියෙ - tiyennə තියෙන්න tiyenə තියෙන balənəwa බලනවා balə බල balannə බලන්න balənə බලන kərənəwa කරනවා kərə කර kərannə කරන්න kərənə කරන innəwa ඉන්නවා in- ඉන් - innə ඉන්න innə ඉන්න gannəwa ගන්නවා gan- ගන් - gannə ගන්න gannə ගන්න 6. PRESENT TEMPORAL GERUND Sinhalese forms ‘when’ clauses by using the verbal adjective with -koTə -කොට added to it: The verbal adjective plus koTə is referred to as the PRESENT TEMPORAL GERUND. sanduda enəkoTə rupiyal pahee muddəreak geennə. සන්දුද එනකොට රුපියල් පහේ මුද්දරයක් ගේන්න . When you come on Monday, bring a five-rupee stamp. [page 105] siigiriyəTə yanəkoTə kaar-ekak gannə. සීගිරියට යනකොට කාර් - එකක් ගන්න . When you go to Sigiriya, take a car. bas-ekee innəkoTə suruTTu bonnə epaa. බස් - එකේ ඉන්නකොට සුරුට්ටු බොන්න එපා . Don't smoke cigars when (you are) on the bus. mahattea siigiriyəTə yanəkoTə mamə kaar-ekə eləwənəwa. මහත්තයා සීගිරියට යනකොට මම කාර් - එක එලවනවා . When the master goes to Sigiriya. I drive the car. 7. THE CONSTRUCTION -y … -у -යි … -යි When the conjunction -y … -у -යි … -යි is added to a word that ends in a consonant, -u- -උ- is added before the -y -යි. putekuy duwekuy පුතෙකු යි දුවෙකු යි a son and a daughter bas-ekǝkuy Tæksiyəkuy බස් - එකකුයි ටැක්සියකුයි a bus and a taxi When the word to which the -uy -උයි is added to a direct indefinite Class 4 noun, the result is the same as when a case ending is added. That is, -ea -අයා is replaced by -ee- -ඒ- or -e- -එ-. Thus: kaDeak කඩයක් kaDeekəTə කඩේකට kaDeekuy කඩේකුය් iskooleak ඉස්කෝලයක් iskoolekəTə ඉස්කෝලෙකට iskoolekuy ඉස්කෝලෙකුය් When a word to which -uy -උයි is added ends in - ŋ -න්, the ŋ න් generally becomes n න්. Thus liyu ŋ ලියුන් ‘letters’ but liyunuy pooskaTuy ලියුනුයි පෝස්කටුයි, ‘letters and postcards’. The -n- -න්- is also inserted when -y -ය් is added to lamay ලමයි, the plural of lamea ලමයා, and the result is lamayinuy ලමයිනුයි. } 8. witərə ‘ONLY’ AND witəray ‘ABOUT’ witərə 'only' contrasts with witərə 'about' in that witərə 'only' will appear in the indefinite form when non-final in a sentence, and will take the assertion marker -y when final in an emphatic sentence, whereas witərə 'about almost always appears without any ending in both situations. Both forms commonly occur with quantity phrases, and then follow the entire phrase. The noun or numeral preceding either witərə 'only or witərə'about may be definite, indefinite or plural and in any case that the construction requires: mamə sumaaneak witərə wæDə kərənəwa. I am working for about a week. mamə sumaaneak witərak wæDə kərənəwa. I am working for only a week. mamə koləm̆bə yanne heTǝ witerǝ. It's about tomorrow that I'm going to Colombo (i.e. tomorrow or so'). [page 106] mamə koləm̆bə yanne heTə witəray. It's only tomorrow that I'm going to Colombo. keselge Di pahak witərə geenne. Bring about five bananas. keselge Di pahak witərak geenna. Bring only five bananas. mahattea koləm̆bəTə witere bas-eken yanawa. The master is going about (as far as) Colombo by bus. mahattea koləm̆bəTə witərak bas-eken yanawa. The master is going only to Colombo by bus. 9. NUMERALS 9.1 The numeral 5 has the following forms: Definite Inanimate Animate Indefinite paha pas denaa pahak pas denek 9.2 Case Forms of Numerals Numerals have forms for the same four cases as nouns in both the definite and indefinite. They have no plural forms. The inanimate forms of the first five numerals have the forms. of Class 2 nouns, although paha ends in a rather than a. Thus: Definite Indefinite Direct eka ekak Dative ekaTa ekakəTə Genitive ekəkə Instrumental eken ekakin As with other Class 2 nouns, the genitive definite must be given for each: eka 'one' deka 'two' tune 'three' hatere 'four' paha 'five' Genitive dekee tunee hatare pahee [page 107] The animate forms of all numerals have the forms of Class 5 nouns: Definite Indefinite Direct ekkenaa 'one' Dative ekkenaaTe ekkenekuTa Genitive ekkenaage ekkenekuge Instrumental ekkenaagen ekkenekugen Direct tun denaa 'three' tun denek Dative tun denaaTa tun denekuTə Genitive tun denaage tun denekuge Instrumental tun denaagen tun denekugen 9.2 Use of the Genitive Definite of Numerals The genitive definite form of numerals is used in the construc-tion 'a five-rupee stamp'; literally, 'a stamp of five rupees'. rupiyal pahee muddereak sate hatere muddareak sate tunee keselgeDi næddə? sata dekee suruTTu hon̆də a five-rupee stamp a four-cent stamp No three-cent bananas? Two-cent cigars are not good. In similar constructions with 'one cent', 'one rupee', etc., the number 'one' is not used, but the word for 'cent' or 'rupee! is in the genitive definite: rupiyelee Tik-T-ekak denne. Give me a (one) rupee ticket. satee muddǝreak onnə. I want a (one) cent stamp. 10. THE SINHALESE WRITING SYSTEM 10.1 More Vowel Symbols 10.11 e, ee Short e following a consonant is written with the symbol G placed before the consonant symbol: GC də me ye se Tə ne With consonant combinations or double consonants, that is, where the first of two consonant symbols has the inherent vowel removed, a following e is written with s before the second: *The n of tun is commonly pronounced n before denaa. [page 108] නන nne යන්නෙ yanne tte පැත්තෙ patte Long ee is written by placing before the consonant symbol and also adding the symbol used to remove the inherent vowel: G මේ dee see mee Tee kee Dee 10.12 0,00 Short o after a consonant is written by placing before and after the consonant symbol. Note that these are the same symbols used to write e and aa, and that it is their combination that indicates o ko po මො mo ro ho bo to the symbol. Long oo is written by writing o and adding Note that this is the same symbol used for removing the inherent vowel from many consonant symbols as well as for writing long ee but that it is placed differently: පෝ hoo poo noo සො SOO රෝ roo මෝ moo 10.2 More Consonant Symbols The following consonant symbols should be added to those already learned: 10.21 อ ca ja 10.22 f fis commonly written by using the symbol for p,, preceded by the letter 'f'. The combination fo is treated like a single consonant symbol in adding vowels: fee ගෝල් Ĵස් gool fees Occasionally the 'f' will be omitted so that spelling such as cai cơ may be met with. Since f is rare in Sinhalese and occurs mostly in words borrowed from English, such spellings [page 109] will cause no special difficulty. 10.23 r Combinations ras the second consonant in a consonant combination is gener-ally written with under the first consonant symbol. The result is treated like a single symbol when vowels are added: 3 trii ත්‍රී රෝස් trii roos Such combinations may also be found written with the customary r symbol 6, i.e. đồ cóď, but the writing with is more common. 10.24 y Combinations y as the second consonant in a consonant combination is gener-ally written with the symbol Note that the symbol for remov-ing the inherent vowel is not used on the first consonant symbol and that the combination is treated as a single consonant symbol when vowels are added: 232 dyaa විද්‍යාලෙ vidyaale 10.3 The Inherent Vowel With i.e. by a plain consonant symbol When preceded by a, a, or aa, or one with, will have the inherent vowel a regardless of position within the word: මහත්තයා mahattea පහ paha Exercises A. [page 101] john epaa, matə adə muddərə tiyenəwඅ. එප, මට අද මදදර තයනවඅ. no. i have stamps today. san̆duda සඳද monday enakotə එනකට when coming geenəwa ගනව bring san̆duda enakotə rupiyal pahee muddəreak geennə. සඳද එනකට රපයල පහ මදදරයක ගනන. when (you) come on monday, bring a five-rupee stamp. salli සලල money mennə salli. මනන සලල. here is the money. mailman nææ. salli san̆duda gannə puluwəni. න. සලල සඳද ගනන පලවන. no, (i) can get the money on monday. additional vocabulary days of the week monday සඳද san̆duda tuesday අඟහරවද an̆gəharuwaada wednesday බදද badaada thursday බ‍රහසපතනද brahaspətinda friday සකරද sikuraada saturday සනසරද senəsuraada sunday ඉරද irida grammar 1. new nouns class 1 pooskaat-ekə පසකට -එක ‘the postcard’ class 2 liyumə ලයම ‘the letter’; gen, liyume ලයම; pl. liyuŋ ලයම rejistər liyuma රජසටර ලයම ‘the registered letter’; gen. rejistər liyume රජසතර ලයම; pl. rejistər liyuŋ රජසතර ලයම balaaporottuwə බලපරතතව ‘the expectation’; gen. balaaporottuwe බලපරතතව; pl. balaaporottu බලපරතත class 3 adə අද ‘today’ (no plural) [page 102] some nouns of class 3 have a direct form in -a -අ instead of the usual - ə -අ. like other nouns of this class, the genitive is identical with the direct (in the definite). the dative and the instrumental add -tə -ට and - iŋ -ඉන respectively to the direct, but unlike the of the other class 3 noun, the -a -අ of these nouns is not lost before the - iŋ -ඉන of the instrumental. the names of the days of the week are all of this type. thus: direct san̆duda සඳ ද ‘ monday’ dative san̆dudatə සඳදට genitive san̆duda සඳද instrumental san̆dudain සඳදඉන these nouns do not have indefinite or plural forms class 4 muddǝree මදදර ‘the stamp’; pl. muddərə මදදර paarsǝlee පරසල ‘the parcel’; pl. paarsal පරසල (some people may have a plural paarsələ පරසල) salli සලල ‘the money’, like eloolu එලල and paləturu පලතර appears in the plural. 2. verbs 2.1 new verbs: geenǝwa ගනව ‘bring’ nætiwenǝwa නතවනව ‘get lost, not exist’ bedənəwa බදනව ‘distribute, deliver (mail)’ 2.2 passive equivalent: ‘they do’ bedənəwa බදනව is a transitive verb, though bedanne nææ බදනන න in the conversation is translated as the passive ‘aren’t delivered.’ colloquial sinhala has no real passive equivalent for the english passive (‘is done’, etc.). instead, it commonly uses the ordinary verb with no subject expressed, as in this example. this is actually a kind of equivalent for english sentences with a non-specific ‘they’ as in ‘they (people in general) do that a lot now’. however, sinhala never expresses the ‘they’ in this construction, but uses a “zero pronoun”. thus: mee wædəpəlee huŋ̆gak wædə kərənəwa, nee da? ම වඩපල හඟක වඩ කරනව , න ද ? ‘they (people) do a lot of work in this workshop, don’t they.’ or ‘a lot of work is done in this workshop, isn’t it?’ 3. ‘have, has’ 3.1 the sinhala construction for ‘have, has’ (possession) is formed with the dative case of the possessor, the direct case of the thing possessed, and the verb tiyenəwa තයනව or innəwa ඉනනව. thus, matə sigəræt tiyenəwa. මට සගරත තයනව . i have cigarettes. literally, this is to/for me there are cigarettes’. mahatteatə kaar-ekak tiyenəwa මහතතයට කර - එකක තයනව the gentleman has a car. arə noonatə putek innəwa. අර නනට පතක ඉනනව . that lady has a son. [page 103] notice that the choice of inn ə wa ඉනනව or tiyenəwa තයනව depends upon whether the thing possessed is animate or inanimate, regardless of the possessor. as with other constructions with these verbs, the negative is næ æ න substituted for the simple form: matə sigəræt n ææ . මට සගරට න . i don't have cigarettes. mahatteatə kaar-ekak nææ. මහතතයට කර - එකක න . the gentleman does not have a car. arə noonatə putek nææ. අර නනට පතක න . that lady doesn't have a son. this ‘have’ construction may have its literal meaning also, depending upon context, so that matə liyuŋ tiyenawa. මට ලයම තයනව . matə liyuŋ nææ. මට ලයම න . may mean either ‘i have letters’, ‘i don’t have letters’, or ‘there are letters for me’, ‘there are no letters for me.’ hence, matə adə liyun nædda? මට අද ලයම නදද ? aren't there any letters for me today? may also mean ‘haven’t i any letters today?’ 3.2 instead of the construction with the dative case and tiyenəwa තයනව or innawa ඉනනව, sinhalese may use the construction with la ŋ̆ ge ලඟ that was met in lesson 2. this is likely to equate with an english ‘with one’, ‘on one’, ‘at my place’, ‘here’: mamə la ŋ̆ ga sigəræt tiyen ə w a . මම ලඟ සගරට තයනව . i have cigarettes on me. api la ŋ̆ g ə hon̆də suruttu tiyen ə w a . අප ලඟ හඳ සරටට තයනව . we have good cigarettes here (i.e. with us, at our place, at our shop). 4. æti ඇත ‘might be, might have’ there are in sinhalese constructions identical to those in section 3, or to ‘there is, there are’, constructions, but with æti ඇත replacing innəwa ඉනනව, tiyenəwa තයනව. these constructions imply ‘might be, might have, but with the implication that the situation discussed is fairly likely to be true or to come about. [page 104] saməharəwitə hetə æti. සමහරවට හට ඇත . perhaps there might be some tomorrow. dæ ŋ bas æti. දන බස ඇත . there might be buses now. matə sigəræt æti. මට සගරට ඇත . i might have cigarettes. mahatteatə kaar-ekak æti. මහතතයට කර - එකක ඇත . the gentleman might have a car. arə noonatə putek æti. අර නනට පතක ඇත . that lady might have a son. api la ŋ̆ ge sigeræt æti. අප ලඟ සගරට ඇත . we might have cigarettes (on us). 5. the verbal adjective form of the verb a new verb form occurs in conversation 8—the verbal adjective. this is made by adding -nə -න to the stem of the verb. stem-final -ə - අ is not changed before this ending, although it becomes -a- -අ- before the -nnə -නන of the infinitive. this means that the verbal adjective will differ from the infinitive in these ways: 1. the verbal adjective adds -nə -න and the infinitive adds -nnə -නන. 2. stem-final -ə- -අ - is not changed before the -nə -න ending, but it becomes a අ before -nnə -නන . however, note that when the verb stem ends in -n- -න-, the verbal adjective and the infinitive will be identical. examples: verb stem infinitive verbal adjective enəwa එනව e- එ - ennə එනන enə එන yanəwa යනව ya- ය - yannə යනන yanə යන bonəwa බනව bo- බ - bonnə බනන bonə බන tiyenəwa තයනව tiye- තය - tiyennə තයනන tiyenə තයන balənəwa බලනව balə බල balannə බලනන balənə බලන kərənəwa කරනව kərə කර kərannə කරනන kərənə කරන innəwa ඉනනව in- ඉන - innə ඉනන innə ඉනන gannəwa ගනනව gan- ගන - gannə ගනන gannə ගනන 6. present temporal gerund sinhalese forms ‘when’ clauses by using the verbal adjective with -kotə -කට added to it: the verbal adjective plus kotə is referred to as the present temporal gerund. sanduda enəkotə rupiyal pahee muddəreak geennə. සනදද එනකට රපයල පහ මදදරයක ගනන . when you come on monday, bring a five-rupee stamp. [page 105] siigiriyətə yanəkotə kaar-ekak gannə. සගරයට යනකට කර - එකක ගනන . when you go to sigiriya, take a car. bas-ekee innəkotə suruttu bonnə epaa. බස - එක ඉනනකට සරටට බනන එප . don't smoke cigars when (you are) on the bus. mahattea siigiriyətə yanəkotə mamə kaar-ekə eləwənəwa. මහතතය සගරයට යනකට මම කර - එක එලවනව . when the master goes to sigiriya. i drive the car. 7. the construction -y … -у -ය … -ය when the conjunction -y … -у -ය … -ය is added to a word that ends in a consonant, -u- -උ- is added before the -y -ය. putekuy duwekuy පතක ය දවක ය a son and a daughter bas-ekǝkuy tæksiyəkuy බස - එකකය ටකසයකය a bus and a taxi when the word to which the -uy -උය is added to a direct indefinite class 4 noun, the result is the same as when a case ending is added. that is, -ea -අය is replaced by -ee- -ඒ- or -e- -එ-. thus: kadeak කඩයක kadeekətə කඩකට kadeekuy කඩකය iskooleak ඉසකලයක iskoolekətə ඉසකලකට iskoolekuy ඉසකලකය when a word to which -uy -උය is added ends in - ŋ -න, the ŋ න generally becomes n න. thus liyu ŋ ලයන ‘letters’ but liyunuy pooskatuy ලයනය පසකටය, ‘letters and postcards’. the -n- -න- is also inserted when -y -ය is added to lamay ලමය, the plural of lamea ලමය, and the result is lamayinuy ලමයනය. } 8. witərə ‘only’ and witəray ‘about’ witərə 'only' contrasts with witərə 'about' in that witərə 'only' will appear in the indefinite form when non-final in a sentence, and will take the assertion marker -y when final in an emphatic sentence, whereas witərə 'about almost always appears without any ending in both situations. both forms commonly occur with quantity phrases, and then follow the entire phrase. the noun or numeral preceding either witərə 'only or witərə'about may be definite, indefinite or plural and in any case that the construction requires: mamə sumaaneak witərə wædə kərənəwa. i am working for about a week. mamə sumaaneak witərak wædə kərənəwa. i am working for only a week. mamə koləm̆bə yanne hetǝ witerǝ. it's about tomorrow that i'm going to colombo (i.e. tomorrow or so'). [page 106] mamə koləm̆bə yanne hetə witəray. it's only tomorrow that i'm going to colombo. keselge di pahak witərə geenne. bring about five bananas. keselge di pahak witərak geenna. bring only five bananas. mahattea koləm̆bətə witere bas-eken yanawa. the master is going about (as far as) colombo by bus. mahattea koləm̆bətə witərak bas-eken yanawa. the master is going only to colombo by bus. 9. numerals 9.1 the numeral 5 has the following forms: definite inanimate animate indefinite paha pas denaa pahak pas denek 9.2 case forms of numerals numerals have forms for the same four cases as nouns in both the definite and indefinite. they have no plural forms. the inanimate forms of the first five numerals have the forms. of class 2 nouns, although paha ends in a rather than a. thus: definite indefinite direct eka ekak dative ekata ekakətə genitive ekəkə instrumental eken ekakin as with other class 2 nouns, the genitive definite must be given for each: eka 'one' deka 'two' tune 'three' hatere 'four' paha 'five' genitive dekee tunee hatare pahee [page 107] the animate forms of all numerals have the forms of class 5 nouns: definite indefinite direct ekkenaa 'one' dative ekkenaate ekkenekuta genitive ekkenaage ekkenekuge instrumental ekkenaagen ekkenekugen direct tun denaa 'three' tun denek dative tun denaata tun denekutə genitive tun denaage tun denekuge instrumental tun denaagen tun denekugen 9.2 use of the genitive definite of numerals the genitive definite form of numerals is used in the construc-tion 'a five-rupee stamp'; literally, 'a stamp of five rupees'. rupiyal pahee muddereak sate hatere muddareak sate tunee keselgedi næddə? sata dekee suruttu hon̆də a five-rupee stamp a four-cent stamp no three-cent bananas? two-cent cigars are not good. in similar constructions with 'one cent', 'one rupee', etc., the number 'one' is not used, but the word for 'cent' or 'rupee! is in the genitive definite: rupiyelee tik-t-ekak denne. give me a (one) rupee ticket. satee muddǝreak onnə. i want a (one) cent stamp. 10. the sinhalese writing system 10.1 more vowel symbols 10.11 e, ee short e following a consonant is written with the symbol g placed before the consonant symbol: gc də me ye se tə ne with consonant combinations or double consonants, that is, where the first of two consonant symbols has the inherent vowel removed, a following e is written with s before the second: *the n of tun is commonly pronounced n before denaa. text: Lesson 9 Lesson 9 [page 119] Conversation: Borrowing a Book } Mr. Wirasekara is has met in town. remembers that he chatting with his friend Mr. Perera, whom he As the conversation progresses, Mr. Wirasekara had intended to borrow a novel from his friend. MR. WIRASEKARA nawekataawe the novel pote the book nawekataa pota the novel (book) ohee lange hon̆də nawekataa pot nædde? Don't you have any good novels? MR. PERERA potak denna puluwəni. I can give you a book. hawəsə the afternoon gedərə the house, home hawese apee gedərəTə ennə puluwan də? Can you come to (my) house in the afternoon? WIRASEKARA maTə dæn kiyəwanna pot mokut na09. I haven't any books to read now. ee nisaa therefore, because of that ee nisaa enne onnə. Therefore, I'd better come. PERERA mamə lange huŋ̆gak tiyenne ingirisi nawəkataa pot. Mostly, I have English novels. [page 120] WIRASEKARA eekeTə kamak nae. That doesn't matter. wenawa become parakku wenewa get late ohee gedərə yanə koTə parakku wenawa da? Will it be (getting) late when you get home? PERERA пaвеe. mama dan yanawa. No. I'm going now. WIRASEKARA maTə dan ennə puluwəni. I can go now. kamak næddə? Is that all right? PERERA Nasce. enna. No. Come. leesi easy eekə leesiy. That will be easy. toora gannawa choose, select honda potak toora gannə (You) can choose a good book. puluwani. at once, right now, ikmənəTə quickly ikmənəTə enna. Come right now. mamə adə yanne bas-eken. Today, I'm going by bus. WIRASEKARA Name magee kaar-ekə tiyenəwa. No. I have my car. (Literally: There is my car'.) enne. kaar-eken yannə puluwəni. Come. We can go by car. [page 121] PERERA ehemə də? Is that so? eeka hon̆day. That's fine. gærej-eke the garage ade magee kaar-eke gærej-ekee. Today my car is in the garage. WIRASEKARA repeaar-ekə the repair ay, repeaar-ekak da? Why? Is it being repaired? (Literally: repair?') 'Why, a PERERA səəwis kərənəwa service (a car) Maare. səəwis kərənəwa. No. They are servicing it. aapahu back aapahu gannə puluwan hawese. I can get it back in the after-noon. WIRASEKARA oheeTə tiyenne osTin-ekak, nee? You have an Austin, haven't you? PERERA ow. Yes. WIRASEKARA ehenan in that case, then, if that is so wooker gærej-eka the Walker Garage ehenan səəwis kəranne wookər gærej-ekee. In that case it's being ser-viced at the Walker Garage. [page 122] PERERA ow. Yes. WIRASEKARA PERERA dæn yanəkətə gærej-ekee nawatinnə oonə də? Do you want to stop at the garage when we go now? yamu let's go naene, dæn gedərə yamu. No. Let's go home now. oheeTə parakku wenawa, nee? You'll be late, won't you? passe later maTə passe ennə puluwani. I can come (back) later. Grammar 1. NEW NOUNS Class 1 gærej-eke ‘the garage’ repeaar-eka ‘the repair’ Class 2 nawəkataawa ‘the novel’; gen. nawakataawe; pl. nawəkataa pota ‘the book’; gen. potee; pl. pot Either nawakataawə or nawəkataa pote (literally: the novel-book’) may be used as the equivalent of English ‘the novel’. ingirisi ‘English’ has noe in the direct singular, but has the other case forms of a Class 2 noun: Dative: ingirisiyəTə; Genitive: ingirisiyen; Instrumental: ingirisiyen, (no plural). Like “English,” ingirisi may be used as an adjective in phrases like ingirisi pot ‘English books. Some people have ingriisi instead. [page 123] Class 3 adə ‘today’; (no plural) hawəsə ‘the afternoon (roughly from 2 p.m. to 6 p.m.) gedərə ‘the house, home’; pl. gedərəwal The genitive form gedərə is the usual equivalent of English ‘at home in the sense ‘in one’s own house’ as opposed to game ‘at home’ in one’s own or native village. 2. NEW VERBS kiyəwənəwa ‘read’ toora gannawa ‘choose, select’ səəwis kərənəwa ‘service (a car)’ wenawa ‘become’ parakku wenawa ‘get late, be late’ 3. parakku wenawa parakku wenawa with no subject expressed has the sense 'it's getting late. With a subject in the direct case it may imply either voluntary or unavoidable lateness: mame parakku wenawa. I'll be late (because I must do something). bas-eka parakku wenewa. The bus is late. With the equivalent of the English subject in the dative case, parakku wenǝwa 1mplies that one will be late for something if he does or does not do a given thing, and that the lateness is thus avoidable: oheeTə parakku wenawa, nee? You'll be late, won't you (if we stop at the garage on the way)? maTə parakku wenawa I'll be late (if I stay here). 4. IDIOMS WITH kamak The English equiva-kamak name is a common idiomatic expression. lent is usually something like 'there's no need, 'there's no problem' or 'it's all right. kamak is actually the indefinite of a Class 2 noun kama 'business, matter'; but it rarely occurs outside of such idiomatic expressions as kamak nasse. Two expres-sions in Conversation 9 are built on kamak nam9: [page 124] kamak næddə? Is it all right. Does it matter; Will it be a problem for you? eekətə kamak nææ. That's all right; That doesn't matter; There's no problem about that. 5. mokut mokut may occur without a preceding noun in negative sentences or questions, with an English equivalent anything' With wene 'other, else' it means anything else (as in Lesson 3): maTə mokut onnə nææ. I don't want anything. mahatteaTə mokut oonə də? Do you want anything? maTə wenə mokut oona nææ /epaa. I don't want anything else. mahatteaTə wenə mokut oonə də? Do you want anything else? mokut may also occur like a quantity word after a noun with the meaning 'any in negative statements or questions: maTə dan kiyəwannə pot mokut nææ. I don't have any books to read now. mahatteaTə pot mokut oonə də? Do you want any books? For most speakers, mokut is restricted to negative statements or questions, though some can apparently use it in positive sentences with the meaning 'some (thing) maTə mokut gannə onnə. I want to buy something maTə paləturu mokut gannə oona. I want to buy some vegetables. Note that Tikak often has the English equivalent 'some' when it follows a noun, whether in statements or questions, but unlike mokut it generally carries the implication small amount, a little, a few': a maTə paləturu Tikak gannə onnə. mahatteaTə pot Tikak gannə oonə də? I want to buy some little) fruit. (a Do you want to buy some (a few) books? [page 125] 6. THE mu FORM 6.1 yamu ‘let’s go’ It is formed by adding illustrates a new verb form: the mu form. mu to the verb stem. Stem final-a does not change to -a-: Verb yanewa 'go' bonawa 'drink' kərənəwa 'do' elawenewa 'drive! elawə- nawətinəwa 'stop, stay' geenewa 'bring' Stem ya- bo- kera- nawati- gee- -mu Form yamu bomu kərəmu elewemu nawatimu geemu gannawa 'get, buy' has alternate mu forms gammu and ganimu. Either may be used. innawa has an irregular mu form indimu. 6.2 The mu form serves as a first person plural imperative. The usual English equivalent is 'let's'. or 'let us'...: yamu bomu eeke gammu metənə nawetimu Let's go. Let's drink (or smoke). Let's buy that one. Let's stop here. 6.3 We have seen that the simple form of the verb is changed to an emphatic form in emphatic sentences. But when the sentence is emphatic, the mu form of the verb does not change its shape. Thus: api gaməTə yamu. Let's go to the village. api yamu gaməTə. Let's go to the village. api mee keselgeDi kamu. Let's eat these bananas. api kamu mee keselge Di. Let's eat these bananas. 7. THE SINHALESE WRITING SYSTEM V 7.1 Vowel Symbols Vowels that begin a word are written with a set of symbols different from those added to consonants: 4 a aa 1 11 23 12 ε وح uu e ee 0 00 [page 126] Examples: අතන ආයෙත් aayet ඒක ඇපල් උඩරට atənə æpəl uDa raTe එතකොට ete koTe ඔය eeka oye ookə 7.2 Nasals 7.21 Half-nasals m, n, ἤ m occurs only before b, and mb is written with the single symbol @. koləm̆bə n̆ occurs only before d and D and only before g. Both n and n̆ are written with the symbol following consonant: attached to the symbol for the C nd හොඳ honda 00 ලඟ lange 7.22 The Symbol n in combinations in which it precedes k org is always written with the symbol. : nk ලංකාව lankaawe norn preceding T, D, h, or s are often written with The only word in which. is thus used that has occurred so far is සිංහල sinhələ. may also be used to write final n, as stated in the next section.. 7.23 Final n At the end of a word, n may be written by 3 oro : පොතෙන් poten යන්නම් yannan නැත්තං nættan [page 127] For the most part, spellings of final n must be memorized for individual words, but some general statements can be made: 1. Final n in the instrumental ending for any class will be written with : බස් එකෙන් සුරුට්ටුවෙන් bas eken suruTTuwen කොළඹින් කඩෙන් kolambin kaDen 2. The nnan form of the verb is always written with final: කරන්නම් kərannan එන්නම් ennan 3. If a word which ends in n has some other form with m or n where a vowel follows, η will be written with or as the case may be. Thus: ගම gama 'the village gan 'villages' පුලුවනි puluweni පුලුවන් puluwan 4. The situations in which is used to write final n must be learned as they occur. The only one that has occurred so far is nættan Exercises A. title: Lesson 10
text: Lesson 10 Lesson 10 [page 132] Conversation: Buying a Book John enters a bookstore and asks a clerk where the school books are. The clerk directs him to another counter. JOHN iskoolə potə koten school book iskoolǝ pot tiyenne koten də? where (what place) Where are the school books? FIRST CLERK arə kawnTəree laŋgəTə yannə. Go to that counter over there. SECOND CLERK mahatteaTə pot mokut oonə də? Did you want any books sir? JOHN siŋhəla igənəgannəwa sinhələ igənəgannə həndə pot monǝwa də? Sinhala, Sinhalese learn What books are good for learning Sinhala? SECOND CLERK koccərə dannewa how much, how many know mahattea sinhəla koссəгə dannǝwa də? How much Sinhala do you know? [page 133] kataakərənəwa speak, call Tikak kataakərannə puluwəni. I can speak a little. akurə the letter of the alphabet JOHN akuru dannawa. I know the letters of the alphabet. I want to learn Sinhala quickly. maTə ikmənətə sinhələ igənəgannə onnə. SECOND CLERK pattǝree pattǝree kiyəwənəwa də? the newspaper Do you read the newspaper? JOHN kiyəwənəwa. I read (them). namut teerenǝwa but understand namut teerenne bohomə Tikay. But I understand very little. SECOND CLERK mee pota kiyəwannə puluwan də? Can you read this book? madi not enough, insufficiently JOHN kiyəwannə puluwəni. I can read (it). teerənəwa madi. I don't understand enough. meeka? SECOND CLERK This one? [page 134] taremak somewhat, to some extent JOHN meekə tarǝmak teerenǝwa. This one I understand somewhat. SECOND CLERK ehemə də? Is that so? tunweni pantiyə ookə tuŋweni pantiyə potak. paTan gannəwa mahattea tunweni pantiyen paTan ganne. third grade, level, class That one is a third grade book. You begin, start (should) start from the third grade. ehenan in that case, if that is SO JOHN ehenan maTə tuŋweni pantiye pot dekak dennə. In that case, give me two third grade books. SECOND CLERK mahatteaTə mee dekə hon̆day. JOHN These two are fine for you. gaanə kiiyədə gaanə? the price What is the price? SECOND CLERK rupiyal tunak dennə. (Give me) three rupees. Additional Vocabulary Numerals 6-12 Inanimate hayə hatə namee (or naməyə) nine dahee (or dahaya) ekolaha dolaha English six seven eight ten eleven twelve Animate hayə denaa hat denaa aTə denaa namə denaa daha denaa ekolos denaa dolos denaa [page 135] Grammar 1. NEW NOUNS Class 2 akura 'the letter of the alphabet; gen. akure; pl. akuru gaanə 'the price'; gen. gaane; pl. ganan (note the change -aa- toa in the plural) pantiyə 'the grade'; gen. pantiye; pl. panti sinhələ 'Sinhala, Sinhalese'; gen. sinhəlee; (no plural) Class 4 kawnTaree 'the counter'; pl. kawnTərə patǝree 'the newspaper'; pl. pattərə 2. NEW VERBS iqənəqannəwa 'learn' kataakərənəwa 'speak' kiyəwənəwa 'read' teerenewa 'understand' paTan gannəwa 'begin, start, commence' dannəwa 'know' NOTE: dannəwa has no past tense in Spoken Sinhala, but dænəgannəwa ia used instead. Thus: dænəgatta. 3. NOUN COMPOUNDS iskoolə potə, nawəkataa potə, siigiri galə and koləmbə bas are examples of NOUN COMPOUNDS. Noun compounds of this type consist of two nouns, which together act as a single noun. The whole compound may thus take any case or defini- [page 136] niteness ending. They require mention here because the first noun is in a special form: the uninflected NOUN STEM. The noun stem for many nouns is identical with the direct plural form (thus 1skoole and nawakataa are both the stem and plural forms of iskoole and nawəkataawa), but for some it is different. Compounds should be learned as units as they occur, since they are commonly idioms with special meanings, and the stem form will not be given for each new noun. One stem that should be learned early is lanka, the stem form of lankaawe, since it is of frequent occur-rence in titles. 4. koten da koten də is an interrogative phrase composed of the interroga-tive kotənə 'at what place' plus də. kotənə is the corresponding interrogative form of the metənə set and carries the same impli-cation of a specific locality. All of the members change tene toten when they occur directly before də just as they do before the dative ending (Lesson 4, 10.2). kotənə takes the same forms as the rest of the set: Direct kotənə Dative kotenTe Genitive kotənə Instrumental kotenin Thus: palaturu koten da? Where is the fruit? atənə. or Over there atenTə yanna. Go over there. 5. koccərə, kiiyak, kiidenek koccərə (də) means either 'how much' or 'how many'. kiiyak (də) and kiidenek (də) mean only 'how many'. koccere, like kiiyak and kildenek, behaves like a quantity word and follows a noun in the plural. While kiiyak is only inanimate, and kiidenek is only animate, koccere is both animate and inanimate: lamay koccərə innəwa də? or lamay kiidenek innəwa də? pot koccərə tiyenəwa də? or pot kiiyak tiyenəwa də? How many children (have you)? How many books are there? [page 137] Since kiiyak and k11denek mean only 'how many', they almost never occur with those nouns like salli, palaturu, eloolu, etc., which do not occur in the singular in Sinhalese. koccərə must be used with these nouns, even though the English equivalent may be either 'how much' or 'how many', depending on the particular noun in English: ohee lange salli koccərə tiyenawə də? How much money do you have on you? ara kaDee tiyenne eloolu koccərə də? How many vegetables in that shop? Note that koccərə, kiiyak, and kildenek, unlike most interroga-tives which are used only with the emphatic form of a verb, may be used with the simple or the emphatic form: mehee pot koccərə tiyenəwa də? How many books are here? mehee tiyenne pot koccərə də? How many books are here? 6. NUMERALS 6 12 6.1 The animate forms of the numerals 'nine' and 'ten' have the forms of Class 4 nouns. The rest of the numerals 'six' through 'twelve', like 'one' through 'five' (8, 9.2) have the forms of Class 2 nouns: six hayə gen. haye seven hata gen. hatee eight aTə gen. aTee nine namee (OR naməyə) ten dahee (OR dahayə) eleven ekolaha gen. ekolahe twelve dolaha gen. dolahe namee and dahee have the following forms in the indefinite and with the assertion marker: Indefinite with-y namee nameak nameay dahee dahayak dahayay Note that nameak is the form we would expect from a Class 4 noun, the rest are not. [page 138] 6.2 The animate forms of these numerals are: six haye denaa Beven hat denaa eight aTə denaa namə denaa nine daha denaa ten ekolos denaa eleven dolos denaa twelve Note that all of these, like the animate forms of 'three', 'four', and 'five' ', tun denaa, hatere denaa, pas denaa, are made with the form denaa, which has the case forms of a Class 5 noun: tun denaaTa, tun denaage, tun denaagen, etc. All animate numer-als in Sinhalese except one and two (ekkenaa, denna) are formed with denaa. The form of the numeral that precedes denaa is the NUMERAL STEM. In a few cases, such as hatərə, hayə, aTo, the numeral stem will be identical with the inanimate form, but for most numerals it will be different. 7. teerenawa ‘UNDERSTAND’ teerenewa 'understand takes a subject in the dative case and an object in the direct case: maTə ee pattərə tarəmak teerenawa. I understand those newspapers to some extent. lameaTə teerenne mee pote. The child understands this book. 8. madi ‘NOT ENOUGH’, ‘INSUFFICIENTLY’ madi 'not enough', 'insufficiently' represents a new type of word: 1. It may follow a simple verb, and then means 'not suffici-ently, 'not enough': maTə teerenewa madi. I don't understand sufficiently. mamə weDə kərənəwa madi. I don't work enough. 2. It forms sentences of its own by substituting for innewa or or tiyenəwa in 'have' or 'there is constructions. It then means Thasn't (haven't) enough' or 'isn't (aren't) enough': [page 139] kalutərəTə bas madi. There aren't enough buses to Kalutara. mehee paleturu madi. There isn't enough fruit here. are iskoole lamay madi. There aren't enough children in that school. maTə nawəkataa pot madi. I haven't enough novels. maTə salli madi. I haven't enough money. mahatteaTə daruwo madi. The gentleman hasn't enough children. Just as the 'have' construction with tiyenawə or innewa may have its literal meaning 'there is something for someone, so the construction with madi substituted for innawa or tiyenawə may have the sense something isn't enough for someone: maTə pot dekak madi. Two books aren't enough for me. 3. In all of these constructions, it may occur with or without the assertion marker with no difference in meaning. The assertion marker added to 1 gives 11: maTə teerenawa madi1. or maTə teerenawa madi. kalutərəTə bas madii. kaluteraTə bas madi. I don't understand sufficient-ly. There aren't enough buses to Kalutara. or 9. paTan gannəwa paTan gannawa 'begin' takes a direct object: daruwo heTə iskoole paTan gannawa. The children begin school tomorrow. 'To begin at' or 'start from' is expressed by using the instru-mental case of the noun: meeken paTan ganne. Begin with this one. mahattea tun weni pantiyen paTan ganna. You (should) begin at (or 'start from') the third grade. [page 140] paTan gannəwa may also be used with a dependent infinitive: mahattea wæDə kərannə paTan gannawa. The master is starting to work. 10. lange lange in the dative case is used to indicate motion up to a place rather than into a place: ee gamətə yannə. Go to that village (into it). ee gama laŋgəTə yannə. Go to that village (up to it, near it). arə kawnTəree langəTə yannə. Go to that counter. mee kawnTeree langəTə enne. Come to this counter. When the destination is a person or persons, the construction with lange is always used, never that with a dative case noun: taatta langəTə enne. are mahatturu langəTə yannə. Come to father. Go to those gentlemen. 11. THE INFINITIVE WITH ADJECTIVES The infinitive has appeared modifying nouns (balannə ten) and other verbs (balanne yannə). In this conversation it appears modifying an adjective: sinhələ gənəgannə hon̆də (pot) (books) good for learning Sinhalese similarly: balannə hon̆də (tænak) (a place) good to see gannə hon̆də (eloolu) (vegetables) good to buy or good for buying nawətinnə hon̆də (hooTelee) (a hotel) good to stay at Exercises A. Substitute orally: 1. iskoola pot tiyenne where here in the shop at this counter [page 141]

text: Lesson 11 Lesson 11 [page 146] Conversation: Extending an Invitation John is invited by his acquaintance, Mr. Gunasekara, an officer in a tea estate, to see some traditional dances at the latter's village. GUNASEKARA næTumə kæməti the dance like (v.) mahattea uDəraTə næTun balannə kæməti də? Would you like to see upcountry dances? OW, OW. ay, mehee næTumak tiyenəwa də? JOHN Yes, yes! Why, is there a dance here? GUNASEKARA rææ the night adə rææ tonight adə rææ apee gamee hoňdə næTumak tiyenəwa. prəsiddə famous næTTuwa dancer bohomə prəsiddə næTTuwo enǝwa. (Some) very famous dancers are coming. maTə ennə puluwəni. adə matəǝ wena wæDak nææ. There is a good dance at our village tonight. kiiyəTə at what time kiiyətə də ennə oonə? At what time should I come? JOHN I can come. I have no other work today. [page 147] GUNASEKARA nameeTa at nine. nameeTə witərə enne. Come (at) about nine. mahattea paarə dannəwa də? Do you know the way (literally: 'the road')? JOHN nææ, mamə paarə danne nææ. No, I don't (know the road). GUNASEKARA (-t) ekkə putat ekkə -with with the (our) son ehenan apee putat ekkə ennə In that case, come with our son. eaa he, she eaa inne arə kaDee. He is in that kaDee. JOHN eheeTə kaar-ekə geniyannə puluwan də? Can one take a car there? GUNASEKARA amaaru difficult apee gedərə laŋgəTə kaar-ekə geniyannə amaaruy. kaar-ekə watte nawattannə. Leave the car at the estate. hæbæy payin however, in fact on foot hæbæy, watte in̆dəla payin yanne onnə. However, you must go on foot from the estate on. It is difficult to take a car up to our home. [page 148] JOHN murakaarea the watchman watte murakaareek innewa də? Is there a watchman in the estate? GUNASEKARA ow, murekaareek innawa. Yes, there is (a watchman). geeTTuwa issərəha the gate in front of kaarekə geeTTuwa issərəha nawattannə puluwəni. You can leave the car in front of the gate. JOHN iwərə done, finished iwere wenawa rae wenewa be late at night næTun iwərəwenəkoTə da?Will it be late at night when the dances end? rase wenewa come to an end GUNASEKARA eli wenawa eli wenə kan naTənəwa dance get light, approach dawn until dawn ow, eli wenə kan naTənəwa. Yes, they dance till dawn. ee nisaa apee gedərə nawətinnə onnə. Therefore, you had better stay at our home. JOHN mokut geennə oonə də? Should I bring anything? GUNASEKARA kameraawe the camera mahattea langə kəməraawak tiyenewa, nee? You have a camera here, haven't you? [page 149] JOHN ow. Yes. GUNASEKARA eekə geennə. Bring that. pintuure the picture hon̆də pintuurə Tikak gannə puluwani. You can take some good pictures. JOHN kataa kərənəwa call hon̆day, lamea yanəkoTə matə kataa karannə kiyannə. Fine. Tell the boy to call me when he goes. Grammar 1. NEW NOUNS Class 2 naTume the dance’; gen. næTume; pl. næTun geeTTuwa ‘the gate’; gen. geeTTuwe; pl. geeTTu kæməraawe ‘the camera’; gen. kameraawe; pl. kæməra Class 3 ‘the night’ has identical direct and genitive forms, and an instrumental in in and thus belongs to Class 3. The forms are: Definite Indefinite Plural Direct rasek 19999 Dative rameTa ramækəTə Genitive rææka Instrumental rein rææækin Class 4 pintuure 'the picture'; pl. pintuurə [page 150] Class 5 naTTuwa 'the dancer'; pl. naTTuwo murakaarea 'the watchman'; pl. murəkaareo 2. NEW VERBS ell wenawa 'become light, dawn' naTənəwa 'dance' kataa kərənəwa 'call, talk, speak (a language)' 1wərə wenewa 'to get done, to come to an end' is an Idiomatic phrase composed of the adjective iwərə 'finished, completed and wenewa. 3. THE THIRD PERSON PRONOUN (meaa) SET Another set of location words is used as an equivalent of the third person pronoun. This set, with the usual distinction in location, is: meaa he, she, this person oyaa area he, she, that person (near you) eaa he, she, that person (over there) he, she, that person (in question) The plural forms are made by adding -la: meaala, oyaala, areala, eaala 'they'. meaa will serve as a model for the case forms of the entire set: Direct meaa Dative meaaTa Genitive meaage Instrumental meaagen Note, however, that the final short throughout the inflection. given later. a in area is short and is kept The plural case forms will be All four members of the set are used as third person singular pronouns for equals and inferiors. They are not generally used for superiors. In addition to this use, one of the set, i.e., oyaa is also used as a second person pronoun to address intimate equals: oyaa enəkoTə, kaar-eken enna. When you (intimate) come, come by car. [page 151] ohee enekoTe, kaar-eken enne. When you (more formal) come, come by car. Here as with other second person pronouns, no simple rule can be given for when it may be used, since such usage differs from group to group and area to area. In general, it is safer not to use oyaa as a second person pronoun unless the person addressed is a very intimate friend. 4. LIKE, LIKE TO kæməti With kaməti 'like', the equivalent of the English subject is in the direct case, and the object is in the dative case. kæməti takes the assertion marker, and as with other forms in i , the result is ii . Thus the form is kamətii when it is not followed by an item like da or nææ : are mahattea ee pattareeTə kæmətii. That gentleman likes that newspaper. eaa osTin-ekəkətə kamati da? Does he like an Austin? Note that with oona 'want’ the English subject is in the dative case whereas with kæməti it is in the direct case. The English object with oona is in the direct case whereas with kaməti it is in the dative case: mama mee potəTə kamətii. I like this book. maTə mee pote onnə. I want this book. kæməti may have a dependent verb in the infinitive, with or without its own object and modifiers: mahattea uDeraTə næTun balanna kaməti də? Do you like to see up-country dances? siigiriyəTə yanakoTə mamə ee taanaayamee nawatinnə kamatii. When I go to Sigiriya, I like to stay in that rest house. ohee are kaDee eloolu gannə kæməti də? Do you like to buy vegetables at that shop? The negative of kaməti is formed by adding name. Thus: mahattea are potaTə kaməti naeee. The master doesn't like that. book. mahattea oya suruTTuwaTə kæmeti nædda? Don't you like that cigar? [page 152] 5. t ekka 'WITH' ‘With’, indicating accompaniment, is expressed by the post-position-tekke. The t is added to the preceding noun (in the direct case) and ekka follows: putaat ekkə with the son lameat ekka with the child When the preceding noun ends in a consonant (as when it is in the indefinite) thet is preceded by -u-: lameekut ekkə with a boy mahatteekut ekka with a gentleman mame plus -t may appear as maat. Hence: maat ekke ‘with me’. 6. issərəha ‘IN FRONT OF’ The postposition issərəha ‘in front of’ takes the direct case: geeTTuwe issərəha in front of the gate kaDee issərəha in front of the shop etənə isseraha in front of that place 7. ‘AT WHAT TIME?’ The Sinhalese expression for ‘at what time’ is kiiyəTə də? ‘At about what time’ is kiiyəTə witərə də? In the corresponding answers (’at nine’, etc.), the dative case of the numeral is used: nameeTa at nine nameeTə witərə at about nine Similarly: nameeTə witərə ennə puluwan də? Can you come at about nine? mama enne pahate witərə. I am coming at about five. (Note that witərə in these expressions takes no assertion marker or indefinite ending since it is witare ‘about’, not witərə ‘only’). 8. kataa kərənəwa kataa kərənəwa may mean either ‘call’ or ‘speak’. As ‘call’ it takes the dative case of the person called: [page 153] taatta maTə kataa kərənəwa. Father is calling me. mahatteaTə heTə ram kataa kərannə. Call the master tomorrow night. As ‘speak’ it takes the direct case: mame dæn sinhələ kataa kərənəwa. I speak Sinhalese now. mehee kataa karanne sinhələ witəray. They only speak Sinhalese here (i.e., ‘only Sinhalese is spoken here’). It may also be used with t ekke in the sense ‘talk with’: maTə mahatteat ekkə Tikak kataa kərannə onnə. I want to talk a bit with the gentleman. ehenan lameat ekkə kataa karanna. If so, talk with the boy. 9. kiyənəwa kiyənəwa with an infinitive has the sense ‘tell (someone) to’. Thus: lamea yanakoTə maTə kataa kərannə kiyannə. Tell the boy to call me when he is going. This sentence means ‘Tell the boy now that he should call me when he is going. Note that lamea is the subject of yanəkoTə and not the object of kiyanne. When the person told to do some-thing is expressed in Sinhalese, it is in the dative case. Thus: lameaTə maTə kataa karannə kiyanne. Tell the boy to call me. Similarly: mahattea siigiriyəTə yanakoTə ee taanaayəmee nawətinnə kiyanna. Tell the gentleman to stop at that rest house when he goes to Sigiriya. Note that mahattea is the subject of yanekoTe, as in lamea yanekoTə above. Compare: mame lameaTə weDe karannə kiyənəwa. I am telling the boy to work. [page 154] Here lameaTə directly expresses the person told, and is not the subject of waDə kəranne. Exercises A. text: Lesson 12 Lesson 12 [page 160] Conversation: Calling on a Friend Mr. Perera, wishing to speak with his friend Mr. Wirasekara, goes to the latter’s house. A servant answers the door. MR. PERERA mahattea gedərə innəwa də? Is the master at home? SERVANT taama still, yet kantooruwe the office nææ, taamə kantooruwe. No. He is still at the office. PERERA gedərə enəwa come home kiiyəTə də gedərə enne? What time is he coming home? SERVANT wahanawa close kantooruwa wahanne hatərələ. The office closes at four. eewi is likely to come pahaTə witərə gedərə eewi. hambe wenewa meet, see (to speak with) ary, mahattea hambe wennə onnə də? Why, did you want to see the master? He is likely to come home about five. [page 161] ow, maTə mahattea Tikak hamba PERERA wenne onnə. hariyəTə exactly hariyəTə mə exactly (emphatic) hariyəTə mə pahaTə eewi da? Yes. I want to see the master for a little (while). Is he likely to come exactly at five? SERVANT kiyannə base. rae wenawa samehare dawaswələ on some days saməharə dawaswələ enəkoTe rase wenawa. be late in the afternoon, towards night nan hambe wenne onnə nan Tikak inne. waaDi wenawa sit enne. mehen waaDi wenne. welaawa the time dæn welaawa tunay. Now it (the time) is three o'clock. can't I can't say. On some days, when he comes home it is late in the afternoon. if If you want to see him, wait a little (while). Come. Sit here. PERERA kiiyə də? What time? SERVANT tunay. Three. [page 162] PERERA tawa still, yet welaa time tawe huŋ̆gak welaa tiyenəwa, nee də? There is still a lot of time (left), isn't there? Tawme the town yanna tiyenəwa have to go maTə TawməTə yannə tiyenewa. passe later I have to go to (the) town. ennan will come mame passe ennan. I'll come (back) later. mamə pahaTə ennan. I'll come at five. mahatteaTə kiyannə. Tell the master. koheewat somewhere, anywhere yaawi is likely to go nættan mahattea koheewat yaawi. Otherwise, the master is likely to go somewhere. SERVANT namə the name mahatteage name? Your name? PERERA Joon pereera John Perera SERVANT kiyannan will tell hon̆day. mamə kiyannan. All right. I'll tell (him). haya wenǝkoTə towards six may mahattea haye wenəkoTə enəwa may. surely The master will surely come by six. [page 163] kame the food ada re kamamətə koheewat yanne na9. Tonight he won't go anywhere to eat (literally, 'for food'). ee nisaa therefore, because of that amaaruWe the difficulty ee nisaa hambe wenne amaaruwak Therefore, it won't be difficult to see (him). PERERA Tælifoon karannan will call (on the telephone) Fine. If I am coming, I'll call. hon̆day. mamə enəwa nan Tælifoon kerannan. Grammar 1. NEW NOUNS Class 2 kantooruwe ‘the office’; gen. kantooruwe; pl. kantooru Tawme ‘the town’ gen. Tawme; pl. Tawn namə ‘the name’; gen, namee; pl. nan ‘the food’; gen, kaame; pl. kaame (or, rarely, kassen) NOTE: The dative kæemətə is a common expression for ‘to a meal’, ‘to eat’: ade re kamətə koheewat yanne nese, Tonight he isn’t going any-where for supper (to eat). welaawe ‘the time’; gen, welaawe; pl. welaa NOTE: The plural form is usually used where English has ‘time’ without an article, as in ‘There is a lot of time left.’ [page 164] amaaruwa ‘the difficulty’; gen. amaaruwe; pl. amaaru NOTE: The indefinite form occurs in the common idiomatic expression amaaruak nase ‘not difficult’, as in ee nisaa hambe wennə amaaruwak Therefore it won't be diffi-cult to see (him). пaвa. The same thing may be said using the adjective amaaru ‘difficult’ with name: ee nisaa hambe wennə amaaru nasee. Therefore it won’t be diffi-cult to see (him). much as English can say ‘It’s not difficult to see him’ or ‘There’s no difficulty about seeing him’. 2. NEW VERBS wahanewa ‘close’ hambe wenəwa ‘meet, see (to speak with)’ waaDi wenawa ‘sit’ 3. THE w1 FORM OF THE VERB 3.1 The wi form is made by adding wi to the verb stem with these stem changes: 1. When the stem ends in a vowel, the vowel is lengthened if possible: Verb Stem -w1 Form yanewa ya- yaawi enawa e- eewi wenawa we- weewi tiyenəwa tiye- tiyeewi nawətinəwa nawati nawatiiwi 2. If the stem-final vowel is a ora, it is lengthened to -aa: balenawa bala- balaawi kərənəwa kara- karaawi bedaawi bedənəwa beda- wahaawi wahanawa waha- [page 165] 3. When the stem ends in n, 11 is added before wi: gannewa gan- ganiiwi dannewa dan- daniiwi 4. A few stems are irregular: innewa in- indiiwi If a new verb has an irregular wi form, that form will be given along with the verb. 3.2 The use of the wi form is illustrated by: pahaTə witərə gedərə eewi (He) is likely to come home about five. nattan mahattea koheewat yaawi. Otherwise, the master is likely to go somewhere. dæn mahattea eewi. The master will probably come now. lamea irida koləmbəTə yaawi. It is likely that the boy will go to Colombo on Sunday. The wi form indicates future time and implies some lack of certainty. There is no single English equivalent that will translate this form under all circumstances, so that it may be variously rendered by such equivalents as 'may, might, will probably, is likely to', depending upon context. In general, the implication of the wi form is similar to that of English 'it is likely that', or 'will probably'. The wi form may be either second or third person, singular or plural, but it occurs as second person only in rare instances. It is never first person. In questions, də immediately follows the wi form: eaa ade rame naTumak balanna yaawi də? Is he likely to go to see a dance tonight? 4. THE -nnan FORM OF THE VERB 4.1 Thennan form is made by adding -nnan to the verb stem with the same stem changes that take place with the nne of the infini-tive: [page 166] Verb Infinitive -nnan Form yannan yanawa yannə enawa enne ennan innawa inne innan kərənəwa kərannə kərannan nawatinawa nawətinne nawetinnan 4.2 Thennan form of a verb refers to an event in the future, and is used only with a first person subject, either singular or plural, implied or stated. It may be used as a polite way of asking permission: mamə yannan? May I go? api ennan? May we come? Another use of this form is as a polite way of agreeing to do something, or saying that you will do something if it is all right with the person you are talking to: mama kiyannan. I'll tell him (if that's what you want me to do). Tælifoon karannan. I'll telephone. api pahaTə ennan. We'll come at five (if it's all right with you). 4.3 Sentences with nnan verbs can never be questions formed with the question marker də. They do not have negatives. } 5. THE CONJUNCTION nan 'if' The conjunction nan 'if', like the question marker də may, in a simple statement, occur after the simple verb. In an emphatic statement it may occur after the emphasized item, but not after the emphatic form of the verb. Also like də, it may occur after onnə, puluwan and kæməti in sentences with these forms, or after the predicate attribute in equational sentences. kalutərəTə yanawa. kalutərəTə yanawa də? kalutərəTə yanawa nan, meeken yanna. (You are) going to Kalutara. Are you going to Kalutara? If you are going to Kalutara, go by this one. [page 167] mahattea inne gedərə. mahattea inne gedərə də? mahattea inne gedərə nan, mame Tælifoon kerannan. hambe wennə oona. hamba wenne onnə də? hamba wenne onnə nan Tikak inne. mee sigeræT hon̆day. mee sigəræT hon̆də də? mee sigəræt hon̆də nan, pækæt-ekak denne. 6. (-Ta) ... basse CAN'T' The negative of puluwan 'can' is base, as in kiyanne base. (I) can't say. The construction with be is identical to the puluwan construc-tion: that is, the subject is in the dative case and a dependent verb is in the infinitive form: maTə pattaree kiyəwannə puluwəni. maTə patteree kiyəwannə bee. lameaTə sinhələ puluwəni. lameaTə sinhələ baxe. The master is at home. Is the master at home? If the master is at home, I'll telephone (him). (You) want to meet (him). Do you want to meet him? If you want to meet him, wait for a while. These cigarettes are good. Are these cigarettes good? If these cigarettes are good, give me a pack. I can read the paper. I can't read the paper. The boy knows Sinhalese. The boy doesn't know Sinhalese. 7. THE 'AM TO', 'AM SUPPOSED TO CONSTRUCTION The verb tiyenawə (but not innawa) may be used with the subject in the dative case and a dependent verb in the infinitive form with the meaning 'am to' 'am supposed to'. This construction is. similar in form to the Tə puluwan 'can' and Tə .. oona 'want' construction. The dependent verb may have Its own subject and modifiers: maTə TauməTə yannə tiyenawə. maTə adə rase kaDeeTə yannə tilyenewa. oheeTə pahaTə koləmbə innə tiyenawə. I am supposed to go to town. I am supposed to go to the shop tonight. You are to be in Colombo at five. [page 168] mahatteaTə eloolu gannə tiyenawə. lameaTə mahattea hayəTə hambə wenna tiyenawə. The master is supposed to buy vegetables. The boy is to meet the master at six. 8. TELLING TIME 8.1 In asking the time at any given moment (as opposed to at what time something will occur or has occurred--see Lesson 11) any one of several expressions involving kiiyə də may be used: welaawe kiiyə də? What time is it (literally, How much is the time)? den welaawe kiiyə də? What time is it now? dæn kiiyə də? What time is it now? The order may be changed with no change in meaning: kiiyə də welaawe? kiiyə də dæn welaawa? kiiyə də dæn? 8.2 In answering the questions above, used with the appropriate numeral: the assertion marker is ekay 'one (o'clock)' or dæn ekay 'It's one (o'clock) now.' dekay 'two (o'clock)' or den dekay 'It's two (o'clock) now.' 9. wenawa IN TIME EXPRESSIONS 9.1 When used with a specific hour of the day, wenewa implies that it will be that time when something else occurs: mahattea enakoTə haya wenawa. It will be six when the mas-ter comes. koocciyə yanakoTə aTə wenewa. It will be eight when the train goes. If wenekoTə is used with a specific time, it implies that something will happen by that time: mahattea haya wenəkoTə enewa. The master will come by six. koocciyə aTə wenəkoTə yanawa. The train will go by eight. 9.2 rase wenawa means either 'getting towards night' or 'getting well into the night', depending upon context. Thus it may equate with either 'be late in the afternoon' or 'be late at night'. [page 169] næTun iwərə wenəkoTə rasee wenǝwa də? saməharə dawaswelə enəkoTə ræse wenawa. Will it be late at night when the dances end? On some days it's late in the afternoon when (he) comes home. 10. taama AND tawe While taame and tawe may both be rendered by English 'still' or sometimes 'yet', there is a clear distinction between them. taamə indicates that something is as it has been in the past. tawa implies that there is still some left, or still some distance to go. Thus: mahattea taamə kantooruwe. lamea taamə koləmbəTə yanawa. The master is still at the office. The boy is still going to Colombo ('as he has been' or 'he hasn't reached there yet'). But: tawe huŋ̆gak welaa tiyenawə. tawe hetəpmə pahak tiyenawə. There is still much time left. There are still five miles (to go). 11. may When may is added to a simple (English certainly, surely') or context: verb, it implies either certainty 'nothing but', depending upon mahattea haya wenǝkoTə enewa may. lamea weDə kərənəwa may. mamə kalutərəTə yanəwa may. The master will surely come by six. The boy is surely working. or The boy does nothing but work. I am surely going to Kalutara. or I do nothing but go to Kalutara. [page 170] mahattea sigəræl bonewa may. The master does nothing but smoke cigarettes. 12. waaDi wenewa waaDi wenawa 'sit (down)' takes the instrumental case of the location: mehen waa Di wenna. arahen waaDi wenne. Sit here. Sit down over there. Exercises A. text: Lesson 13 Lesson 13 [page 182] Conversation: Arranging a Visit Mr. Perera's nephew, Sirisena, has arranged to visit his uncle in Kandy during the school vacation. Mr. Perera, who meets him in Colombo, asks about his plans. MR. PERERA බය ලමයා වන කොට චන්නෙ කෝට්ටියෙන්, නේද? When you come, you are coming by train, aren't you? STRISENA ඇක්ස්ප්‍රස් එක ඔව්. හයට ඇක්ස්ප්‍රස් එකක් තියෙනවා. the express (train) Yes, there is an express at six. PERERA හයේ කෝච්චිය අට හමාර නුවර හයේ කෝට්ටය නුවරට යන්නේ අට හමාරට, නේද? six o'clock train eight-thirty Kandy The six o'clock train reaches Kandy at eight-thirty, doesn't it? For the whole journey it takes (only) two and a half hours. PERERA අතර මග ඔව්. ඒක අතර මග නවත්තන්නෙ මම අට හමාරට ඉස්ටේසමට එන්නම්. on the way Yes. It doesn't stop on the way, does it? I'll come to the station at eight-thirty. SIRISENA කරදරේ කරදර වෙනවා මාමා කරදර වෙන්න එපා. මට ටැක්සියකින් එන්න පුලුවනි. the trouble go to trouble don't Don't go to any trouble, uncle. I can come by a taxi. මම කාරෙක ගේන්නම්. මට හෙට වෙන වැඩක් නෑ. පරක්කු ඉස්ටේසමේම මම පරක්කු නම් ඉස්ටේසමේ ම ඉන්න. ටැක්සියක් ගන්න එපා. කොහොම හරි මම කොහොම හරි අට හමාරට එන්නම්. බැරි ඩ්‍රයිවර් එවනවා PERERA I'll bring the car. text: Lesson 14 Lesson 14 [page 193] Conversation: Looking for a Doctor John goes to his neighbor Mr. Gunawardana to find out where he could find a good doctor. JOHN කිට්ටුව දොස්තර near the doctor මේ කිට්ටුව හොඳ දොස්තර කෙනෙක් ඉන්නවාද? Is there a good doctor near here? MR. GUNAWARDANA දොස්තර කෙනෙක් ඉන්නෙ හැතැප්ම තුනක් එහා. beyond, away There is a doctor three miles away. එයින් මෙහා ඇපොතිකරි from that this way the apothecary එයින් මෙහා ඉන්නෙ ඇපොතිකරි කෙනෙක් ද්වීතරයි. This way from the doctor's (literally: 'from that') there is only an apothecary. ඇයි? අසනීපයක් ද? Why? Is someone sick (liter-ally: 'An illness?')? ඔව්. අපේ ලමයාට ටිකක් අසනීපයි. JOHN Yes. Our son is a bit sick. [page 194] GUNAWARDANA හදිස්සිය හදිස්සියක් නම් ඇපොතිකරි ලගට යන්න. මෙහේ ඇපොතිකරි හුඟක් හොඳයි. the emergency If it is an emergency, go to the apothecary. The apothecary here is very good. JOHN යනඑක ඒත් හොඳ දොස්තර කෙනෙක් ලගට යන එක හොඳයි, නේද? even then the going Even then, it's good to go to a good doctor, isn't it? THE THIRD PERSON PRONOUN උන්නැහේ is used by people of a respectable social level to මහත්තයා on the other hand, is a polite form that can be used by anyone to refer to a refer to those (male) of equal status. person of equal or higher status. Clergymen and relatives are not referred by either form. c is also used after personal names as a title like 'Mister' (again by those of equal status). ໖໖ is very rarely used in directly addressing someone. As a pronoun (that is, not as 'Mister'), a is a member of another set of location words, but there is no member corresponding to a (මේ) මුන්නැහේ (අර) අරුන්නැහේ (ඒ) උන්නැහේ this gentleman that gentleman (over there that gentleman (in question) The plural is made by adding - ලා : මුන්නැහේලා 'these gentlemen'; අරුන්නැහේලා, උන්නැහේලා 'those gentlemen'. [page 197] 3. THE 'TOO, ALSO CONSTRUCTION 3.1 In Sinhalese, is added to a noun to express 'too, also', as in 'I too have to go', or 'I can come, too'. Thus: මම එනවා. වමත් එනවා. I am coming. I am coming, too. ໖໖ has a variant ở which may be used interchangeably with it, so that in place of the last example, we may have මාත් එනවා. I am coming, too. 3.2 If the noun is inflected for case, the follows the case ending. මට යන්න තියෙනවා. මටත් යන්න තියෙනවා. මහත්තයාට දෙන්න. මහත්තයාටත් දෙන්න. I have to go. I have to go, too. Give (it) to the gentleman. Give (it) to the gentleman, too. 3.3 When the word ends in a consonant, vowel is added be-fore : බස් එකෙන් යන්න. Go by the bus. බස් එකෙනුත් යන්න. Go by the bus, too. මට පොතක් තියෙනවා. I have a book. මට පොතකුත් තියෙනවා. I have a book, too. (6) SET 4. THE CASE FORMS OF THE BASIC Like the other location sets, the basic (6) set of location words has case forms. Direct මේ Dative ออ Instrumental මෙයින් There is no genitive form. They are ඔයිට ඔයින් අර 430 J අරින් ชอ එයින් 5. මෙහේ Members of the ce set, in the genitive case (which is identical with the direct case, Lesson 4) may be used before nouns with the sense of this (that) place'. Thus: [page 198] මෙහේ ඇපොතිකරි එහේ තානායම් the apothecary here (literally: 'the apothecary of this place') the rest house there (literally: 'the rest house of that place') 6. VERBAL NOUNS A verbal noun may be formed by adding on to the verbal adjec-tive form of the verb. Thus: යනවා බලනවා ගන්නවා go see, notice buy, get යන එක (the) going බලන එක (the) seeing (the) buying, getting One of the uses of a verbal noun in Sinhalese is as an equivalent of an English verb form in "-ing" used as the subject of a sentence. දොස්තර කෙනෙක් ලඟට යන්න. දොස්තර කෙනෙක් ලඟට යන එක හොඳයි. කෝච්චියෙන් එනවා. කෝච්චියෙන් එන එක හොඳයි. Go to a doctor. Going to a doctor is good. (He is) coming by train. Coming by train is good. 7. WHILE, DURING ६ 'while, during' is a postposition that follows a noun in the genitive case, or an adverb of place like 'at home'. ගෙදර දී වත්තෙ දි ගම දී ගමේ දී ගමනේ දී Thus: තාත්තා ගම දී වැඩ කරනවා. බස් එකේ දි සුරුට්ටු බොන්න එපා. while at home while in the estate while at home while in the village during the Journey Father works while (he is) at home. Don't smoke cigars while in the bus. [page 199] 8. කිට්ටුව කිට්ටුව 'near, in the vicinity of' is a postposition taking a noun or pronoun in the direct case: ගම කිට්ටුව in the vicinity of the village ගෝල්ෆේස් හෝටලේ කිට්ටුව near the Galle-Face Hotel set, in the direct case, may occur before Members of the කිට්ටුව : මේ කිට්ටුව ඒ කිට්ටුව in this vicinity in that (in question) vicinity 9. 'BEFORE' ඉස්සර 'before' (of time) takes a dependent noun or pronoun in the dative case: ඊට ඉස්සර පහට ඉස්සර before that before five 10. අසනීප The form ຜບ 'sick' is an adjective which takes its subject in the dative case and is used with the assertion marker: අපේ ලමයාට අසනීපයි. Our child is sick. අසනීප may be qualified by you or ටිකක් : අපේ ලමයාට ටිකක් අසනීපයි. Our boy is a bit (or 'somewhat') sick. මහත්තයාට හුඟක් අසනීපයි. The gentleman is very sick. 11. INSTRUMENTAL CASE The instrumental case is used to express 'in' with time ex- pressions: මිනිත්තුවකින් පැයකින් දවසකින් පැය තුනකින් in a minute in an hour in a day in three hours [page 200] 12. එහා, මෙහා 12.1 The word om 'that way and on this way' have the forms of a Class 3 noun, but occur only in the definite singular. Thus: Direct එහා මෙහා Dative එහාට මෙහාට Genitive එහා මෙහා Instrumental එහායින් මෙහායින් 12.2 The form ons may equate with English 'away' when there is no point of reference specifying direction. දොස්තර කෙනෙක් ඉන්නෙ හැතැප්ම තුනක් එහා. There is a doctor three miles away. 12.3 Another use of ໖ and em; contrasts the directions 'this way' and 'that way'. ටිකක් එහා හුඟක් මෙහා a little distance that way a good distance this way එහාට යන්න. Go that way. ටකක් මෙහාට එන්න. Come a little this way. 12.4 When point of reference is specified, om means 'beyond', 'on the other side of and Gems means on this side of'. The point of reference will be in the instrumental case: හෝටලේ තියෙන්නෙ කඩෙන් හැතැප්ම තුනක් එහා. The hotel is three miles on the other side of the shop. දොස්තර ඉන්නෙ වත්තෙන් හැතැප්ම කීපයක් මෙහා The doctor is several miles this side of the estate. ගෝGỈ ස් හෝටලෙන් ටිකක් එහාට යන්න. Go a little distance beyond the Galle-Face Hotel. When location rather than motion is indicated, as in some of the sentences in sections 3 and 4, the forms, මෙහා are in the genitive case (although of course for a noun of this type, the direct and genitive are identical). [page 201] 13. ໖ 'ON VACATION' و නිවාඩු the plural of the noun ໖໖ is used to equate with English 'on vacation'. In this use its subject is in the dative case: මට නිවාඩු. I am on vacation. [page 197] 3. the 'too, also construction 3.1 in sinhalese, is added to a noun to express 'too, also', as in 'i too have to go', or 'i can come, too'. thus: මම එනව. වමත එනව. i am coming. i am coming, too. ໖໖ has a variant ở which may be used interchangeably with it, so that in place of the last example, we may have මත එනව. i am coming, too. 3.2 if the noun is inflected for case, the follows the case ending. මට යනන තයනව. මටත යනන තයනව. මහතතයට දනන. මහතතයටත දනන. i have to go. i have to go, too. give (it) to the gentleman. give (it) to the gentleman, too. 3.3 when the word ends in a consonant, vowel is added be-fore : බස එකන යනන. go by the bus. බස එකනත යනන. go by the bus, too. මට පතක තයනව. i have a book. මට පතකත තයනව. i have a book, too. (6) set 4. the case forms of the basic like the other location sets, the basic (6) set of location words has case forms. direct ම dative ออ instrumental මයන there is no genitive form. they are ඔයට ඔයන අර 430 j අරන ชอ එයන 5. මහ members of the ce set, in the genitive case (which is identical with the direct case, lesson 4) may be used before nouns with the sense of this (that) place'. thus: [page 198] මහ ඇපතකර එහ තනයම the apothecary here (literally: 'the apothecary of this place') the rest house there (literally: 'the rest house of that place') 6. verbal nouns a verbal noun may be formed by adding on to the verbal adjec-tive form of the verb. thus: යනව බලනව ගනනව go see, notice buy, get යන එක (the) going බලන එක (the) seeing (the) buying, getting one of the uses of a verbal noun in sinhalese is as an equivalent of an english verb form in "-ing" used as the subject of a sentence. දසතර කනක ලඟට යනන. දසතර කනක ලඟට යන එක හඳය. කචචයන එනව. කචචයන එන එක හඳය. go to a doctor. going to a doctor is good. (he is) coming by train. coming by train is good. 7. while, during ६ 'while, during' is a postposition that follows a noun in the genitive case, or an adverb of place like 'at home'. ගදර ද වතත ද ගම ද ගම ද ගමන ද thus: තතත ගම ද වඩ කරනව. බස එක ද සරටට බනන එප. while at home while in the estate while at home while in the village during the journey father works while (he is) at home. don't smoke cigars while in the bus. [page 199] 8. කටටව කටටව 'near, in the vicinity of' is a postposition taking a noun or pronoun in the direct case: ගම කටටව in the vicinity of the village ගලෆස හටල කටටව near the galle-face hotel set, in the direct case, may occur before members of the කටටව : ම කටටව ඒ කටටව in this vicinity in that (in question) vicinity 9. 'before' ඉසසර 'before' (of time) takes a dependent noun or pronoun in the dative case: ඊට ඉසසර පහට ඉසසර before that before five 10. අසනප the form ຜບ 'sick' is an adjective which takes its subject in the dative case and is used with the assertion marker: අප ලමයට අසනපය. our child is sick. අසනප may be qualified by you or ටකක : අප ලමයට ටකක අසනපය. our boy is a bit (or 'somewhat') sick. මහතතයට හඟක අසනපය. the gentleman is very sick. 11. instrumental case the instrumental case is used to express 'in' with time ex- pressions: මනතතවකන පයකන දවසකන පය තනකන in a minute in an hour in a day in three hours [page 200] 12. එහ, මහ 12.1 the word om 'that way and on this way' have the forms of a class 3 noun, but occur only in the definite singular. thus: direct එහ මහ dative එහට මහට genitive එහ මහ instrumental එහයන මහයන 12.2 the form ons may equate with english 'away' when there is no point of reference specifying direction. දසතර කනක ඉනන හතපම තනක එහ. there is a doctor three miles away. 12.3 another use of ໖ and em; contrasts the directions 'this way' and 'that way'. ටකක එහ හඟක මහ a little distance that way a good distance this way එහට යනන. go that way. ටකක මහට එනන. come a little this way. 12.4 when point of reference is specified, om means 'beyond', 'on the other side of and gems means on this side of'. the point of reference will be in the instrumental case: හටල තයනන කඩන හතපම තනක එහ. the hotel is three miles on the other side of the shop. දසතර ඉනන වතතන හතපම කපයක මහ the doctor is several miles this side of the estate. ගgỉ ස හටලන ටකක එහට යනන. go a little distance beyond the galle-face hotel. when location rather than motion is indicated, as in some of the sentences in sections 3 and 4, the forms, මහ are in the genitive case (although of course for a noun of this type, the direct and genitive are identical). [page 201] 13. ໖ 'on vacation' و නවඩ the plural of the noun ໖໖ is used to equate with english 'on vacation'. in this use its subject is in the dative case: මට නවඩ. i am on vacation. exercises a. substitute orally: 1. ම කටටව is there a good doctor is there an uncle of yours is there a school book are there good shops are there good apothecaries 2. ඒ හටල තයනන 3. beyond the shop three miles beyond that estate five miles this side of my house a little this side of that (spot) very far from there my son my uncle my uncle's son the doctor the watchman of this estate are there any vegetable shops are there sinhalese hotels is there a famous dancer are there good watchmen is there a well-known garage a little beyond mr. perera's estate beyond the office in the up-country near the apothecary's house beyond colombo ටකක අසනපය. the driver of this bus the watchman's father this gentleman that gentleman (in question) this patient [page 202] [page 203] [page 204]

'People like that shop. [page 209] 2. NEW VERBS වහිනවා 'rain' 3. PAST TENSE 3.1 Forms In the past tense there is a simple past and an emphatic past which act as past equivalents of the simple and emphatic pres-ents which have already been learned. The simple form of both the present and the past tense ends in a oraa and the emphatic form of both the present and the past tense ends in e or-ee.
